method: Multi-agent sourced survey run in this session: one agent derived the onboard workload from the repository (PR #662 autonomy stack, BEHAVIOR_SPEC, SIM_TO_REAL_PLAN, the study's power and hardware code); five agents surveyed platform categories with sources; five independent agents fact-checked each category (corrections, confirmations, unverifiable claims, missed options); one agent synthesized architectures; two critics checked numbers and workload fit; a final agent revised. Numbers carry their basis (vendor, third-party measured, estimate) and source URLs.

workload.task: Camera capture, stereo depth and RGB-depth registration (OAK-D Lite at 60-75 cm, OAK-D Pro W at 100-120 cm, now mounted in the head)
workload.rate_hz: 10 Hz consumed by the follower today (capture_hz 10); 15-30 Hz available and useful for obstacle depth
workload.latency_budget_ms: <= 60 ms acquisition age assumed; <= 60 ms skew allowed between RGB, depth, 2 ToF and IMU; whole chain <= 200 ms from the oldest measurement to a motion request
workload.current_implementation: The camera's RVC2 VPU computes depth. The host receives rectified RGB plus registered 16UC1 depth at 640x400 as ROS 2 sensor_msgs/Image. Python converts them (image_array copies to float32 and masks invalid pixels) and message_filters.ApproximateTimeSynchronizer pairs five topics. The code assumes a torso-fixed, centred, rectified pinhole camera (46.5 deg VFOV crop).
workload.recommended_implementation: Keep rectification, undistortion (needed for the Pro W's ~150 deg DFOV lens), RGB-depth alignment and the Pro W IR dot projector on the camera. Use the camera's host-synchronised timestamps. Ingest with depthai-ros / C++ composable nodes instead of Python conversion. Use 320x200 depth for obstacles and 416-640 px RGB for people. Have the camera MJPEG-encode the operator stream.
workload.compute_need: Depth costs the host nothing (RVC2: 4 TOPS total, 1.4 TOPS AI). Camera power: 2.5-3 W base, up to +0.5 W stereo, +0.5 W encoder, +1 W NN; OAK-D Lite max ~5 W, Pro W up to 15 W with IR. Host needs USB 3: ~1.3 MB per 640x400 RGB+depth frame, i.e. ~13 MB/s at 10 Hz or ~38 MB/s at 30 Hz uncompressed. Python conversion and sync take ~1-3 ms per frame on one core.

workload.task: Sensor time synchronisation and per-frame camera pose (new because the camera moved from the torso to the head)
workload.rate_hz: Every camera frame (10-30 Hz); the MCU samples neck encoder and IMU at >= 100-200 Hz for interpolation
workload.latency_budget_ms: Neck angle and torso attitude must be aligned to frame exposure within ~10-20 ms. Expression motion of +/-9.7 deg at 0.55 Hz reaches ~0.6 rad/s, i.e. ~1 deg per 30 ms, which is ~3.5 cm height error at 2 m against the 0.085 m floor-residual threshold.
workload.current_implementation: Not handled. PR #662 rejects packets with > 60 ms skew and requires hardware timestamps aligned to ROS wall time, but it treats the camera as fixed to the torso. The current form-study design puts the camera in the skull roof at +5 deg, so the extrinsics change with the neck joint.
workload.recommended_implementation: The MCU timestamps encoder and IMU samples on a clock synced to Linux (PTP-style ping over the host link). Linux then composes camera pose = torso attitude (IMU) x neck forward kinematics at the frame timestamp, before back-projection. Verify against surveyed targets, as bench check 1 in ROS2.md asks.
workload.compute_need: Negligible (a few 4x4 transforms per frame). The requirement is timestamped, synchronised I/O, not throughput.

workload.rate_hz: 10 Hz today (one detector call per synchronised frame); target >= 10 Hz
workload.latency_budget_ms: Detection + tracking + planning must fit in <= ~140 ms (the 200 ms deadline minus <= 60 ms acquisition) and average < 100 ms to hold 10 Hz with the single latest-frame worker
workload.current_implementation: The hardware ROS node accepts only --detector opencv_hog: OpenCV's CPU HOG + linear-SVM pedestrian detector (64x128 window, scale 1.05, winStride 8) on the full 640x400 RGB, with range from the median depth in the box. The simulator path uses a logistic classifier on metric depth silhouettes (17 depth slabs x morphological close + connected components), trained on synthetic masks and validated only against simulated people. No code uses the Jetson GPU or the OAK VPU for inference.
workload.recommended_implementation: Use a small DNN person detector (YOLO-nano or SSD-MobileNet class, INT8) at 320-416 px input, validated on truncated bodies. With the PR geometry (0.366 m lens, +12 deg, 46.5 deg VFOV), a 1.75 m person is fully in view only beyond ~1.96 m, but the spec follows at 1.5-2.5 m and never closer than 1.0 m. HOG's full-body template fails in exactly that near band. Run it on an accelerator: first choice is the OAK's own RVC2 (spatial detection gives box + 3D position from aligned depth), otherwise a host NPU/GPU. Keep the depth-silhouette check as a secondary cue.
workload.compute_need: Measured on this host (4-vCPU Xeon 2.1 GHz, OpenCV 4.14, synthetic 640x400, single thread): HOG 64-81 ms p50 (94 ms p95), ~40 ms on 4 threads; depth-silhouette detector 11-20 ms; at 320x200, 9 ms and 3.7 ms. HOG cannot simply be downscaled: its window needs a person >= 128 px tall, which holds within ~6.4 m at 640x400 but only ~3.2 m at 320x200, and the follower searches to 5.5 m. Estimated 2-3x slower per core on Cortex-A76/A78AE (Pi 5 / Orin Nano CPU), so HOG alone takes ~130-280 ms single-thread. DNN replacement: YOLO-nano class is 6.5-8.7 GFLOPs at 640 px and ~1.6-3.7 GFLOPs at 320-416 px (published figures), i.e. 16-55 GFLOP/s at 10-15 Hz. That is a small load for a >= 1 TOPS INT8 NPU (OAK RVC2 1.4 TOPS AI) but most of a Pi 5 CPU.

workload.task: Appearance / re-identification (no silent target switching; reacquisition after occlusion)
workload.rate_hz: Per detection per frame (10 Hz); reacquisition across occlusions of up to 2 s
workload.latency_budget_ms: On ambiguity, stop and report re-select within 500 ms; decide reacquisition within 1-3 frames of reappearance
workload.current_implementation: A 200-bin exposure-normalised chroma histogram in two height bands per detection, compared by histogram intersection. Association needs colour distance < 0.46. An ambiguity latch fires when a competing match is within 0.20 cost or an overlapping track has a similar colour (state ambiguous_reselect, robot stops). The selected person's signature is frozen at selection. Tracks are dropped after 0.9 s, and the selection is cleared after 0.75 s of absence (lost_reselect), so the spec's reacquisition after <= 2 s occlusion cannot be met.
workload.recommended_implementation: Run a deep re-ID embedding (OSNet x0.25-x1.0 or MobileNet class, 128-512-d) on each person crop. Keep a gallery of the selected person's embeddings, collected only while unambiguous. Gate matches by cosine distance combined with motion and depth. Keep the stop-on-ambiguity margin test. Keep the selected identity alive (robot stopped, 'occluded') for >= 2-3 s before 'lost_reselect'. Never auto-select a new person.
workload.compute_need: Current: < 1 ms per detection on CPU. Robust: 0.08-0.98 GMAC per 256x128 crop (OSNet x0.25 to x1.0, published). For <= 5 people at 5-10 Hz with the light variants that is ~0.4-14 GMAC/s, which fits on the same NPU as the detector (RVC2 for x0.25-x0.5; Hailo or Jetson GPU for x1.0 at full rate). Gallery matching < 0.1 ms on CPU.

workload.task: Tracking, target selection and follow state machine
workload.rate_hz: 10 Hz per frame; operator select/start/stop events; Linux watchdog tick at 40 Hz (25 ms)
workload.latency_budget_ms: Selection needs a track seen <= 300 ms ago with >= 2 frames; reacquisition needs 3 consecutive frames; on target loss, stop within 1.0 s
workload.current_implementation: OnboardFollower (Python, one RLock): greedy association in metric (left, forward) with a gate of 0.24 m + 1.45 m/s x dt plus the colour gate. Holds track IDs, selection, arming, operator heartbeat ownership, and the states occluded / confirming / lost / ambiguous.
workload.recommended_implementation: Constant-velocity Kalman tracks in the gravity-aligned ground frame, with ego-motion compensation from MCU odometry (IMU yaw rate + leg odometry). Hungarian or ByteTrack-style association with re-ID cost. Keep the explicit operator selection/start gates and no automatic reselection. Implement in C++ or vectorised Python.
workload.compute_need: < 1-2 ms per frame on one Linux core for <= 10 tracks; no accelerator. Association cost is negligible next to detection.

workload.task: Obstacle detection from stereo depth + 2 x ToF (+ 2D lidar at 100-120 cm)
workload.rate_hz: Depth at the camera rate (10 Hz now, 15 Hz preferred); each VL53L5CX 8x8 at up to ~15 Hz (ST figure, unverified in the repo survey); STL-19P lidar 10 Hz (6-13 Hz), ~500 points per scan
workload.latency_budget_ms: Depth path <= 200 ms to a motion request. The ToF near-range / floor-drop stop should act within one ToF frame (~67 ms) and must not depend on Linux. At the 0.30 m/s nominal speed (120 cm), 200 ms is 6 cm of travel.
workload.current_implementation: Every frame back-projects the full 640x400 depth using IMU roll/pitch, twice (once for detection, once inside steer for the expected-floor mask). Checks: >= 70 % valid depth in each of 3 sectors; points 0.045-0.71 m high within 2 m, compressed to a 25 mm grid; two scalar ToF ranges against a level-floor model (range outside 0.32-2.0 m or residual > 0.085 m triggers near_range_stop). The hull and height band are 60 cm-specific constants. No code reads the lidar. The current design uses 8x8-zone VL53L5CX sensors, not two scalar ranges.
workload.recommended_implementation: Build a 2.5D local height/occupancy grid (~5 cm cells, ~4 x 4 m, 1-2 s decay, ego-motion compensated) that fuses downsampled depth (320x200), both 8x8 ToF zone arrays and, at 100-120 cm, the 360 deg lidar scan. The lidar covers flanks and tail sweep during pivot turns, which the camera and ToF cones cannot see. Parameterise the hull per size. Duplicate the ToF near-range / floor-drop stop on the MCU.
workload.compute_need: Measured (Xeon, single thread): back-projection 3.7-4.6 ms at 640x400, 0.8 ms at 320x200. ToF (2 x 64 zones x 15 Hz, ~2k ranges/s) and lidar (~5k points/s) are negligible. A robust grid at 320x200 is estimated at ~5-15 ms per update on one A76-class core in C++ or vectorised code. The MCU ToF guard takes < 0.1 ms per frame.

workload.rate_hz: Planner at the camera rate (10 Hz); a 25 ms (40 Hz) timer republishes the request
workload.latency_budget_ms: Oldest measurement to request <= 200 ms; the receiver expires requests after <= 200 ms; operator stop honoured within 300 ms
workload.current_implementation: steer() checks 9 constant-curvature arcs (+/-31 deg, 0.27 m arc, 0.65-1.30 m horizon, 5 cm steps) against a padded 60 cm hull (-0.62..0.49 x +/-0.29 m) and scores them against the target bearing. Speed is 0.08-0.12 m/s with a 0.45 m/s^2 ramp, and it stops at 1.95 m (at_distance). Output is a geometry_msgs/TwistStamped (forward, yaw) on follow/cmd_vel to a separate locomotion bridge that does not exist yet.
workload.recommended_implementation: Run the same arc/DWA search over the local grid in C++ (or a Nav2-style controller), with turn-in-place checks for the tail sweep. Use per-size speeds (0.21-0.30 m/s nominal, >= 0.35 rad/s walking turn, >= 0.5 rad/s in place) and a 1.5-2.5 m follow distance, never < 1.0 m. Requests are clipped to the policy's trained command range (0-0.20 m/s, +/-0.5 rad/s for the 60 cm policy), rate-limited and expired on the MCU.
workload.compute_need: Measured steer(): 4.9 ms (clear) to 21 ms (cluttered, ~23k close points) per call on one Xeon core. Estimated ~10-60 ms on an A76-class core in Python, ~1-5 ms in C++.

workload.task: Operator web view (image encoding + detections) and control actions
workload.rate_hz: The page polls /view every 190 ms (~5 Hz) and posts a heartbeat after each poll; the server JPEG-encodes every processed frame (10 Hz)
workload.latency_budget_ms: Operator lease 0.80 s; heartbeat loss leads to a controlled stop within 1.0 s; stop honoured within 300 ms
workload.current_implementation: Python ThreadingHTTPServer bound to loopback, reached through SSH port forwarding. Serves a base64 JPEG plus track boxes as JSON. Actions are select/start/stop/heartbeat with session ownership. JPEG encoding runs inside the detection worker.
workload.recommended_implementation: Use on-camera MJPEG (OAK encoder) or a hardware encoder, pushed over WebSocket/WebRTC, with detections as a JSON overlay. Decouple encoding from the detection worker. Serve authenticated TLS on the robot (or use a VPN) instead of SSH. Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Orin Nano both lack a hardware H.264 encoder (vendor specs), so on-camera encoding is the cheap path.
workload.compute_need: Measured: 640x400 JPEG + base64 takes 0.8-1.0 ms on the Xeon (est. ~2-3 ms on A76) and is ~92 KB per frame, ~0.45 MB/s (3.7 Mbit/s) at 5 Hz over Wi-Fi. The HTTP server load is negligible.

workload.task: Locomotion policy inference (with normalisation, phase reference and fitted gait adapter)
workload.rate_hz: 50 Hz today (MJCF timestep 2 ms x frame_skip 10); 100 Hz possible
workload.latency_budget_ms: The policy was trained with an 8 ms drive command delay and zero-order hold, so sample -> inference -> CAN target should stay at ~<= 8 ms with low jitter (SIM_TO_REAL_PLAN asks for < 10 ms loop latency)
workload.current_implementation: SB3 PPO actor: actor.predict(stats.normalize_obs(obs), deterministic=True) in Python/PyTorch with a VecNormalize pickle and SHA-256 bundle checks. A 6-coefficient fitted gait adapter and a phase-based reference (1.40 Hz oscillator) wrap it. The 57-value input is 14 joint angles, 14 rates, gravity, gyro, 2 foot loads, phase sin/cos, 2 expression, 14 previous actions and 3 command values. There are 14 outputs (12 legs + neck + tail). No ONNX export exists and no policy bundle is committed.
workload.recommended_implementation: Export the deterministic actor to ONNX plus the normalisation mean/var/clip as plain arrays. Run it on the MCU as a fixed-size float32 MLP, in the same 50 Hz loop that samples encoders/IMU/foot loads and sends CAN targets, with the bundle SHA-256 pinned in firmware. Fallback: ONNX Runtime C++ on an RT-isolated Linux core, with an MCU-side timeout.
workload.compute_need: Actor 57->64->64->14 with tanh: 8,782 parameters (35 KB float32), 8,640 MACs per step. Measured 4.8 us in NumPy on the Xeon. Estimated 20-50 us on a 600 MHz Cortex-M7 (Teensy 4.1), < 0.3 % CPU at 50 Hz. Even the ~200k-parameter [512,256] MLP used for the large species (~164k MACs) would take ~0.3-0.6 ms on the M7.

workload.task: State estimation: IMU attitude, gyro, foot loads, odometry
workload.rate_hz: IMU sampled at >= 200-1000 Hz; gravity estimate at the policy rate (50 Hz in sim); BEHAVIOR_SPEC measures the trunk at 100 Hz; attitude to Linux at the camera rate
workload.latency_budget_ms: Fresh within one policy period (20 ms); attitude stamped within 60 ms of each camera frame
workload.current_implementation: Sim only: gyro-propagated gravity with an accelerometer correction gated on |a| (update_gravity) at 50 Hz, plus noisy encoders, gyro and foot loads. The ROS node expects sensor_msgs/Imu with orientation covariance and uses roll/pitch for back-projection. There is no base-velocity estimator; the deployable actor uses only encoders, IMU gravity/gyro, foot loads, command and previous action.

Publish timestamped attitude, odometry and neck angle to Linux for camera pose and tracking ego-motion.
workload.compute_need: The complementary filter is < 100 FLOP per update. A 15-18 state contact-aided EKF at 200-500 Hz is estimated at <= 5-10 % of a 600 MHz M7. No Linux compute.

workload.rate_hz: Targets at the policy rate (50 Hz, zero-order hold as trained); telemetry (position, velocity, torque/current, temperature) at 100-250 Hz per drive

workload.task: Watchdogs, command arbitration and the stop chain
workload.rate_hz: Linux follower watchdog every 25 ms; MCU checks every control cycle (>= 50 Hz, ideally 200-1000 Hz)
workload.latency_budget_ms: Operator heartbeat 0.80 s; sensor stale 0.35 s; request age 200 ms; skew 60 ms; operator stop <= 0.3 s; heartbeat loss leads to a controlled stop <= 1.0 s, then stand
workload.current_implementation: All watchdogs live in the Linux Python process. OnboardFollower.watchdog checks heartbeat, monotonic time and stale sensors. SensorService.tick zeroes output on inference overrun, stops on stale or rejected packets, and requires a fresh selection. A clean shutdown publishes zero; a crash publishes nothing. ROS2.md lists the receiving bridge's expiry/arbitration, an independent embedded watchdog and a hardware traction disconnect as physical commissioning tasks.
workload.recommended_implementation: Keep the Linux checks. Add on the MCU: velocity-request expiry (<= 200 ms) and arbitration, a Linux-alive heartbeat, the MCU's own hardware watchdog, drive communication/limit faults, bus voltage/current and cell alarms, the ToF near-range stop, e-stop sense and traction-contactor drive. A Linux crash must end in a controlled stop-and-stand run by the MCU.
workload.compute_need: Negligible on either side. What matters is placement (on the MCU, independent of Linux) and a hardwired stop path.

requirements.minimum_spec:
The minimum spec meets BEHAVIOR_SPEC section 3 with the robust implementation, at all four sizes.

(a) Real-time MCU. Keep the Teensy 4.1 already in the control allowance. Requirements: Cortex-M7 class >= 400-600 MHz with a single-precision FPU; >= 512 KB RAM (the actor is 35 KB); >= 2 CAN controllers (Teensy has 3, one FD); 2 x I2C, >= 3 UART, SPI, ADC; a hardware watchdog; a timestamped host link. Load: CAN to 12 drives at 200-250 Hz (~30 % of each 1 Mbit/s bus); the policy at 50 Hz, 100 Hz-capable (< 0.3 % CPU); IMU at 0.5-1 kHz; ToF guard; request expiry/arbitration; e-stop. About 0.5-1 W inside the existing 4 W line.

(b) Neural accelerator, >= ~1 TOPS INT8. Load: a YOLO-nano-class person detector at 320-416 px and >= 10 Hz (~16-55 GFLOP/s), plus a light re-ID net (OSNet x0.25-x0.5 class) on <= 5 crops at 5-10 Hz (~0.4-14 GMAC/s). The OAK cameras' own RVC2 (1.4 TOPS AI), already carried for depth at every size, is the first candidate: no extra board, about +1 W. Acceptance test: the detector holds >= 10 Hz with stereo, alignment and MJPEG running. If it does not, add a host NPU (>= 13 TOPS, Hailo-8L class) or use a Jetson.

(c) Linux host. Requirements: 4 x Cortex-A76-class cores >= 2 GHz, 8 GB RAM (4 GB workable), NVMe/SSD, 1 x USB 3 for the camera, USB or UART to the MCU, Wi-Fi, and Ubuntu + ROS 2 support. Expected load with C++/vectorised perception is ~1-1.5 cores, leaving ~50 % headroom: obstacle grid + planner 5-15 ms per update at 10-15 Hz, tracking < 2 ms, ROS transport, streaming, logging. A Raspberry Pi 5 (8 GB) meets this. The Jetson Orin Nano Super does too, but its GPU sits unused unless detection runs on it.

Not sufficient on any of these ARM CPUs: the as-written PR #662 Python/HOG path. It takes ~80-105 ms per frame on one 2.1 GHz Xeon core (measured); an estimated 2-3x slower A76/A78AE core gives ~140-320 ms, against a 100 ms frame period and a 200 ms deadline. Detection must therefore move to an accelerator whichever host is chosen.

Power, mass and cost, first order, by the method of designlab/compute_options.py:
- Power: host ~4-7 W plus MCU ~1 W, against the 31 W Jetson budget at the rails. Through the 0.88 converter this removes ~27 W from the bus.
- Runtime: 60 cm 96 -> ~69 W (34 -> ~48 min); 75 cm 113 -> ~85 W (29 -> ~39 min); 100-120 cm ~13-18 % less power.
- Mass and cooling: ~0.1-0.15 kg against 0.294 kg; ~0.6 L/s airflow against ~2.6 L/s for 31 W at a 10 K rise.
- Cost: a Pi 5 8 GB + cooler is booked at $185.95 (tariff-elevated, HARDWARE_BOM.md:60,219). The Jetson is $249 list ($399 street in parts.json) + $120 integration.
requirements.growth_spec:
The growth spec covers voice commands, stronger detectors and pose, deep re-ID, mapping, and possibly vision-conditioned locomotion. It matters most at 100-120 cm, where cost is reported as a note and is not a gate (DECISION_LOG.md:23, P8).

(a) Accelerator, >= 20-70 TOPS INT8 (GPU or NPU). Loads:
- YOLO-s/m or a pose model at 640 px and 15-30 Hz (~0.3-1 TFLOP/s; YOLOv8s is 28.6 GFLOPs at 640);
- OSNet x1.0 re-ID (~1 GMAC per crop) for up to 10 people at 10 Hz (~0.1 TMAC/s);
- optional segmentation for drop-offs and glass.

(b) CPU of 6-8 A78AE-class cores or better, 8-16 GB RAM, >= 256 GB NVMe. Loads:
- 2D lidar SLAM (slam_toolbox class, ~0.5-1 core at 10 Hz scans) and/or visual-inertial odometry (1-2 cores or GPU);
- Nav2-style global + local planning;
- on-device ASR: wake word + Whisper tiny/base class (39-74 M parameters), ~1 core for ~1 s per command on CPU or a small GPU share, with a beamforming mic array.

(c) MCU unchanged. The policy stays an MLP; even a 200k-parameter [512,256] actor is ~0.3-0.6 ms on the M7. A vision-conditioned policy encoder would run on the Linux accelerator and pass a latent to the MCU at 10-50 Hz.

Power: 15-40 W module plus ~6 W carrier/cooling. At 100-120 cm (150-200 W walking) this is ~10-25 % of walking power. At 60-75 cm the same set costs 30-40 % of power and runtime, so the growth tier is best kept to the larger sizes.

Examples, with cost noted:
- Jetson Orin Nano Super 8 GB (current choice): 67 TOPS, $249 list / $399 street + $120 integration, 25 W + 6 W budget. Covers moderate growth.
- Jetson Orin NX 16 GB: 78 TOPS dense / 157 sparse in Super mode, 10-40 W, $1,099 module + $111-410 carrier. Covers full growth at 100-120 cm.
- Raspberry Pi 5 + Hailo-8 (26 TOPS) class: the low-power middle option, without CUDA (models are compiled on an x86 host).
interfaces: Camera -> Linux: USB 3 through the neck with a service loop (build.py:509-511). 640x400 RGB + 16-bit depth is ~1.3 MB per frame: ~13 MB/s at 10 Hz, ~38 MB/s at 30 Hz raw, less with on-camera MJPEG. The OAK-D Pro W can draw up to 15 W with IR (parts_2026-11-07.json parts[9]), so power it from its own 5 V rail rather than an SBC USB port (a Raspberry Pi 5 supplies only about 1.6 A in total to its USB ports, vendor spec).

Linux <-> MCU: one deterministic, timestamped link: Teensy 4.1 USB 2.0 HS device (480 Mbit/s), UART at >= 2 Mbit/s, or 100 Mbit Ethernet. Up, at 50-100 Hz: 14 joint positions/velocities/torques, IMU attitude and rates, foot loads, 2 x 64 ToF zones and faults (~1-2 KB per message). Down, at 10-40 Hz: velocity/expression requests and a heartbeat. Includes a clock-sync exchange so neck-angle and IMU samples can be interpolated at camera timestamps.

MCU -> leg drives: 2 x classic CAN at 1 Mbit/s, 6 drives per bus, isolated transceivers. Teensy 4.1 has 3 FlexCAN controllers, one CAN FD (RAPTOR_SCALING_AND_ALTERNATIVES.md:492). Bus load is ~30 % at 200 Hz request/response. At 120 cm the RobStride neck joins a CAN bus (hardware.py:86).

MCU -> expression servos at 60-100 cm: Dynamixel TTL half-duplex (Protocol 2.0) through the TTL bridge on the 12 V appendage rail (assumptions.json:30; platform/engineering/README.md:85; hardware.py:77-85).

ToF -> MCU: 2 x VL53L5CX on I2C (separate buses, or LPn-sequenced address assignment). Each sensor needs ~90 KB of driver firmware loaded at boot. 8x8 zones at up to ~15 Hz (unverified ST figure) (parts[21]; hardware.py:78).
IMU -> MCU over SPI/I2C: BNO085 fusion, or a raw 6-axis IMU at >= 500 Hz. The OAK's own IMU (BMI270 on the Lite, BNO086 on the Pro W) can also stamp camera motion (parts[8],[9]).

2D lidar STL-19P (100-120 cm): UART at 230400 baud, ~5000 points/s, 6-13 Hz scan with PWM speed control (parts[15]). Connect to Linux via USB-UART, or to an MCU UART if a 360 deg proximity stop is wanted.
Foot load cells + amplifiers -> MCU ADC/SPI at >= 100-500 Hz (build.py:386; assumptions.json:31).

Power and safety I/O on the MCU: bus voltage/current sense, cell-monitor alarm, pack temperature, e-stop sense input and traction contactor/disconnect output, all hardwired so the stop works without Linux (platform/engineering/README.md:73,85; ROS2.md:31).

Compute power rail from the 6S (20-25.2 V) or 12S (40-50.4 V) bus: the Jetson carrier needs 9-20 V (today a 12 V D36V50F12 at 4.5 A; platform/engineering/README.md:58,85). A Raspberry Pi 5 needs 5 V at 5 A (a >= 25 W 5 V buck). At 12S the 48 V power bay carries a 48 -> 12 V converter (build.py:446-449).
Wi-Fi to the operator page: ~92 KB per 640x400 JPEG at 5 Hz is ~3.7 Mbit/s. Optional wireless e-stop handset (parts_2026-11-07.json parts[42]).
Storage: NVMe/SSD for ROS bags (raw RGB-D ~13 MB/s at 10 Hz, ~47 GB/h).
Audio (growth): a USB mic array with on-chip AEC/beamforming (XVF3800 class, USB/I2S, 16 kHz; parts[50]).
software_constraints: ROS 2 (rclpy, message_filters, sensor_msgs, geometry_msgs) on Ubuntu with Python 3 and NumPy (ROS2.md:7-18; ros2_node.py:192-199). Any host needs a supported arm64 Ubuntu/ROS 2 pairing, e.g. Ubuntu 24.04 + Jazzy on a Pi 5, or JetPack 6 (Ubuntu 22.04) + Humble on a Jetson.

The only hardware detector option is OpenCV 4.x HOG from objdetect (ros2_node.py:202,216-217; ROS2.md:7,12); OpenCV 5 builds lack the HOG entry point (ROS2.md:41). Downscaling does not make HOG cheaper: its 64x128 window needs a person >= 128 px tall, which holds within ~6.4 m at 640x400 but only ~3.2 m at 320x200, while the follower searches to 5.5 m (perception.py:134).

Perception runs in one Python worker thread and drops all but the latest frame (ros2_node.py:128,137-149). The rclpy executor (25 ms watchdog timer), the HTTP threads and the worker share one GIL. Throughput is therefore bounded by single-core speed, and timer jitter grows under load. More cores do not help until the code is parallelised or moved to C++ or an accelerator. This is a further reason to enforce request expiry on the MCU.

Measured on this development host (4-vCPU Xeon 2.1 GHz, OpenCV 4.14, NumPy 2.5, single thread, synthetic 640x400 frames, the PR's own code): HOG 64-81 ms p50 (94 ms p95; ~40 ms on 4 threads); depth-silhouette detector 11-20 ms; back-projection 3.7-4.6 ms; steer() 4.9-21 ms; full update() 16-24 ms (silhouette) or 73-84 ms (HOG); JPEG+base64 0.8-1.0 ms (~92 KB). At 320x200 everything is ~4x cheaper. Policy MLP: 4.8 us in NumPy. Cortex-A76 (Pi 5) and A78AE (Orin Nano) cores are estimated 2-3x slower per core; benchmark on target. Script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-mesozoic-labs/c17e65d8-8171-548a-aef1-2a557e9379dd/scratchpad/benchscript/run_bench.py.
Hardware timestamps aligned to ROS wall time are mandatory; use_sim_time is refused (ros2_node.py:225-226).

Geometry assumptions to remove before hardware: (1) a torso-fixed, centred, rectified pinhole camera (perception.py:3-5,19-31; ros2_node.py:60-73), whereas the current design has a head camera (build.py:495-508) and, on the Pro W, a ~150 deg equidistant lens (sensors.py:20,30-31); (2) two scalar ToF ranges (ros2_node.py:88-93), whereas the design uses 8x8-zone VL53L5CX sensors (hardware.py:78); (3) the 60 cm-specific hull, height band and speeds in steer() (controller.py:56-61,71,91).

Policy deployment today: SB3/PyTorch with a VecNormalize pickle and digest checks (inference.py:29-80). There is no ONNX/TensorRT/TFLite path, and C code cannot read the pickled statistics (SIM_TO_REAL_PLAN.md:220-227). To deploy: export the deterministic actor to ONNX and the mean/var/clip as arrays (SIM_TO_REAL_PLAN.md:326-327); keep the bundle's SHA-256 identity in the exported artefact; reproduce reference_angles, the phase oscillator and the gait adapter exactly (robot_walking.py:36-61; robot_gait_adapter.py:14-40). No policy bundle is committed yet (REPRODUCTION.md:14).

Accelerator toolchains are not interchangeable. OAK RVC2 runs OpenVINO-IR models compiled to .blob through DepthAI. Hailo needs HEF files compiled on an x86 host. Jetson needs TensorRT engines built for the installed JetPack. A bare Pi CPU uses ONNX Runtime, NCNN or TFLite. Keep ONNX as the interchange format and pick detector/re-ID models that compile for the chosen target.
Video encoding: Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Orin Nano have no hardware H.264 encoder (vendor specs; CPU encoding only). On-camera MJPEG/H.264 from the OAK is the cheap path for the operator stream.
The operator page binds to loopback and relies on SSH port forwarding (web.py:1,46-48; ROS2.md:33). A field-usable external page needs on-robot authentication and TLS, or a VPN.

MCU firmware is C/C++ and needs: FlexCAN drivers and the RMD/RobStride CAN protocols; Dynamixel Protocol 2.0; the ST VL53L5CX ULD driver (> 90 KB program memory, parts[21]); an IMU driver; a fixed-step scheduler without dynamic allocation; and the exported MLP as static float32 arrays (35 KB).

Linux real-time patches are not needed if the MCU owns the control loop. If the policy ever moves to Linux, use PREEMPT_RT, an isolated core and C++ inference, with an MCU-side timeout and fallback stance.

options.configuration: NVIDIA developer kit as sold: Orin Nano 8GB module, NVIDIA reference carrier, stock heatsink with fan, the included M.2 Wi-Fi card and a 19 V adapter. Storage is microSD or a user-added M.2 NVMe; neither is counted. Mass is 174 g as sold, per an NVIDIA forum moderator (not independently weighed); the study's tray brings it to 0.29 kg. Counted price and mass leave out the tray, NVMe, cabling and the 6S/12S DC-DC converter. The converter stays because the carrier accepts 9-20 V. For this robot, plan on the 15 W or 25 W mode (both capped); MAXN SUPER is uncapped.
options.cpu: 6-core Arm Cortex-A78AE v8.2 (1.5 MB L2 + 4 MB L3). Max 1.73 GHz in MAXN SUPER, 1.50 GHz in 15 W mode, 1.34 GHz in 25 W mode (vendor nvpmodel table)
options.ai_accelerator: 1024-core Ampere GPU with 32 Tensor cores. GPU max 612 MHz (15 W), 918 MHz (25 W), 1020 MHz (MAXN SUPER). No DLA, no hardware video encoder
options.power_basis: Measured by third parties at the module input only (tegrastats VDD_IN). This excludes the carrier, NVMe, fan and USB-powered loads such as the OAK-D. Idle: 6.1 W in MAXN SUPER (arXiv 2609.13551, Sep 2026); 6.85 W near idle in MAXN (RidgeRun); 4.7 W idle and 6.2 W with two 8 FPS 640x640 FP16 detector streams on a 7 W-mode configuration (NVIDIA forum, JetPack 6.2). Detector load: 11.7-12.3 W mean for YOLO26s TensorRT FP16 at 640x640 and 67-75 img/s, 10.3-10.6 W in INT8 (MAXN SUPER, arXiv 2609.13551); 14.1 W FP16 and 12.5 W INT8 with YOLOv8n running flat out at 225 and 286 FPS (H. Choi, Apr 2026). The whole original kit at the wall measured about 4 W idle and about 17 W peak in 15 W mode (Hackster 2023). Max 25 W is NVIDIA's stated dev-kit maximum (25 W mode); MAXN SUPER is uncapped. Kit power at the DC input is module power plus carrier, NVMe and fan overhead; that overhead is unmeasured, estimated at 2-3 W.
options.interfaces: 4x USB 3.2 Gen2 Type-A (10 Gbps; 3 A VBUS limit per dual stack) for the OAK-D, a lidar USB-UART adapter and the Teensy. 1x USB-C (host, device or recovery). 2x 22-pin MIPI CSI-2 (CAM0 x2, CAM1 x2/x4). 1x GbE. M.2 Key M 2280 PCIe Gen3 x4 and Key M 2230 x2. M.2 Key E fitted with the included Wi-Fi card. DisplayPort. 40-pin header with UART, SPI, I2C, I2S and GPIO: I2C can serve the VL53L5CX sensors and a UART the STL-19P. The module has one CAN controller, but the carrier's J17 CAN header is unpopulated and needs an external 3.3 V transceiver. That is not needed here, because the Teensy owns both leg CAN buses. DC jack accepts 9-20 V.
options.video_encode: No hardware encoder: NVIDIA lists 1080p30 encode on 1-2 CPU cores. Hardware decode is 1x 4K60 H.265. For the operator page, use the OAK-D's onboard H.264/H.265/MJPEG encoder (4K30 / 1080p60) or a low-resolution CPU stream.
options.software: JetPack 6.2.x (Jetson Linux 36.4/36.5, Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.6, TensorRT 10.3) with ROS 2 Humble and Isaac ROS 3.2. Isaac ROS 3.2 Update 1 added JetPack 6.2 and Orin Nano Super support. Alternatively JetPack 7.2 (2 Jun 2026: Jetson Linux 39.2, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, CUDA 13.2.1, TensorRT 10.16.2, DeepStream 8.0) with ROS 2 Jazzy and Isaac ROS 4.6 (Aug 2026); Isaac ROS 5.0 (Sep 2026) moved to ROS 2 Lyrical. JetPack 7.2 has no SD-card image for this kit, so it is flashed from a USB ISO. Power modes (Jetson Linux 36.4.4): the Super flash configuration offers 15 W, 25 W (default) and MAXN_SUPER; the non-Super configuration offers 15 W and 7 W. NVIDIA calls MAXN experimental. Model path: export ONNX, then build a TensorRT engine with Ultralytics export or trtexec (routine). The ONNX policy MLP can run on CPU through ONNX Runtime. A PREEMPT_RT kernel is packaged from JetPack 6.1, but users report boot freezes and CUDA error 801 on some 6.2.x releases; NVIDIA points to 6.2.2 or 7.2.
options.availability: In production. NVIDIA's MSRP rose from $249 to $399 in July 2026; SparkFun sells it at $399, in stock, with a high-demand warning. Developer kits carry no lifecycle date; Orin Nano production modules are listed through Jan 2032.

options.fit_notes: Carries the full 60-75 cm workload, and on the stated workload the 100-120 cm one too. A YOLO11n/26n-class person detector takes about 4.5 ms of GPU time per 640x640 frame in MAXN SUPER and about 6 ms in 15 W mode. Following at 15-30 FPS, tracking and re-ID, depth-based avoidance from the OAK-D, ToF and lidar parsing, and the 50-100 Hz ONNX MLP on CPU therefore fit with room to spare. Measured module power is about 6 W idle and 10-14 W under a saturating detector load. The 25 W + 6 W budget is a ceiling, not a typical draw: running in the 15 W mode with a measured budget could roughly halve the compute draw at the battery (estimate; confirm at the converter input). Risks: the price is now $399. The 9-20 V input keeps the DC-DC converter. There is no hardware encoder, so stream through the OAK-D encoder or CPU. The 8 GB is shared by ROS 2, TensorRT, maps and streaming. The dev-kit carrier is not intended for production. The stock fan needs a ducted intake and outlet in the shell. The 7 W mode is available only with the non-Super flash configuration.

Module prices at 1KU: Orin Nano 4GB $349, Orin Nano 8GB $399, Orin NX 8GB $649, Orin NX 16GB $999, AGX Orin 32GB $1,799, AGX Orin 64GB $2,999. The study's $249 compute line is now $150 low. https://www.cnx-software.com/2026/07/22/nvidia-increases-the-price-of-jetson-modules-and-devkits-by-up-to-101/ https://developer.nvidia.com/embedded/faq https://www.sparkfun.com/products/22098

Lifecycle: Orin Nano, Orin NX and AGX Orin modules are listed through Jan 2032 (AGX Orin Industrial Jul 2033), T5000 through Aug 2035 and T4000 through Jan 2036. Developer kits carry no lifecycle date. NVIDIA's 2026 phase-out driven by LPDDR4 supply (last-time-buy 1 Jul 2026, last ship 15 Jul 2027) covers TX2 NX, TX2i, AGX Xavier and Xavier NX; Orin is not affected. https://developer.nvidia.com/embedded/lifecycle https://www.cnx-software.com/2026/04/30/nvidia-phases-out-several-jetson-modules-due-to-high-lpddr4-ram-prices-and-tight-supplies/

Software: JetPack 6.2.x (Jetson Linux 36.4/36.5, Ubuntu 22.04) brought the Super modes and pairs with ROS 2 Humble and Isaac ROS 3.2. JetPack 7.2 (2 Jun 2026: Jetson Linux 39.2, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, CUDA 13.2.1, TensorRT 10.16.2, DeepStream 8.0) now covers both Orin and Thor. Isaac ROS 4.6 (18 Aug 2026) supports JetPack 7.2 with ROS 2 Jazzy on Orin and Thor; Isaac ROS 5.0 (21 Sep 2026) moves to ROS 2 Lyrical. JetPack 7.2 has no SD-card image for the Orin Nano dev kit, so it is flashed from a USB ISO. ONNX-to-TensorRT conversion for YOLO is routine (Ultralytics export or trtexec). https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/jetpack-7-2-jetson-software-goes-agentic-with-jetson-linux-39-2/372056 https://nvidia-isaac-ros.github.io/releases/index.html

Measured power is far below the study's budget. Third-party tegrastats measurements of the Orin Nano 8GB module (module input only): about 6 W idle; 6.2 W with two 8 FPS 640x640 FP16 detector streams; 10.3-12.3 W running YOLO26s at 67-75 img/s; 12.5-14.1 W with YOLOv8n running flat out at 225-286 FPS (MAXN SUPER). The original kit measured about 4 W idle and about 17 W peak at the wall in 15 W mode. The 25 W + 6 W budget is about 35 W at the battery through the 0.88 converter. A measured-basis planning value of about 12-15 W at the board (estimate: module 8-12 W plus 2-3 W for carrier, NVMe and fan) would be about 14-17 W at the battery, roughly 18-22 W less. That is about 19-23% of the 96 W walking total at 60 cm, if the 35 W fixed-auxiliary figure is this compute budget. Use the 15 W or 25 W mode for a hard cap; MAXN SUPER is uncapped. This needs measuring at the converter input with the real pipeline. https://arxiv.org/html/2609.13551v1 https://hokwangchoi.com/blog/vision-benchmarks/ https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/reducing-idle-power-on-orin-nano-super-dev-kit/358482 https://www.hackster.io/news/jetson-gets-a-rocket-boost-hands-on-with-the-nvidia-jetson-orin-nano-developer-kit-4ef82eac71dd

Basis note: most Jetson power figures are tegrastats VDD_IN, which is module input only. To compare with whole-board figures for SBCs, add the carrier, NVMe, fan and USB-device draw (estimate 2-3 W for a small carrier; unmeasured) plus converter loss.

Detector speed is not the constraint. On Orin Nano Super, YOLO26n with TensorRT FP16 at 640 takes 4.57 ms (Ultralytics). YOLOv8n takes 4.43 ms of GPU time in MAXN SUPER and 6.13 ms in 15 W mode (third party). A 15-30 FPS person detector therefore uses under a fifth of the GPU even in 15 W mode. NVIDIA's DeepStream page lists PeopleNet ResNet34 (960x544, INT8) with the NvDCF tracker at 217 FPS on the pre-Super Orin Nano. Orin NX 16GB is only about 10% faster on YOLO26n FP16 (4.13 ms, measured before Super mode); AGX Orin 64GB is about 1.7x faster (2.62 ms) and Thor about 3.3x (1.39 ms). The current Ultralytics page has replaced its YOLO11n tables with YOLO26n. No person re-ID network benchmark was found for any Orin. No YOLO benchmark was found for Orin Nano 4GB, Orin NX 8GB, AGX Orin 32GB or T4000. https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/nvidia-jetson/ https://archive.docs.nvidia.com/metropolis/deepstream/7.1/text/DS_Performance.html

Video encode: Orin Nano (4GB and 8GB) has no hardware encoder; NVIDIA lists 1080p30 encode on 1-2 CPU cores. Orin NX, AGX Orin and Thor have NVENC. For the operator web page, the OAK-D's own H.264/H.265/MJPEG encoder (4K30 / 1080p60) or a low-resolution CPU stream avoids the gap. https://ie.rs-online.com/web/p/processor-development-tools/2647384 https://media.distrelec.com/Web/Downloads/_t/ds/OAK-D_Lite-eng_tds.pdf

Power input: NVIDIA's dev kits take 9-20 V (Orin Nano) or 7-20 V (AGX Orin), so they need the 6S/12S DC-DC converter. Third-party carriers take the pack directly: Seeed reComputer Mini 12-54 V (both 6S and 12S), Connect Tech Super Hadron-DM 10-60 V, ARK Just A Jetson 5.5-75 V, and Auvidea JNX42 12-48 V. Seeed reComputer Robotics J401 is 19-54 V per the wiki (its product page says 12-54 V), and the Seeed Mini J501 for AGX Orin is 19-48 V. A 19 V minimum is marginal on 6S (19.8 V at 3.3 V/cell before sag). NVIDIA says Super modes above 25 W need at least 8 V VDD_IN and a carrier high-voltage rail. A 5 V-fed carrier such as ARK's therefore limits an Orin NX to 25 W-class modes (inferred). https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/orin-nano-dev-kit-input-voltage/251158 https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/power-consumption-nvidia-jetson-orin-nano-developer-kit-8gb/330902 https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/orin-nx-16gb-on-devkit-super-mode-power-loading-cant-up-to-40w/324604

CAN: Orin Nano and Orin NX modules have one CAN controller; AGX Orin and Thor have two. Orin dev kits need external 3.3 V transceivers (the Orin Nano kit's J17 header is unpopulated); the Thor dev kit has built-in transceivers. Seeed's Robotics carrier adds CAN-FD with onboard transceivers. The Teensy 4.1 owns both leg CAN buses, so Jetson-side CAN is optional, for example as a listen-only monitor; a USB or UART link to the Teensy is enough. https://docs.nvidia.com/jetson/archives/r39.2/DeveloperGuide/HR/ControllerAreaNetworkCan.html

Mass: the Orin Nano dev kit is 174 g per an NVIDIA forum moderator, so the 0.29 kg tray allowance holds. Small wide-input carriers weigh less again: Super Hadron-DM 45 g, ARK 75 g, Seeed Mini carrier 80 g, Robotics J401 carrier 200 g, each plus the module and a heatsink (Connect Tech's active heatsink is 49 g). Seeed's boxed systems are heavier: Mini 345/462 g, Robotics 1.1 kg. AGX Orin dev kit 872.5 g, Seeed Mini J5011 (AGX Orin 32GB) 1.35 kg, AGX Thor dev kit 1.856 kg.

DLA: Orin Nano has no DLA. Orin NX 8GB has one; Orin NX 16GB and AGX Orin have two. NVIDIA's DeepStream page shows PeopleNet at 153 FPS with NvDCF on each Orin NX DLA. At 100-120 cm, the DLA is the low-power way to keep a fixed person detector running while the GPU serves other models. https://archive.docs.nvidia.com/metropolis/deepstream/7.1/text/DS_Performance.html

Real-time: NVIDIA packages a PREEMPT_RT kernel from JetPack 6.1, but users report boot freezes and CUDA error 801 on some 6.2.x releases, and NVIDIA points to 6.2.2 (r36.5) or 7.2. The policy MLP is tiny, so it can run on the Jetson CPU, but its 50-100 Hz loop has to tolerate Linux jitter or move into the deterministic MCU tier. https://nvidia-isaac-ros.github.io/v/release-3.3/getting_started/compute/preempt_setup.html https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/cuda-error-801-with-rt-kernel-nvbuild-sh-r-on-jetpack-6-2-2-expected-behavior/374926

Recommendation by size (judgment from the data above). At 60-75 cm, keep an Orin Nano 8GB: either the $399 dev kit with the converter, or the module on a 6S-capable small carrier (Super Hadron-DM about $809 with module; reComputer Mini $709) to drop the DC-DC stage. Run it in the 15 W mode and set the budget from measurement. At 100-120 cm, the Orin Nano 8GB still carries the stated workload. Step to an Orin NX 16GB (same footprint and carriers; NVENC, two DLAs, 16 GB; $999 module, $1,657.99 as a Seeed Robotics system) if voice/VLM or more cameras are added. AGX Orin (15-60 W, 0.87-1.35 kg, measured idle 7-22 W, $2,749-3,499) and Thor (40-130 W, about 16 W idle, 1.86 kg, $5,499) are not justified by this workload. The Orin Nano 4GB no longer saves meaningful money ($349 vs $399 at 1KU) and halves the GPU and RAM.

Other carriers seen but not entered: Auvidea JNX42 (EUR 215 excluding VAT; 12-48 V; 1x USB 3.1; 2x 4-lane CSI; PoE GbE; CAN Rx/Tx only) and Seeed reComputer Super J3011 ($769; 12-19 V input only, so no input advantage over the NVIDIA kit). Waveshare's Orin Nano Super kit on its own carrier was not evaluated because its input range was not found. https://developer.ridgerun.com/wiki/index.php/NVIDIA_Jetson_Orin_Nano/Introduction/Carrier_Boards/JNX42 https://store.rebotnix.com/product/jnx42/ https://www.seeedstudio.com/reComputer-Super-J3011-p-6444.html
open_questions: Is the 35 W fixed-auxiliary figure the 25 W + 6 W compute budget through the 0.88 converter (35.2 W)? If so, re-budget it from a measurement.

Measure the Orin Nano Super dev kit at the converter input with the real pipeline in the 15 W, 25 W and MAXN SUPER modes. The pipeline is: OAK-D streams, the person detector at the chosen rate, tracker and re-ID, navigation, the web stream and the MLP.
Will the person detector run on the OAK-D's own Myriad X VPU, leaving the Jetson to track, re-ID and plan? That would shrink the required Jetson, or let a smaller computer do the job.
Which person re-ID network is planned, and what is its latency on Orin Nano? No re-ID benchmark was found.
Is the Orin Nano 8GB 7 W mode (non-Super flash configuration only) enough for the 60 cm robot's detector? No benchmark was found.
For 6S builds, does a carrier with a 19 V minimum (Seeed Robotics J401, Seeed Mini J501) survive pack sag near end of discharge? Seeed's J401 input range conflicts between pages (12-54 V vs 19-54 V).
Does Seeed's reComputer Mini support Super mode, and which CAN transceivers does its extension board use? Neither is stated.
Re-run the closed-shell airflow sizing (the 1,285 mm² inlet target was based on 31 W) using measured typical (12-15 W) and peak (25 W) compute power.
Wi-Fi: the NVIDIA kit includes a card, but third-party carriers need an M.2 Key E card. Can the operator-page stream hold up from inside the shell?
Is onboard VLM/LLM voice interaction actually intended? It is the only stated need that would justify an Orin NX 16GB, AGX Orin or Thor.

corrections.claimed: Users report boot freezes and CUDA error 801 on some 6.2.x releases; NVIDIA points to 6.2.2 (r36.5) or 7.2.
corrections.corrected: The cited thread reports CUDA error 801 on JetPack 6.2.2 itself. NVIDIA recommended no fixed version, so 6.2.2 is not a known-good RT target. Treat CUDA on the RT kernel as unproven on JetPack 6: keep the 50-100 Hz policy loop on the Teensy, or test RT plus CUDA yourself before relying on it.
corrections.evidence: User report, 30 Jun 2026: Orin Nano on JetPack 6.2.2 (CUDA 12.6) with a 5.15.185-rt-tegra kernel built using nvbuild.sh -r. deviceQuery fails with error 801 and nvidia-smi cannot get the GPU handle; the same binary works on the stock kernel. NVIDIA (AastaLLL, 2 Jul 2026) replied 'We don't maintain nvbuild.sh on JetPack 6' and only pointed to older r36.4 build guidance. The thread has no resolution.

corrections.claimed: 6.1 W idle in MAXN SUPER (arXiv 2609.13551), measured at the module input (tegrastats VDD_IN).
corrections.corrected: 6.10 W is a locked-clock idle: MAXN SUPER with CPU, GPU and memory clocks pinned by jetson_clocks, fan on. That is close to a worst case. The paper reports 'whole-module' tegrastats power and does not name VDD_IN. With default clock scaling the same kit idles lower: 4.7 W VDD_IN in 7 W mode on JetPack 6.2, and 2.5 W after disabling display, audio and PCIe in the device tree. Plan on roughly 2.5-6.1 W idle depending on mode and clock locking (third-party measured).
corrections.evidence: arXiv method: 20 s idle at the same power and clock settings, with jetson_clocks and active fan, giving 6.10 W. Forum user (Jan-Feb 2026, tegrastats VDD_IN; NVIDIA's DaneLLL says VDD_IN is 'very close to physically measuring the power'): 4.7 W idle and 6.2 W active, then 2.5 W idle and about 6 W active after trimming.

corrections.claimed: YOLO26s, detector only, 640x640, TensorRT FP16, MAXN SUPER: 66.8 fps, 15 ms.
corrections.corrected: These are end-to-end figures, not GPU time. The range 66.76-74.56 img/s and 13.41-14.98 ms is Ultralytics 'prediction latency', which includes pre- and post-processing. TensorRT inference alone was 6.16-6.18 ms in FP16 (about 162 FPS) and 6.07-6.25 ms in INT8. INT8 gave no end-to-end gain (74.54 vs 74.56 img/s), so pre/post-processing was the bottleneck. Other rows in this entry are GPU-only, so this row is not directly comparable. Setup: JetPack 6.2.1 (L4T 36.4.7), TensorRT 10.7.0, MAXN SUPER with jetson_clocks.
corrections.evidence: arXiv 2609.13551 (11 Sep 2026) results table across four datasets: throughput, prediction latency and inference latency for FP16 and INT8.

corrections.field: benchmarks (DeepStream PeopleNet + NvDCF 217 FPS; YOLOv8 + NvDCF 155 FPS)
corrections.claimed: Orin Nano on JetPack 6.0 GA in max power mode, before Super mode existed.
corrections.corrected: These are 15 W-mode vendor figures. The DeepStream page's 'max power mode' is 'sudo nvpmodel -m 0'. On a JetPack 6.0 (non-Super) Orin Nano 8GB, mode 0 is the 15 W mode: 4 GPU TPCs at 624.75 MHz, 6 CPU cores at 1510.4 MHz, EMC 2133 MHz. That covers 217 FPS (PeopleNet ResNet34 + NvDCF), 250 FPS without tracker, and 155/182 FPS (YOLOv8), so they apply directly to the recommended 15 W cap. This assumes the 8GB module; the page says only 'Orin Nano'.
corrections.evidence: DeepStream 7.1 performance page: 'JetPack 6.0 GA is used' and 'Max power mode is enabled: $ sudo nvpmodel -m 0'. Jetson Linux r36.4.4 nvpmodel table: Orin Nano 8GB non-Super mode 0 = 15W (default), mode 1 = 7W.

corrections.claimed: Is the Orin Nano 8GB 7 W mode enough for the 60 cm robot's detector? No benchmark was found.
corrections.corrected: Two data points exist. (1) Third party, emulated hardware: an AGX Orin dev kit flashed as an Orin Nano 8GB ran FP16 TensorRT end-to-end in 7 W mode at 45.7 FPS for YOLO26n (15.58 ms) and 30.4 FPS for YOLO26s (26.76 ms). In 15 W mode it ran 50.3 and 48.1 FPS. Power was 'silicon power' (VDD_GPU_SOC + VDD_CPU_CV, not VDD_IN) at 4.6-4.8 W. Input size was not stated. (2) Real kit, the survey's own forum source: 6.2 W VDD_IN with two 8 FPS 640x640 streams of a ~20M-parameter FP16 detector in DeepStream, in 7 W mode.
corrections.evidence: Dubinsky case study, dated 02.06.2026 (day/month order ambiguous), which notes the emulation may not model thermal throttling. The forum thread's follow-up gives the model size and DeepStream.

corrections.claimed: [103, 90.5, 34.77] (some listings give 100 x 79 x 21 mm)
corrections.corrected: NVIDIA's datasheet figure is 100 x 79 x 21 mm, with height including feet, carrier board, module and thermal solution. 103 x 90.5 x 34.77 mm comes from a reseller page (Switch Science) for the discontinued original kit. Keeping the larger envelope as a packaging allowance is defensible, but label it a reseller figure. A forum user disputed the 21 mm height, and NVIDIA's reply only pointed back to the datasheet.
corrections.evidence: Forum post quoting the datasheet: '100mm x 79mm x 21mm (Height includes feet, carrier board, module, and thermal solution)'. Hackster gives 100x79x21 mm including carrier. Switch Science marks its listing discontinued.

corrections.claimed: 809 ($410 carrier + $399 Orin Nano 8GB module at NVIDIA 1KU MSRP)
corrections.corrected: About $859.82 at single-unit US list prices: $410 NGX027 (WDL, 1-9 units, 38 in stock) plus $449.82 for the module (Seeed). Heatsink, NVMe and Wi-Fi are extra. NVIDIA's FAQ calls $399 'volume suggested pricing at 1KU+', not a single-unit price. The carrier figures (45 g, 87.6 x 58.8 mm, +10 to +60 V) are confirmed by the spec sheet.
corrections.evidence: Seeed sells the module (900-13767-0030-000) at $449.82 and says 'modules must be sold with a carrier board'. Other Seeed single-unit prices: Orin Nano 4GB $371.42, Orin NX 8GB $734.02, Orin NX 16GB $1,077.02; the 1KU prices are $349, $649 and $999.

corrections.claimed: 1079 ($680 carrier + $399 module at 1KU)
corrections.corrected: About $1,129.82 at single-unit prices ($680 carrier + $449.82 module), before heatsink, M.2 2242 SSD and Wi-Fi. ARK's $680, 421 units in stock, 5.5-75 V input, 5.2 V 8 A regulator, 75 g and 100 x 72 x 23 mm are all confirmed.
corrections.evidence: Seeed single-unit module price $449.82; NVIDIA labels $399 as 1KU+ volume pricing.

corrections.claimed: J401 carrier ($195.99) + module ($399 at 1KU) + Super-mode heatsink with fan ($28.99)
corrections.corrected: $674.80 at Seeed single-unit prices ($195.99 + $449.82 + $28.99). The same build with an Orin NX 16GB (the J4012 bare build) is $1,302.00 ($195.99 + $1,077.02 + $28.99).
corrections.evidence: Seeed accessory page lists the carrier at $195.99, heatsink $28.99 and GMSL board $52.99. Seeed bundle page lists the Orin Nano 8GB module at $449.82 and the NX 16GB at $1,077.02.

corrections.claimed: 1100 ('the system's wiki lists 1,100 g; the 200 g figure on the carrier wiki is the carrier alone')
corrections.corrected: Unverified. Seeed publishes no complete-system mass. Both wiki pages put the figure in a table titled 'Carrier Board Specifications' with the same 115 x 115 x 38 mm size; one lists 200 g and the other 1100 g. The product page and the 2026-11-03 datasheet list no weight. Spread over a 115 x 115 x 38 mm envelope (502.6 cm³), 1,100 g averages 2.19 g/cm³, about 81% of solid aluminium (my estimate). That is implausible for a fan-cooled board, so 1,100 g is probably a packaged weight. Weigh a unit. Meanwhile use 200 g carrier + module + heatsink as the low bound and 1.1 kg as the upper bound.
corrections.evidence: wiki.seeedstudio.com/recomputer_jetson_robotics_j401_getting_started: 'Carrier Board Specifications ... 200g'. wiki.seeedstudio.com/recomputer_robotics_j401_getting_started: 'Carrier Board Specifications ... 1100g'. Neither page gives a separate system mass.

corrections.claimed: Input 19-54 V per Seeed's wiki; the product page says 12-54 V. Confirm the 12 V lower limit before relying on it.
corrections.corrected: Treat 19 V as the minimum. Seeed's datasheet for the same J401 platform (J4012 with GMSL, updated 2026-11-03) also states a '19–54 V DC input'. So two Seeed documents say 19 V, and only one marketing line on the J4012 page says 12 V. On 6S that means running only above about 3.17 V/cell.
corrections.evidence: Datasheet text: 'fueled through a wide 19–54 V DC input'. It also gives up to 55 °C in MAXN, against 50 °C on the wiki.

corrections.claimed: 1100 (system listed at 1,100 g)
corrections.corrected: Unverified. This is the same 'Carrier Board Specifications' 1100 g label that another Seeed wiki page gives as 200 g, and it is physically implausible as a device mass (see the J3011 correction). Neither the datasheet nor the product page gives a weight.
corrections.evidence: See the J3011 mass correction; the J4012-GMSL datasheet text has no weight field.

corrections.claimed: The vendor power ceiling rises from 25 W to 40 W, so cap it with the 15 W or 25 W mode.
corrections.corrected: Under NVIDIA's stock modes, a 15 W or 25 W cap leaves the NX 16GB less GPU than an Orin Nano 8GB under the same cap (my inference from clocks; no benchmark). The NX Super 15 W mode runs 2 GPU TPCs at 612 MHz, and the 25 W mode runs 4 TPCs at 408 MHz. The full 4 TPCs at 1173 MHz come only in the 40 W and MAXN_SUPER modes. The Orin Nano 8GB Super runs 4 TPCs at 612 MHz in 15 W and 918 MHz in 25 W. The NX's detector speed advantage therefore needs 40 W or MAXN_SUPER, or a custom nvpmodel profile, at higher power. What a 25 W cap still offers is the DLA path: 2 DLAs at 614.4 MHz.
corrections.evidence: Jetson Linux r36.4.4 NVP model clock table for Orin NX 16GB Super: 15W = 4 CPU at 1420.8 MHz, 2 TPC at 612 MHz; 25W = 8 CPU at 1497.6 MHz, 4 TPC at 408 MHz; 40W = 4 TPC at 1173 MHz. Orin Nano 8GB Super: 15W = 4 TPC at 612 MHz; 25W = 4 TPC at 918 MHz.

corrections.corrected: Unverified. It is the same ambiguous 'Carrier Board Specifications' label as the J3011 and J4012; see the J3011 correction.
corrections.evidence: Two Seeed wiki pages for the J401 carrier list 200 g and 1100 g in identically titled tables.

corrections.claimed: About $300 over the J3011 adds NVENC and one DLA at the same 8 GB.
corrections.corrected: The premium is $301.01 against the $1,119 listing, or $342.00 against the $1,159.99 accessories-page listing. Below 40 W the NX 8GB does not out-run an Orin Nano 8GB in its 25 W mode. The NX 8GB Super 20 W mode caps the GPU at 408 MHz (4 TPCs), and 1173 MHz comes only at 40 W or MAXN_SUPER. The Orin Nano runs 918 MHz at 25 W.
corrections.evidence: Jetson Linux r36.4.4: Orin NX 8GB Super 20W = 6 CPU at 1497.6 MHz, 4 TPC at 408 MHz; 40W = 6 CPU at 1984 MHz, 4 TPC at 1173 MHz. Seeed lists the J4011 at $1,119 on its product page and $1,159.99 on the accessories page.

corrections.field: benchmarks (category finding: no re-ID benchmark on any Orin)
corrections.claimed: No person re-ID network benchmark was found for any Orin.
corrections.corrected: NVIDIA's ReIdentificationNet model card gives AGX Orin numbers. Model: ResNet50 backbone, fixed input B x 3 x 256 x 128, latest deployable_v1.2. FP16 on Jetson AGX Orin: batch 1 at 0.96 ms (1,043.62 img/s), batch 16 at 6.42 ms (2,492.26 img/s), batch 64 at 23.09 ms (2,771.60 img/s). These are vendor trtexec figures. The card lists Orin Nano and Orin NX as test hardware but gives no numbers for them, so the Orin Nano re-ID gap remains.
corrections.evidence: NGC model card performance table, Jetson AGX Orin rows only.

corrections.claimed: Hackster measured 22 W idle in MAXN, over 19 W idle in 15 W mode, and 98 W at the wall; the fit notes say the kit 'idles at a measured 7-22 W'.
corrections.corrected: '7-22 W' is not a like-for-like idle range; the figures are on different bases. Hackster says only the 98 W MAXN-load figure was measured at the wall. It does not say where the 22 W and over-19 W idle figures were measured, and the kit ran JetPack 5.0. The 7 W idle is a user's 'quick measurement' (andrei49, 15 Jun 2026) with no stated method.
corrections.evidence: Hackster review text; NVIDIA forum post by andrei49.

corrections.field: interfaces (CAN count; category finding 'AGX Orin and Thor have two')
corrections.claimed: Thor has two CAN controllers.
corrections.corrected: NVIDIA's own sources disagree. The Jetson Thor product page lists '4x CAN' for the T5000 module. The Jetson Linux CAN page lists 2 controllers for Thor, and the dev kit exposes 2x 13-pin headers with built-in transceivers. Module capability and software-supported count differ. This does not matter here because the Teensy owns CAN.
corrections.evidence: NVIDIA Thor spec table (T5000: '4x CAN'; dev kit: '2x 13-pin CAN header'); Jetson Linux r39.2 and r39.2.1 CAN pages ('Number of controllers': Thor 2).

corrections.claimed: NVIDIA's 2026 phase-out driven by LPDDR4 supply (last-time-buy 1 Jul 2026, last ship 15 Jul 2027) covers TX2 NX, TX2i, AGX Xavier and Xavier NX.
corrections.corrected: The 1 Jul 2026 last-time-buy and 15 Jul 2027 last-ship dates are Connect Tech's dates for its own products, not an NVIDIA EOL notice. NVIDIA's lifecycle page lists TX2 NX, Xavier NX 8/16GB, AGX Xavier 32GB, AGX Xavier Industrial and TX2i as available through July 2027. It also lists the original Jetson Nano through January 2027. None of these is a candidate here.
corrections.evidence: CNX quotes 'CTI last time buy of TX2 NX, TX2i, AGX Xavier, and Xavier NX modules'. NVIDIA's lifecycle table gives the dates above.

missing_options: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 2 module and developer kit, the most relevant future option for the 60-75 cm builds and a reason to keep the carrier choice SODIMM-compatible. Announced 25 Aug 2026. NVIDIA (vendor) gives 78 TOPS, an 8-core Arm CPU and 8 GB, with about 2x the inference performance of Orin Nano Super. It also claims the same performance at 40% less power in the 15 W mode. Electronic Design adds: Ampere GPU, 8x Cortex-A78, LPDDR5X up to 120 GB/s, configurable 15-40 W, same form factor as Orin Nano Super. Module and dev kit due H1 2027; price not announced. https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2026/NVIDIA-Announces-Jetson-Orin-Nano-2-Robotics-Computer-to-Redefine-Entry-Level-Edge-AI/default.aspx ; https://www.electronicdesign.com/technologies/embedded/product/55401539/electronic-design-nvidias-new-nano-jetson-brings-llms-to-robotics

NVIDIA Jetson T2000 and T3000 (mid-range Thor class), announced 15 Jul 2026 for Q1 2027; prices not announced. T2000: 16 GB, 400 FP4 TFLOPS (sparse), 6x Neoverse-V3AE, 1024 CUDA cores, 10GbE, power not announced. T3000: 32 GB LPDDR5X, 865 FP4 TFLOPS, 8x V3AE, 1536 CUDA cores, about 65 W, emulated on the AGX Thor dev kit from JetPack 7.2.1. The T2000 is the first Thor-class part that might fit a 100-120 cm budget if onboard VLM or voice is wanted. https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/jetson-thor-robotics-edge-ai-agent/ ; https://www.servethehome.com/nvidia-announces-expanded-jetson-thor-lineup-with-mid-range-t3000-and-t2000-modules/

Orin NX 16GB or 8GB module fitted to NVIDIA's own Orin Nano Super dev-kit carrier, the lowest-mass NX path that uses a stock NVIDIA carrier. An NVIDIA forum thread shows an NX 16GB running Super modes on that carrier at 19 V input (JetPack 6.2), reaching about 32 W VDD_IN under full CPU+GPU stress (third-party, tegrastats). It keeps the 9-20 V converter. Cooling headroom of the stock heatsink is unverified. Module price about $1,077.02 single-unit at Seeed. https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/orin-nx-16gb-on-devkit-super-mode-power-loading-cant-up-to-40w/324604
unverifiable: Power mode of the Ultralytics Orin Nano Super YOLO26n row (4.57 ms FP16, 3.80 ms INT8). The guide names no mode and does not say whether jetson_clocks was used. Its own setup step 'sudo nvpmodel -m 0' selects the 15 W mode on the Super flash configuration, so 'MAXN SUPER' for this row is not confirmed. The dataset is also unstated (probably COCO128). https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/nvidia-jetson/

Seeed reComputer Robotics J401 boxed-system mass (200 g vs 1100 g; see corrections). Also unclear whether the J3011 includes a 128 GB NVMe: the wiki says it does, but the product page lists no storage and offers a 512 GB add-on for $179. https://www.seeedstudio.com/reComputer-Robotics-J3011-p-6503.html
Connect Tech Orin NX active heatsink at 49 g: the page returned HTTP 403, so the mass and price are unverified. https://connecttech.com/product/nvidia-jetson-orin-nx-active-heat-sink/

ARK Just A Jetson 'Super Power Mode'. ARK's hardware page says the module and all rails draw from one 5 V supply. NVIDIA forum guidance allows 7/15/25 W at 5 V@5 A, but Super modes above 25 W need at least 8 V. MAXN SUPER above 25 W on this carrier is therefore unlikely (my inference), and ARK does not say which mode it means. https://docs.arkelectron.com/embedded-computers/ark-just-a-jetson/hardware

Whether forum posters 'sgursal' (25 W dev-kit maximum, 8 V Super-mode note) and 'Trumany' (174 g, 872.5 g, 9-20 V and 7-20 V) are NVIDIA staff: the fetched pages show no staff badges. Their figures read as official answers but are not datasheet values.

Seeed reComputer Mini extension CAN: the wiki lists '1x CAN JST 4pin (3.3V)', which may be a logic-level port needing an external transceiver; Seeed does not say. https://wiki.seeedstudio.com/recomputer_jetson_mini_getting_started/

Connect Tech NGX027 USB 3.1 VBUS current is not stated; the spec sheet gives only 500 mA each for the auxiliary 3.3 V and 5 V outputs. The OAK-D Lite datasheet gives 4 W typical and 4.5 W max (about 0.9 A at 5 V), and OAK-D Pro W power was not checked. Confirm the port current or plan a powered feed. https://media.distrelec.com/Web/Downloads/_t/ds/OAK-D_Lite-eng_tds.pdf
Auvidea JNX42 (EUR 215 ex VAT, 12-48 V): the cited REBOTNIX store page shows no product data, so it is unverified. https://store.rebotnix.com/product/jnx42/

Cited sources that could not be fetched. The RS Online Orin Nano page returned 403; the '1080p30 encode on 1-2 CPU cores' claim is confirmed on NVIDIA's Jetson Orin page instead. The Isaac ROS release-3.3 PREEMPT_RT page returned 404; the claim that a packaged RT kernel exists from JetPack 6.1 is supported only by a search snippet of the current Isaac ROS page.

Carrier, NVMe and fan overhead of 2-3 W at the dev-kit DC input: no measurement comparing DC-jack power with VDD_IN was found. NVIDIA's ChrisB_NV (Jun 2026) confirms VDD_IN is total module power and that external measurement needs a custom sense point. https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/externally-measuring-current-draw-power/372739

Hackster's original Orin Nano kit figures (about 4 W idle, about 17 W peak at the wall): the article does not name the power mode. They were taken on the pre-Super kit with Wi-Fi, a DisplayPort monitor, keyboard and mouse attached, and include AC-adapter loss.

Current JetPack point release: a Jetson Linux r39.2.1 developer-guide archive exists (last updated 12 Aug 2026), and NVIDIA said T3000 emulation would ship with JetPack 7.2.1. JetPack 7.2.1 is therefore likely current, but its release notes were not checked. https://docs.nvidia.com/jetson/archives/r39.2.1/DeveloperGuide/HR/ControllerAreaNetworkCan.html

Single-unit US module prices from distributors vary: Arrow listings show $249, $369 and $449 with no stock and 24-week lead times. Seeed's $449.82 line is the only consistent single-unit figure found.

Orin Nano and Orin NX module mass is unpublished, so the 45 g, 75 g, 80 g and 200 g carrier totals still exclude the module and heatsink. My web-search budget ran out before I could search further. A follow-up message can resume the search.

options.name: Raspberry Pi 5 8GB + Active Cooler (CPU only)
options.configuration: Counted: Raspberry Pi 5 8 GB board ($175 list, Nov 2026 product brief), official Active Cooler ($5 list) and a 64 GB A2 microSD (about $15, my estimate; Raspberry Pi's SD-card page shows no prices). Not counted: the 5 V/5 A robot buck converter. No NPU, so the person detector runs on the Pi CPU or on the OAK-D's RVC2.
options.cpu: Broadcom BCM2712, 4x Arm Cortex-A76 @ 2.4 GHz (512 KB L2 per core, 2 MB L3), VideoCore VII GPU
options.ai_accelerator: None (CPU NEON only); the head-mounted OAK-D's RVC2 (1.4 TOPS for AI) can host the detector
options.power_basis: Third-party measurements. Jeff Geerling: Pi 5 8GB, C1 stepping, 3.2 W idle and 9.8 W under stress-ng (2GB D0: 2.4 / 8.9 W). CNX Software, wall meter incl. PSU, Active Cooler fitted: 3.0 W idle headless, 8.8 W with stress -c 4, 16.8 W peak with USB drives attached. heise: D0-stepping boards idle at about 2.5 W, and every stepping peaks just under 9 W. The 8.5 W 'typical inference' figure is my estimate for a 4-core NCNN detector, which sits close to all-core stress. Battery side at 0.88 DC-DC (estimate): about 3.6 W idle, 9.7 W while detecting and 11 W max, against the 35.2 W Jetson budget. OAK-D power is excluded; it flows through the Pi's USB ports, up to 1.6 A x 5 V.
options.interfaces: USB: 2x USB 3.0 Type-A, each 5 Gbps simultaneously via RP1, which links to BCM2712 over PCIe 2.0 x4 (16 Gb/s). Measured: 420 MB/s on one SSD, 842/832 MB/s read/write across two. That is ample for one OAK-D (1080p NV12 at 30 fps is about 93 MB/s, plus about 15 MB/s for 640x400 depth; my estimate). 2x USB 2.0, one of which can carry the Teensy 4.1 USB-serial link. Also GbE, 2x 4-lane MIPI CSI/DSI, and 1x PCIe 2.0 x1 FFC (Gen 3 works but is not certified by Raspberry Pi). 40-pin GPIO: I2C for the two VL53L5CX, UART for the STL-19P, SPI. No native CAN: use an SPI MCP2518FD HAT (Waveshare 2-CH CAN FD HAT, $46.99) or USB-CAN. USB downstream current is capped at 1.6 A total with a 5 V/5 A supply (600 mA otherwise), and the fan shares that limit. Set PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000 when feeding from a non-PD 5 V buck.
options.software: OS: Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit (Debian 13 Trixie), or Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 LTS (26.04 is listed as certified on Pi 5). ROS 2: Jazzy binaries are Tier 1 on Ubuntu 24.04 arm64; Lyrical Luth (May 2026, LTS to May 2031) is Tier 1 on Ubuntu 26.04 arm64. Raspberry Pi OS/Debian is Tier 3, meaning a source build or Docker. CPU inference: NCNN (fastest per Ultralytics), OpenVINO, ONNX Runtime, LiteRT, MNN and ExecuTorch, all exported directly from Ultralytics with near-zero conversion effort. The ONNX MLP runs under ONNX Runtime. Real-time: PREEMPT_RT has been in mainline since 6.12, but no RT kernel package was found for Raspberry Pi OS, so you build your own. On Ubuntu, the Pro realtime-kernel raspi variant covers 24.04 (free for up to 5 machines), and ubuntu-realtime is free from 26.04 (a Pi-specific build there is not confirmed).
options.video_encode: No hardware encoder; only a 4Kp60 HEVC decoder. Software libx264 encodes 1080p30 in real time with about 60% of one A76 core in low-latency mode, or 100-150% of a core in high-quality mode (Raspberry Pi white paper, Apr 2026). Alternative: let the OAK-D's RVC2 hardware H.264/H.265/MJPEG encoder (4K30 / 1080p60) do it and forward the bitstream.
options.availability: In production. Raspberry Pi commits to production until at least January 2036. The 8 GB list price went $80 (launch) -> $95 (Dec 2025) -> $125 (Feb 2026) -> $175 (Apr 2026), driven by LPDDR4X costs; Raspberry Pi says it will reverse the rises when memory prices fall.

options.fit_notes:
Without an NPU it can carry: OAK-D depth into a costmap and local planner (depth is computed on the camera), the VL53L5CX (I2C) and STL-19P (UART), the ONNX MLP at 50-100 Hz, and the operator stream (libx264 at about 0.6 core for 1080p30, or forward the OAK's hardware H.264). The MLP's compute is tiny; timing is the problem. OSPERT 2024 measured a stock-kernel worst case of 36.8 ms under heavy stress, against 124 us with PREEMPT_RT. So use an RT kernel with an isolated core, or keep the loop deadline on the Teensy.

Person detection on the CPU is marginal. YOLO26n NCNN at 640 runs about 15 fps inference-only and would load most of the 4 cores. Input of 320-416 would be several times faster (my estimate). Better: run YOLOv6n or YOLOv8n on the OAK's RVC2 (31-65 fps at 416, vendor) and keep tracking and re-ID on the Pi. No Pi 5 CPU re-ID benchmark was found.

Good fit for 60-75 cm on power (about 9.7 W at the battery while detecting, vs 35.2 W for the Jetson budget) and mass (about 75 g vs 290 g).

Risks:
- Little headroom for re-ID plus voice.
- The OAK-D Pro W (100-120 cm) must be powered through its Y-adapter, not the Pi's 1.6 A USB budget.
- A microSD card in a walking robot; a USB SSD or CM5 eMMC is safer.
- List price has risen 119% since launch.

Carrier choice:

- A Hailo forum user reports CM5 + Nano B + AI HAT+ working. The 65x56.5 mm HAT overhangs the carrier, and the AI HAT+ 2 and Sixfab HAT are documented as Pi 5 only.

No CM5-specific YOLO benchmark was found; expect the Pi 5 CPU numbers at the same clock.

Best long-term route for 100-120 cm if Mesozoic Labs later makes its own carrier (5 V buck, CAN-FD, M.2, connectors that lock against vibration).

Recommended Pi configuration for 60-75 cm.

The Hailo-8L runs the person detector: YOLOv8n at 640 measured 61.9 fps (batch 1, hw-only) on a Pi 5; YOLO11n is 157 fps on the vendor's x86 host. It can also run a re-ID embedder for loss and reacquisition (OSNet 165 fps vendor; RepVGG re-ID 4580 fps). That leaves the CPU for tracking, nav, the MLP and streaming.

End-to-end pipelines on the Pi are limited by the host, not the NPU: YOLO26n ran 14.7 fps sync and about 20 fps async in Sixfab's tests. That is adequate for 10-15 Hz person following, but keep pre/post-processing in C++ (a C++ app reached 144 fps on a Hailo-8).

- The HAT is rated 0-50 C ambient.
- The stacking header and PCIe FFC are untested under walking vibration.
- Raspberry Pi does not certify PCIe Gen 3.
- Multi-context models (YOLO11s and larger) slow sharply on the single lane.

Only worth it if the voice stretch goal (Whisper-class speech-to-text plus a small LLM for intent) should run on the robot. It has 8 GB on the module, does a Qwen2.5-1.5B prefill in 320 ms vs 2039 ms on the Pi CPU, and runs Whisper examples through hailo-apps.
