category_findings:
Prices (Nov 2026): Raspberry Pi raised the price of every DRAM-bearing product it sells several times as LPDDR4X costs rose: 1 Dec 2025, 2 Feb 2026, 1 Apr 2026, and 2 Nov 2026 for 16GB.
- Pi 5 list is now $110 (4GB), $175 (8GB) and $385 (16GB), against $60/$80/$120 at launch.
- CM5 8GB/32GB Wi-Fi is $205.
- Accelerators without DRAM held their price (AI HAT+ 13 TOPS $70, 26 TOPS $110), but the AI HAT+ 2 (8 GB on board) went from $130 to $200.
- A Pi 5 8GB + AI HAT+ stack ($265-305 with cooler and SD card) now costs about the same as, or more than, the $249 Jetson Orin Nano Super kit. The case for a Pi is power and mass, not price.
Sources: https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/892-raspberry-pi-5/documents/RP-008348-DS-6-raspberry-pi-5-product-brief.pdf ; https://www.raspberrypi.com/news/price-rises-for-some-16gb-raspberry-pi-products/ ; https://www.raspberrypi.com/news/a-new-3gb-raspberry-pi-4-for-83-75-and-more-memory-driven-price-increases/ ; https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=397523 ; https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/944-raspberry-pi-compute-module-5/documents/RP-008181-DS-5-cm5-product-brief.pdf ; https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/1319-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-2/documents/RP-009655-MM-6-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-plus-2-product-brief.pdf ; https://sixfab.com/blog/raspberry-pi-5-ai-hat-benchmark-deepx-vs-hailo/

Power, measured:
- Bare Pi 5: idle 2.4 W (2GB D0) to 3.2-3.3 W (4/8GB C1); stress-ng 8.9-9.8 W (Geerling). CNX at the wall with the Active Cooler: 3.0 W idle, 8.8 W. heise: 16GB idle 2.95 W, all steppings just under 9 W.
- Whole Pi 5 8GB + NPU HAT system, average during detection: 6.08 W (Hailo-8L), 6.53 W (Hailo-8), 7.59 W (Hailo-10H), 6.73 W (DEEPX DX-M1M). Idle 3.6-3.9 W (Sixfab, inline USB-PD meter, July 2026).
Through the 0.88 DC-DC that is about 7-9 W at the battery, against the 35.2 W the Jetson is budgeted at ((25+6)/0.88): about 26-28 W less.
My estimate of the runtime effect if the Jetson really drew its full budget: +36-41% at 60 cm (96 W walking), +30-34% at 75 cm (110 W), +15-23% at 100-120 cm (150-200 W). The real gain is smaller if the Jetson typically runs well below its 25 W mode.
Sources: https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2024/new-2gb-pi-5-has-33-smaller-die-30-idle-power-savings/ ; https://www.cnx-software.com/2023/11/05/raspberry-pi-5-review-raspberry-pi-os-bookworm-benchmarks-power-consumption/ ; https://heise.de/-10232337 ; https://sixfab.com/blog/raspberry-pi-5-ai-hat-benchmark-deepx-vs-hailo/

Extra power each accelerator adds over a bare Pi:
- Hailo-8L: about 1.5 W typical (vendor).
- Hailo-8: 2.4-3.3 W typical, 8.25 W max (M.2 datasheet).
- Hailo-10H: 2.5 W typical (vendor).
- DEEPX DX-M1M: 3 W sustained (vendor).
- Coral USB: about 2 W typical, 4.5 W peak (900 mA, datasheet).
- AI Camera: about 1.9 W (Hackster, measured).
In Sixfab's system measurements the rise over idle was about 2.3-3.8 W; that includes host-side CPU work.
Sources: https://hailo.ai/products/ai-accelerators/hailo-8l-ai-accelerator-for-ai-light-applications/ ; https://hailo.ai/hailo-files/hailo-8-m-2-key-m-et-datasheet-en/ ; https://hailo.ai/products/ai-accelerators/hailo-10h-m-2-ai-acceleration-module/ ; https://docs.sixfab.com/docs/ai-hat-plus-raspberry-pi-5-specifications ; https://gweb-coral-full.uc.r.appspot.com/static/files/Coral-USB-Accelerator-datasheet.pdf ; https://hackster.io/news/raspberry-pi-s-ai-eye-hands-on-with-the-raspberry-pi-ai-camera-module-383fb34afcf7

Pi 5 CPU-only detection, FP32 at 640, inference only (Ultralytics): YOLO26n 67 ms with NCNN (about 15 fps), 105 ms with OpenVINO, 126 ms with ONNX Runtime; YOLO11n 147 ms with ONNX (6.8 fps), and about 94 ms with NCNN per an earlier revision of the guide.
Other measurements: Q-engineering got YOLOv8n ncnn at 20 fps at 640 on a Pi 5 overclocked to 2.9 GHz; Arm's ExecuTorch INT8 YOLO11n ran 134 ms on 1 thread.
Not found: OpenCV-DNN, MobileNet-SSD or person re-ID benchmarks on the Pi 5 CPU.
CPU-only person detection at 640 would use most of the four cores. Reduce input to 320-416 or move the detector off the CPU.
Sources: https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/raspberry-pi/ ; https://community.ultralytics.com/t/raspberry-pi-5-crash-when-running-yolov11n-ncnn/1525 ; https://github.com/Qengineering/YoloV8-ncnn-Raspberry-Pi-4 ; https://huggingface.co/Arm/yolo11n-int8-xnnpack-executorch-raspberrypi5

Hailo on the Pi 5:
- Hailo Model Zoo (vendor, x86 host, hw-only, batch 1): YOLOv8n at 640 runs 201 fps on Hailo-8L, 1036 on Hailo-8 and 378 on Hailo-10H; YOLO11n 157 / 185 / 309; OSNet-x1.0 re-ID 165 / 215 / 292.
- The Pi 5 has a single PCIe Gen3 lane, and measured numbers are lower: Hailo-8 YOLO11n 104.9 fps hw-only (7.75 ms; Hailo staff call this expected for x1); Hailo-8 YOLOv8n 431 fps with hailortcli but 144 fps in a user's C++ app; Hailo-8L YOLOv8n 61.9 fps at batch 1 and 121.4 at batch 8. Multi-context models (YOLO11s and larger) lose the most.
- Sixfab's end-to-end YOLO26n pipelines reached only 12-15 fps sync and 20-23 fps async on every NPU, so the Pi's CPU-side decode and pre/post-processing is the bottleneck, not the NPU.
All of these comfortably exceed the 10-15 Hz that person following needs.
Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hailo-ai/hailo_model_zoo/master/docs/public_models/HAILO8L/HAILO8L_object_detection.rst ; https://community.hailo.ai/t/official-fps-benchmark-on-hailo-8-using-raspberry-pi-5/18873 ; https://community.hailo.ai/t/the-performance-on-the-raspberry-pi-5-with-the-hailo-8-chip-seems-not-good-as-he-official-results/17473 ; https://community.hailo.ai/t/yolov8n-real-performance-didnt-expected-from-hailo-model-zoo-documentation/18904 ; https://sixfab.com/blog/raspberry-pi-5-ai-hat-benchmark-deepx-vs-hailo/

The head OAK-D's RVC2 can run the person detector on the camera itself (Luxonis):
- YOLOv6n R2: 65.5 fps at 416.
- YOLOv8n: 31.3 fps at 416, 14.3 fps at 640.
- YOLO11n: 28.1 fps at 416.
This runs alongside stereo depth and a hardware H.264/H.265/MJPEG encoder (4K30 / 1080p60), with 1.4 of the 4 TOPS available for AI.
So a plain Pi 5 with no NPU is workable at 60-75 cm. An NPU HAT then only adds headroom for re-ID, pose or a second model. Luxonis staff say OAK cameras work fine with the Pi 5.
Sources: https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/platform/rvc/rvc2 ; https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/products/OAK-D%20Lite ; https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/3825-current-raspberry-pi-os-and-oak-cameras

H.264: the Pi 5 has no hardware H.264 encoder, only HEVC decode. Raspberry Pi's April 2026 white paper shows libx264 encoding 1080p30 in real time with about 60% of one Cortex-A76 core (low-latency preset), or 100-150% of a core for the high-quality preset.
For the operator page, a 720p 15-30 fps stream costs well under one core (my estimate). Better still, take the OAK's on-camera H.264/H.265 bitstream and only forward it (WebRTC/RTSP), drawing the detections on the web page.
Sources: https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/685-app-notes-guides-whitepapers/documents/RP-010033-WP-1-H.264%20encoding%20performance%20on%20Raspberry%20Pi%205_series%20computers.pdf ; https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/platform/rvc/rvc2

USB3 and OAK power on the Pi 5:
- Bandwidth: each USB 3.0 port has its own 5 Gbps controller in RP1, which links to the SoC over PCIe 2.0 x4 (16 Gb/s). Measured: 420 MB/s on one SSD, 842/832 MB/s across two. An OAK stream (about 93 MB/s for 1080p NV12 at 30 fps plus about 15 MB/s of depth, my estimate) fits easily.
- Power is the limit: downstream USB current is capped at 1.6 A total with a 5 V/5 A supply (600 mA otherwise), and the fan shares it.
- OAK-D Lite: 2.5-3 W base plus up to 2 W for its subsystems.
- OAK-D Pro W: 'might consume up to 15W' with IR on; Luxonis recommends an external 15+ W supply via its Y-adapter. Power the Pro W from the robot's 5 V rail at 100-120 cm.
Sources: https://www.raspberrypi.com/news/introducing-raspberry-pi-5/ ; https://www.hackster.io/news/raspberry-pi-5-review-hands-on-with-the-most-powerful-raspberry-pi-yet-57efaf61b10f ; https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html ; https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/products/OAK-D%20Pro%20W ; https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/products/OAK-D%20Lite ; https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/platform/deploy/usb-deployment-guide

Feeding the Pi from the 6S/12S pack: the Pi 5 needs a 5 V source that can deliver 3 A to boot and 5 A for the full 1.6 A USB budget; its typical bare-board active current is 800 mA. With a plain 5 V buck (no USB-PD), set the bootloader property PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000 (it skips PD negotiation) or usb_max_current_enable=1. Raspberry Pi also says the Pi 5 is not certified at PCIe Gen 3, which the AI HAT+ uses.
Sources: https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html ; https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/1081-raspberry-pi-ai-hat/documents/RP-008133-DS-1-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-plus-product-brief.pdf

Real-time behaviour: PREEMPT_RT has been in mainline since Linux 6.12, but no RT kernel package was found for Raspberry Pi OS; users build their own, and a Raspberry Pi engineer suggested a 4 kB-page RT build.
- OSPERT 2024 on a Pi 5 under heavy stress-ng plus iperf3: stock kernel average 14.7 us, max 36.8 ms; RT kernel average 5.9 us, max 124 us.
- Forum RT builds saw 200-460 us maxima and over 1 ms spikes overnight under memory stress, attributed to memory-bus contention.
- Ubuntu ships a realtime kernel with a raspi variant through Ubuntu Pro on 24.04 (free for up to 5 machines); from 26.04 `ubuntu-realtime` is free (a Pi-specific build is not confirmed).
Implication: for the 50-100 Hz policy (10-20 ms period), run it on an RT kernel pinned to an isolated core, or make the Teensy own the deadline.
Sources: https://antonio.paolillo.be/publications/workshops/ecrtsOspert2024_dewit_rtlinux_paper.pdf ; https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=382231 ; https://ubuntu.com/real-time

ROS 2 and OS:
- Jazzy is Tier 1 on Ubuntu 24.04 arm64.
- Lyrical Luth (May 2026, LTS to May 2031) is Tier 1 on Ubuntu 26.04 arm64; Debian Trixie is Tier 3. Ubuntu 26.04 LTS is certified on the Pi 5.
- Raspberry Pi OS is Tier 3, so ROS 2 runs from a source build or Docker.
The trade-off: the AI HAT+/rpicam/IMX500/DEEPX integrations are first-class on Raspberry Pi OS (the DEEPX HAT supports only Trixie), while on Ubuntu the Hailo PCIe driver must be built from source. The practical choices are Raspberry Pi OS with ROS 2 in a Ubuntu container, or Ubuntu 26.04 with a hand-built HailoRT.
Sources: https://discourse.openrobotics.org/t/ros-2-lyrical-luth-released/55021 ; https://discourse.openrobotics.org/t/ros-2-jazzy-jalisco-released/37862 ; https://docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/How-To-Guides/Installing-on-Raspberry-Pi.html ; https://ubuntu.com/raspberry-pi ; https://ubuntu.com/blog/hackers-guide-to-the-raspberry-pi-ai-kit-on-ubuntu ; https://docs.sixfab.com/docs/ai-hat-plus-raspberry-pi-5-specifications

CAN: the Pi has no native CAN.
- SPI CAN-FD HATs work through SocketCAN mcp251xfd overlays; for example the Waveshare 2-CH CAN FD HAT (MCP2518FD/MCP2562FD, $46.99). A Pi 4 user reported MCP2518FD frames dropped under high system load, and no Pi-5-specific validation was found.
- USB-CAN adapters are the other route (not evaluated).
Since the Teensy 4.1 already owns both leg CAN buses, the simplest link is Pi to Teensy over USB serial or UART. A Pi-side CAN interface is then needed only for bus monitoring and logging.
Sources: https://waveshare.com/2-ch-can-fd-hat.htm ; https://www.waveshare.com/wiki/2-CH_CAN_FD_HAT ; https://forum.opencyphal.org/t/how-to-use-the-raspberrypi-with-mcp2518fd-to-debug-uavcan/1091

Coral lifecycle: treat as end-of-life.
- Google archived pycoral (3 Jul 2025), libedgetpu (14 Oct 2025) and edgetpu (19 Apr 2026, 'no longer maintained').
- coral.ai product pages now redirect to developers.google.com/coral (the new Coral NPU IP platform), and the USB datasheet only lists Debian 10 with Python 3.5-3.7.
- On the Pi 5, YOLOv8n takes 22 ms at 320 and 54 ms at 512; at 640 most ops fall back to the CPU. Maximum ambient is 25 C at max clock.
- The M.2/PCIe version needs the gasket driver, a 4K-page kernel, MSI-X device-tree changes and ASPM off.
Sources: https://github.com/google-coral/pycoral ; https://github.com/google-coral/libedgetpu ; https://github.com/google-coral/edgetpu ; https://developers.google.com/coral ; https://gweb-coral-full.uc.r.appspot.com/static/files/Coral-USB-Accelerator-datasheet.pdf ; https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/coral-edge-tpu-on-raspberry-pi/ ; https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2023/pcie-coral-tpu-finally-works-on-raspberry-pi-5/

Other Pi accelerators:
- AI Kit: discontinued, replaced by the AI HAT+ 13 TOPS at the same $70.
- Hailo-8 M.2 modules ($179.99) on the $12 M.2 HAT+ match the AI HAT+ 26 TOPS within 0.1% but cost about $80 more, so they only make sense on a CM5 carrier with an M.2 slot.
- Sixfab's DEEPX DX-M1M HAT (25 TOPS, $95, June 2026) had the highest NPU throughput in Sixfab's own test (YOLO26n 178.7 vs 96.7 fps for Hailo-8). It is Raspberry Pi OS Trixie only, Pi 5 only, and its certifications are pending.
- AI Camera (IMX500, $70): YOLO11n at 640 on the sensor in 58.8 ms, about 1.9 W, but 2D only; it would duplicate the OAK-D.
Sources: https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/ai-kit/ ; https://www.waveshare.com/product/ai/boards-kits/raspberry-pi/hailo-8.htm ; https://shop.sixfab.com/products/ai-hat-plus-raspberry-pi-5 ; https://docs.ultralytics.com/integrations/sony-imx500/ ; https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/ai-camera/

CM5 with a small carrier:
- Same SoC as the Pi 5. Tom's Hardware measured 2.65 W idle and 6.66 W under stress (passive cooling).
- The CM5 is 55x40x4.7 mm and rated -20 to +85 C, against the Pi 5's 0-70 C.
- The Waveshare CM5-NANO-B (55x41 mm, $17.99) has one USB 3.2 Gen1 port (enough for the OAK-D) and a 16-pin PCIe FFC; a Hailo forum user reports CM5 + Nano B + AI HAT+ working.
- Seeed's CM5 MINIMA has an M.2 2242 slot for a Hailo module but only USB 2.0.
- A custom carrier (5 V buck, CAN-FD, M.2, locking connectors) is the natural long-term route for the 100-120 cm robots.
Sources: https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/944-raspberry-pi-compute-module-5/documents/RP-008181-DS-5-cm5-product-brief.pdf ; https://www.tomshardware.com/raspberry-pi/raspberry-pi-compute-module-5-review ; https://waveshare.com/CM5-NANO-B.htm ; https://community.hailo.ai/t/smallest-rpi-cm5-m-2-hailo-carrier-options/18959 ; https://www.cnx-software.com/2025/07/31/cm5-minima-raspberry-pi-cm5-carrier-board-features-m-2-2230-2242-socket-for-hailo-ai-accelerator-or-nvme-ssd/

Thermal and mechanical:
- Ambient ratings: Pi 5 0-70 C; AI HAT+ and AI HAT+ 2 0-50 C (the HAT+ 2 heatsink is recommended for sustained loads); CM5 -20 to +85 C; Coral USB 25 C max at max clock.
- With the Active Cooler the Pi 5 stayed at about 66 C under load without throttling; with a heatsink only, it throttled (CNX). The torso needs forced air past the stack.
- Mass: Pi 5 + Active Cooler about 75 g (29 g cooler per a retailer listing, plus about 46 g board, my estimate), and about 100 g with an AI HAT+ (estimate), against 290 g for the Jetson with tray.
- Footprint: 85x56 mm (Pi 5) or 55x41 mm (CM5 + Nano B).
Sources: https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/892-raspberry-pi-5/documents/RP-008348-DS-6-raspberry-pi-5-product-brief.pdf ; https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/1319-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-2/documents/RP-009655-MM-6-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-plus-2-product-brief.pdf ; https://www.cnx-software.com/2023/11/05/raspberry-pi-5-review-raspberry-pi-os-bookworm-benchmarks-power-consumption/ ; https://www.waveshare.com/raspberry-pi-5-official-active-cooler.htm

Voice stretch goal: the AI HAT+ 2 (Hailo-10H, 8 GB) runs Whisper-class speech-to-text through Hailo's app examples (forum, Mar 2026) plus small LLMs for intent. Raspberry Pi measured a 96-token Qwen2.5-1.5B prefill at 320 ms on the Hailo-10H vs 2039 ms on the Pi 5 CPU.
No Pi 5 CPU speech-to-text benchmark was collected.
Sources: https://www.raspberrypi.com/news/when-and-why-you-might-need-the-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-plus-2/ ; https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=396322

Bottom line for this category (my assessment):
- 60-75 cm: Pi 5 (4 or 8 GB) + AI HAT+ 13 TOPS, or a plain Pi 5 with the detector on the OAK RVC2. Both cover the workload at roughly a quarter of the Jetson's budgeted power.
- 100-120 cm: Pi 5 8GB + AI HAT+ 26 TOPS, or the AI HAT+ 2 if voice must be on-board. A CM5 on a small or custom carrier is the tidier mechanical option.
- Avoid Coral (USB or M.2) and the discontinued AI Kit.
- The weak spots against Jetson: CPU-side pre/post-processing throughput, no hardware video encoder, no CUDA/TensorRT ecosystem, and a self-maintained RT kernel.
open_questions: What does the Jetson Orin Nano Super actually draw on this workload? The 26-28 W saving and the runtime gains assume it uses its full 25 W + 6 W budget. A bench measurement of the Jetson stack would size the real saving.

Should the person detector run on the OAK-D's RVC2 (frees the Pi, no NPU needed) or on a Hailo HAT (higher fps and model choice, frees the OAK for depth)? Bench both with the real pipeline: depth at the required resolution, detection, H.264 stream and tracking together.
Which re-ID model will the loss/reacquisition logic use, and what does it cost on the Pi 5 CPU? No CPU re-ID benchmark was found; Hailo vendor figures exist for OSNet-x1.0 and RepVGG-A0.

Run the 50-100 Hz policy on the Pi under PREEMPT_RT (self-maintained kernel on Raspberry Pi OS, or Ubuntu's realtime kernel), or make the Teensy 4.1 own the timing, or run the small MLP on the Teensy itself?
OS choice for ROS 2: Raspberry Pi OS with ROS 2 in Docker (best Hailo/DEEPX/IMX500 support) or Ubuntu 26.04 + ROS 2 Lyrical (Tier 1, but the Hailo driver is hand-built)?
How hot will the torso/head get while walking? The AI HAT+ / HAT+ 2 are rated only to 50 C ambient, so forced airflow may be required.
Will the 40-pin stacking header and 16-pin PCIe FFC survive walking vibration? Consider a CM5 on a custom carrier with locking connectors for the 100-120 cm robots.
Which board stepping (C1 or D0) ships in current 4GB/8GB stock? Idle differs by about 0.8 W.
Do the OAK-D Pro W's IR projector and flood LED need to run? If so, it needs a Y-adapter fed from a 15+ W robot 5 V rail, not the Pi's 1.6 A USB budget.
Is a Pi-side CAN-FD interface needed at all, or is a USB/UART link to the Teensy enough? If needed, MCP2518FD SPI HATs on the Pi 5 (RP1 SPI and interrupt latency) are unvalidated.
How long will prices keep rising? Pi prices rose four times in 12 months (16GB now $385). Raspberry Pi promises rollbacks when memory costs fall; consider buying ahead for all prototypes.

The shared web-search budget ran out before these could be checked: AI HAT+ / AI HAT+ 2 / Coral USB masses, a measured Pi 5 board mass, current official SD-card and CM5-cooler prices, OpenCV-DNN and MobileNet-SSD CPU benchmarks on Pi 5, and a Pi 5 CPU speech-to-text benchmark (whisper.cpp/Vosk). Estimates are labelled as such; a follow-up search can close these gaps.

corrections.claimed: Raspberry Pi raised the price of every DRAM-bearing product it sells several times: 1 Dec 2025, 2 Feb 2026, 1 Apr 2026, and 2 Nov 2026 for 16GB.
corrections.corrected: Not every product was raised, and the list of dates is incomplete. On 1 Apr 2026 the 1GB/2GB Pi 4 and Pi 5 ($35-65) and the Pi 400 ($60) were held. On 2 Nov 2026 the Pi 500+ was held, and Raspberry Pi said it had 'avoided making blanket increases across the entire product line'. The Pi 5 1GB has stayed at $45 since it launched in Dec 2025. corrections.field: fit_notes (vision speed vs the 26 TOPS HAT)
corrections.claimed: For vision it is not faster than the 26 TOPS HAT on small detectors. Vendor zoo: YOLOv8n 378 fps at batch 1 vs 1036 on the Hailo-8.
corrections.corrected: Speed depends on the model, and the YOLOv8n row is cherry-picked. In the same vendor zoo (i5-9400 host, batch 1) the Hailo-10H is faster on the current nano models: YOLO11n 309 vs 185 fps, YOLO26n 234 vs 154, OSNet-x1.0 re-ID 292 vs 215. It is slower on YOLOv8n (378 vs 1036), YOLOv6n (506 vs 1250) and SSD-MobileNet-v1 (452 vs 1015). At batch 8 the Hailo-8 leads (YOLO11n 541 vs 343; YOLO26n 427 vs 311). On a Pi 5, Sixfab's NPU-async YOLO26n was 83.5 vs 96.7 fps. The survey's own benchmark rows (YOLO11n 309 vs 185) contradict its conclusion.
corrections.evidence: Parsed HAILO10H_object_detection.rst (DFC v5.5.0), HAILO8_object_detection.rst (DFC v2.20.0) and the person_re_id .rst files.

corrections.field: power_w_typical_inference / power_basis (same applies to the 26 TOPS, Hailo-10H, DX-M1M and Hailo-8 M.2 entries)
corrections.claimed: 6.08 W average for the whole system during sync inference runs (6.53 / 7.59 / 6.73 W for the other NPUs), used as the person-detection 'typical'.
corrections.corrected: The averages are reported correctly, but they are not measurements of a person-following pipeline. They average seven models, mostly heavy ones: YOLOv8l, YOLOv8x, YOLO11l and DeepLabV3, plus YOLO26n, EfficientNet-Lite0 and MobileNetV2. Runs were sync single-request with video decode on the Pi. The precision is not stated (the survey's INT8 label is an assumption), no Pi CPU cooler is stated, and no OAK-D was attached. Label these as a third-party mixed-model proxy.
corrections.evidence: Sixfab lists the seven models, '640 x 640 for YOLO models', an inline USB-PD meter, idle 3.6-3.9 W, and no quantization precision.

corrections.field: power_w_max (same applies to rpi5_8gb_ai_hat_plus_2_hailo10h at 14 W and rpi5_8gb_sixfab_ai_hat_dx_m1m at 15 W)
corrections.claimed: 12 W max (estimate: Pi stress-ng 9.8 W plus about 2 W for the NPU).
corrections.corrected: Not supported as a maximum. The same Sixfab test measured whole-system peaks of 9.2-17.8 W 'depending on chip and model' and does not break them out by chip. Any of the HATs may therefore have peaked near 17.8 W. Use about 18 W as the worst case until per-chip peaks are measured. Sixfab's own DX-M1M spec gives roughly 13-15 W for the system.
corrections.evidence: Sixfab test configuration table: 'Peak power during inference 9.2 W to 17.8 W depending on chip and model.'

corrections.field: fit_notes ('a C++ app reached 144 fps on a Hailo-8'); also rpi5_8gb_ai_hat_plus_26tops benchmark row
corrections.claimed: Keep pre/post-processing in C++ (a C++ app reached 144 fps on a Hailo-8).
corrections.corrected: The 144 fps result (Hailo forum, 5 Sep 2025, Hailo-8 M.2 at Gen3 x1, firmware 4.20.0) ran the HEFs without post-processing. It is not an end-to-end detection figure and does not show that C++ pre/post-processing removes the host bottleneck.
corrections.evidence: Forum thread: own C++ app 144 FPS 'used the HEFs without post-processing'; hailortcli run 431 FPS; the link reported 'Width x1 (downgraded)'.

corrections.claimed: YOLOv8n at 640 measured 61.9 fps (batch 1, hw-only) on a Pi 5 8GB, HailoRT 4.19.
corrections.corrected: The post (9 Mar 2026) reports 61.9 fps at batch 1 and 121.4 at batch 8 with HailoRT 4.19.0 and Model Zoo v2.13 HEFs, whose documentation then promised 182 / 464 fps. It does not name the measuring tool, does not say hw-only, and does not give the Pi's RAM size. Drop 'hw-only' and '8GB'.
corrections.evidence: Forum post contents; Hailo staff reply: 'The Model Zoo numbers are raw chip throughput, not application-level FPS.'

corrections.field: configuration ('The single PCIe lane is taken by the HAT, so there is no NVMe'); also the 26 TOPS, AI HAT+ 2 and DX-M1M entries
corrections.claimed: The HAT takes the only PCIe lane, so NVMe is impossible.
corrections.corrected: A PCIe packet-switch board makes NVMe possible alongside the accelerator. The Geekworm X1004 (ASMedia ASM1182e) supports a Hailo-8 plus an NVMe boot SSD on the Pi 5. They share PCIe 2.0 x1 bandwidth (Gen 3 does not pass through the switch), which would further reduce multi-context Hailo throughput. This matters for the survey's own microSD vibration risk.
corrections.evidence: Geekworm wiki: 'X1004 uses ASMedia ASM1182e PCIe switch', 'do not support PCIe 3.0', and 'X1004 also supports hailo-8 ai accelerator and can also support booting from another SSD'.

corrections.claimed: Launched 15 Jan 2026 at $130, rose +$50 on 1 Apr 2026, and the July 2026 brief lists $200.
corrections.corrected: Each fact is correct, but $130 + $50 = $180, so another rise of about $20 came before the July 2026 brief (MM-6, $200). No announcement for it was found. $200 is current: the product page says 'Available now for $200' and Sixfab's October 2026 table agrees.

corrections.claimed: Even then the AI HAT+ 2 is faster: a 96-token Qwen2.5-1.5B prefill takes 320 ms on the Hailo-10H vs 2039 ms on the Pi 5 CPU.
corrections.corrected: The only published comparison is prefill / time-to-first-token (96 tokens, QWEN2.5-1.5B-4int, CPU via llama.cpp, Pi RAM size not stated). There are no decode tokens/s and no power figures, so 'faster' is shown for prompt processing only, not for generation.

corrections.claimed: libx264 encodes 1080p30 in real time with about 60% of one A76 core in low-latency mode, or 100-150% of a core in high-quality mode.

MemryX Cascade 100R Raspberry Pi 5 HAT+: 4x MX3 chips, 25 TFLOPS, 1-12 W, 42 MB on-chip weight storage, PCIe Gen 3 over the Pi 5 FPC, 85x56 mm. A second LLM/VLM/voice option besides the AI HAT+ 2. M5Stack's Pi kit (AI-8850, $215) is marked EOL and out of stock; standalone card availability is unconfirmed. https://docs.m5stack.com/en/ai_hardware/LLM-8850_Card ; https://shop.m5stack.com/products/ai-8850-llm-accelerator-m-2-kit-8gb-version-ax8850

Official Raspberry Pi CM5 IO Board (160x90 mm, M.2 M-key PCIe socket plus 2x USB 3, 5 V USB-C input): the first-party CM5 carrier with both an NPU slot and USB 3 for the OAK-D, and the natural reference design for the proposed custom carrier. The survey's Nano B has no M.2 slot and the MINIMA has no USB 3. https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/compute-module-5-io-board/

PCIe packet-switch HATs for the Pi 5, e.g. Geekworm X1004 (ASM1182e, Gen 2): NVMe boot plus a Hailo-8 at the same time. This removes the microSD-in-a-walking-robot risk the survey raises, at the cost of shared Gen 2 x1 bandwidth. https://wiki.geekworm.com/X1004

Configuration not surveyed: Pi 5 + M.2 HAT+ with an NVMe boot SSD and no NPU, with person detection on the OAK RVC2. It is the cheapest way to remove the microSD risk for the CPU-only 60-75 cm option. M.2 HAT+ from $12, 2230/2242, up to 3 A, production to Jan 2032. https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/m2-hat-plus/
unverifiable: Search limit: this run's web-search budget was already used up (the shared limit was hit on the first query). Verification therefore used direct fetches of the cited URLs and known primary pages only. No search for new 2026 Pi-ecosystem products or for independent re-measurements was possible; a follow-up with search budget could close these gaps.

cm5_8gb_wifi_nano_b power figures: 2.65 W idle, 6.66 W passive stress, 8 W with fan, 10.99 W at 3 GHz, and the stated CM5 4GB/32GB IO-board configuration. The Tom's Hardware review returned only its 123-character title to the fetcher. The CM5 brief itself is confirmed (DS-5 redirects to DS-13, Nov 2026): CM5108032 $205, CM5104032 $140, 55x40x4.7 mm, -20 to +85 C, production to Jan 2036. Waveshare Nano B ($17.99, 55x41 mm, 1x USB 3.2 Gen1, 16-pin PCIe Gen2/3 x1, 5 V/5 A) and Nano A (0.015 kg, $14.99) are confirmed.
CM5 module mass 0.018 kg: the Farnell IT and UK listings returned HTTP 503. Berrybase lists the CM5 passive cooler at EUR 5.50 incl. VAT, 0.036 kg gross.

Coral prices: USB Accelerator $58.56-63.22 (Arrow returned HTTP 503); Coral M.2 G650-04686-01 about $29.90 (Octopart returned HTTP 403; element14 back-order page returned HTTP 503). Everything else on Coral is confirmed: datasheet v1.4 (4 TOPS, 2 TOPS/W, 500 mA min / 900 mA peak, 25 C max ambient at max clock / 35 C reduced, Debian 10, Python 3.5-3.7); archive dates pycoral 3 Jul 2025, libedgetpu 14 Oct 2025, edgetpu 19 Apr 2026; coral.ai product pages 302 to developers.google.com/coral and the coral.ai datasheet URL 404s; gasket-driver repo 404; Ultralytics Pi 5 8GB tab (YOLOv8n 22.2/16.7 ms at 320, 53.5/41.6 ms at 512; YOLOv8s 40.1/32.2 ms at 320).
AI Camera: Sony's claim that IMX500 inference adds under 100 mW has no URL. The Hackster 1.87 W of 4.12 W figure is confirmed but its measurement method is not stated.

'Hailo's starter kit is about $179' (Hailo-8 M.2 entry): no URL. Also unconfirmed whether Waveshare's $179.99 Hailo-8 listing is the extended-temperature ET part (HM218B1C2HAE) that the -40 to 85 C rating applies to.

All masses are estimates with no measured source: Pi 5 board about 46 g; Pi + cooler 75 g; stacks with HATs 100-110 g; CM5 + Nano B 63 g; Coral stack 110 g. The 0.029 kg Active Cooler (Waveshare) and 0.036 kg CM5 cooler (Berrybase, gross) are retailer shipping weights. Waveshare's Pi 5 and AI HAT+ pages give no weight.
Current board stepping of 4GB/8GB Pi 5 stock: C1 idles at about 3.2-3.4 W (Geerling; heise), D0 at about 2.4-2.5 W. Not verified, so Geerling's C1 idle numbers may not match boards bought now.

Estimated prices: microSD about $15 (Raspberry Pi's SD-card page shows no prices) and CM5 cooler about $5. The Active Cooler's $5 list comes from the 2023 launch post; Raspberry Pi's product page now shows no price, and Waveshare sells it at $5.99.

Seeed's YOLOv8n 136.7 fps at batch 8: a custom compile (DFC 3.27, hailo_model_zoo 2.11) with PCIe generation and tool not stated, so it is not directly comparable to the other rows.
Precision of the Sixfab benchmark models is not stated in the article; the survey's INT8 labels are assumptions, though plausible for Hailo and DEEPX toolchains.

Jetson Orin Nano Super $249, used for price comparisons: NVIDIA's product page lists no price. It is outside this category and was not re-verified.

options.fit_notes: Most NPU TOPS in the category, but the measured 14.2 W idle on the same SoC is already about half the Jetson's 31 W budget, the board is 115x100 mm, and no YOLO benchmark was found. Not a fit for battery runtime.

category_findings: RK3588/RK3588S boards are the strongest fit in this category for the minimum autonomy spec. Rockchip's model zoo lists YOLOv8n INT8 640x640 at 76.3 FPS on one of the three NPU cores (vendor, inference only; https://github.com/airockchip/rknn_model_zoo). An independent Sci. Rep. study (21 Jan 2026) measured 24.5 ms on one core and 21.3 ms on three cores with unmodified Ultralytics weights, at 3.68 W whole-device power under continuous inference (USB power meter; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36862-y). The roughly 2x gap fits Rockchip's restructured YOLOv8 head (my inference), so the export recipe matters.

Measured idle and CPU-stress power at the wall (Jeff Geerling, https://sbc-reviews.jeffgeerling.com/): Orange Pi 5 1.0/10 W, Orange Pi 5 Max 1.4/10.9 W (12.8 W HPL), ROCK 5C 1.6/9.5 W, Radxa CM5 1.2/8.4 W, ROCK 5B 3.6/17 W. The RK3576 ROCK 4D measured 2.7 W idle and 7 W CPU stress (https://www.linuxlinks.com/radxa-rock-4d-single-board-computer-running-linux-power-consumption/2/). My estimate for the full robot autonomy load on an RK3588 board (detector + tracker/re-ID + ROS 2/Nav2 + OAK-D host + H.264 stream + ONNX MLP) is 6-9 W against the 31 W (25 + 6 W) Jetson budget. That is about 22-25 W less at the board and about 25-28 W less at the battery through the 0.88 converter. Board plus cooler mass is about 45-125 g against the 0.29 kg Jetson with tray (board masses from vendor pages, cooler masses estimated).

No board in this category has a published measured power figure for NPU inference except the unnamed RK3588 board in Sci. Rep. 2026 (3.4-4.2 W across nine YOLO models at 640). Every other 'typical inference' figure here is an estimate. The chosen board should be measured with the real workload (OAK-D attached, ROS 2/Nav2 running) before the runtime model is fixed.

Cross-platform YOLOv8n, same method (Au-Zone EdgeFirst, INT8 640x640, end-to-end preprocess-inference-postprocess; https://huggingface.co/EdgeFirst/yolov8-det): Jetson Orin Nano TensorRT INT8 23.3 ms / 282 FPS realized; Raspberry Pi 5 + Hailo-8L 19.8 ms / 65 FPS; i.MX 95 Neutron (EVK) 32.8 ms / 61.5 FPS latency mode, 80 FPS throughput mode; i.MX 8M Plus (FRDM) 78.9 ms / 13.1 FPS; NXP Ara240 M.2 card on FRDM 16.3 ms / 107 FPS. Rockchip is not in that suite. The Orin Nano keeps roughly 3-5x more detector throughput headroom than any SBC NPU here.

Toolkit maturity, my ranking. 1) Rockchip RKNN is the most mature: native Ultralytics export (format='rknn', FP16 or INT8 with calibration, x86 host only; https://docs.ultralytics.com/integrations/rockchip-rknn/); model zoo v2.5.0 with YOLOv5-v11 and YOLO26, pose, segmentation and speech (Whisper base RTF 0.196 on RK3588, zipformer streaming RTF 0.059, vendor; https://github.com/airockchip/rknn_model_zoo); used in production by Frigate and by PhotonVision on FRC robots (Orange Pi 5). 2) NXP eIQ: YOLOv8 runs on the i.MX 95 Neutron NPU per EdgeFirst, but YOLO11/YOLO26 are not yet supported and forum users report timeouts. 3) MediaTek NeuroPilot: vendor publishes YOLOv8s only, Ultralytics models are not supplied pre-converted, and the ONNX Runtime NPU EP exists only on Genio 520/720 (https://genio.mediatek.com/doc/iot-aihub/ai_hub/benchmark.html). 4) TI TIDL on BeagleY-AI: acceleration only on TI's Yocto Edge AI image, not BeagleBoard Debian (https://docs.beagleboard.org/boards/beagley/ai/demos/using-edge-ai.html), no published AM67A YOLOv8n figure, and TI E2E reports of TIDL hangs.

Mainline Linux on RK3588: GPU (6.10), CPU DVFS (6.11), PCIe/USB3 (6.7-6.10) and HDMI are upstream (Collabora, Dec 2024: https://www.collabora.com/news-and-blog/news-and-events/rockchip-rk3588-upstream-support-progress-future-plans.html). H.264/H.265 decoders and VICAP capture landed in early 2026, but the ISP is still not upstream (https://www.collabora.com/news-and-blog/news-and-events/mainline-video-capture-and-camera-support-for-rockchip-rk3588.html). The open Rocket NPU driver is in Linux 6.18 with Mesa 25.3 Teflon, RK3588 only (https://www.phoronix.com/news/Rockchip-NPU-Linux-Mesa); RK3576 NPU support is not merged (https://www.cnx-software.com/2026/07/15/reverse-engineering-brings-rk3576-npu-support-to-open-source-rocket-driver-for-mainline-linux/). In practice a robot build uses the Rockchip 6.1 BSP (Radxa OS, Orange Pi Ubuntu 22.04, Armbian vendor kernel) with RKNN, and ROS 2 Humble/Jazzy run on Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 arm64. The Ubuntu-Rockchip project was archived on 2026-04-29 (https://github.com/Joshua-Riek/ubuntu-rockchip/releases). The OAK-D is a USB camera, so the missing mainline ISP does not block the camera path.

Supply and price, November 2026: the 2026 DRAM shortage inflated SBC prices about 1.5-2.5x. CNX (April 2026): Orange Pi 5 Ultra 16 GB $125 to $309; ROCK 5B+ 8 GB $90 to $129.99 and sold out; Raspberry Pi 5 8 GB $80 to $175; Jetson Orin Nano dev kit sold out in most places (https://www.cnx-software.com/2026/04/28/what-a-difference-two-years-make-comparing-sbc-prices-in-2024-and-2026/). On 2026-11-07: most Radxa RK3588 boards are sold out at Arace and Ameridroid; Orange Pi boards are in stock on Amazon at $169-$367; FriendlyElec's NanoPC-T6 LTS, CM3588 and NanoPi M5 are in stock at FriendlyElec; BeagleY-AI is in stock at $70; NXP FRDM boards show 'Pending Stock'. Buy spares when the board is chosen.

Longevity: Radxa guarantees ROCK 5B/5B+/5T and CM5 until at least September 2032 and ROCK 4D until September 2034 (product briefs, e.g. https://dl.radxa.com/rock4/4d/docs/radxa_rock4d_product_brief.pdf). MediaTek lists Genio 1200 until 2032 and Genio 700 until 2034 (https://genio.mediatek.com/genio-700). NXP's longevity program covers the i.MX 95 for at least 10 years (https://www.nxp.com/products/i.MX95). Orange Pi, Khadas and FriendlyElec publish no end dates.

Interfaces and power integration. Every RK3588 board has at least one USB 3 port for the OAK-D. Radxa ROCK 5B+/5T share 2 A across their four USB-A ports (https://dl.radxa.com/rock5/5b+/docs/radxa_rock5bp_product_brief.pdf), so the OAK-D Pro W with its IR projector should get 5 V from a separate rail. NanoPC-T6 LTS (12 V DC), ROCK 5T (9-20 V DC), ROCK 5B+ (USB-C PD 9-20 V or fixed 5-20 V), NanoPi M5 (6-20 V) and CM3588 (5-20 V) accept a 12 V rail directly. Orange Pi boards (5 V/4-5 A), ROCK 5C/4D and BeagleY-AI (5 V/3 A) need a dedicated 5 V buck. RK3588 CAN-FD pins appear on Orange Pi and Radxa 40-pin headers without transceivers; NXP FRDM boards carry TJA1051 transceivers. The Teensy already owns the two leg CAN buses, so host CAN is optional.

RK3588 multi-core NPU: Sci. Rep. 2026 found that spreading one model over several cores cuts YOLO latency by under 10%, while running one context per core raises throughput (+48% in a Khadas Edge2 pipeline; https://news.lavx.hu/article/running-yolov8n-at-the-sensor-s-ceiling-a-140-mb-real-time-uav-detection-pipeline-on-cheap-rk3588s-boards). Suggested split: detector on core 0, re-ID embedding on core 1, voice or spare on core 2. A third-party report claims 199 FPS YOLOv8n at 640 on all three cores with a zero-copy MPP/RGA pipeline; its scope (inference only or end-to-end) is not stated (https://github.com/airockchip/rknn_model_zoo/issues/454).

Hardware video encode for the operator web stream exists on every option here. RK3588/RK3588S: H.264/H.265 up to 8K30. RK3576: 4K60. AM67A: 4K60. Genio 1200: 4K60. Genio 700: 4K30. i.MX 95: 4Kp30. i.MX 8M Plus: 1080p60. QCS6490: 4K30. The Jetson Orin Nano has no hardware video encoder.

Missing data. No YOLOv8n benchmark was found for TI AM67A, Qualcomm QCS6490 boards, CIX P1, or RK3576 from a third party. MediaTek publishes YOLOv8s only (INT8 640, NPU only: Genio 510 24.0 ms, 700 17.0 ms, 1200 28.4 ms, 520 9.02 ms, 720 8.04 ms; https://genio.mediatek.com/doc/iot-aihub/ai_hub/benchmark.html). No person re-ID network benchmark was found for any board in this category. Rockchip vendor YOLO11n: 64.0 FPS on RK3588 and 87.5 FPS on RK3576 (single core, inference only).

Other boards seen but not detailed: Orange Pi 5 Pro (RK3588S, 89x56 mm, 62 g, 1x USB 3.1, 8 GB $203.99 on Amazon), Orange Pi CM5 module (12 g, 4 GB/32 GB $174.99), Radxa ROCK 5A (4 GB $154.95 at Ameridroid, in stock), FriendlyElec NanoPi M6 (Ameridroid 8 GB kit $274.95), and Orange Pi 4 Pro (Allwinner A733, 3 TOPS, 4 GB $65.99), whose NPU toolkit was not assessed. DEBIX Model A (i.MX 8M Plus) is listed at $145.99-$299 by its vendor according to search results; the vendor page could not be loaded on 2026-11-07. Radxa Dragon Q8B is on pre-order (ships 2026-11-15, 8 GB $209) and Geerling measured 4.9 W idle and 20.9 W stress.

Sizing, my assessment. For 60-75 cm, a compact RK3588 board (Orange Pi 5 Max, ROCK 5C, or a Radxa CM5/CM3588 custom carrier) covers detection and tracking, depth-based local navigation, the ONNX MLP and H.264 streaming at about 6-8 W and under 100 g. For 100-120 cm, the NanoPC-T6 LTS (in stock, 12 V input) or ROCK 5T/5B+ (9-20 V input, dual CSI) fit. Keeping the Jetson there is defensible only if heavier models (pose, segmentation, larger detectors, on-device LLM) are planned, since the 3-5x detector headroom costs about 20 W.

Research limit: the web search budget for this run was used up near the end. Measured power for NanoPC-T6, ROCK 5T, ROCK 5B+, Orange Pi 5 Plus and Khadas Edge2, the ROCK 4D and FRDM board dimensions, and QCS6490/AM67A YOLOv8n benchmarks were not searched further; the values given for them are labelled estimates.
open_questions: Should the person detector run on the OAK-D's own Myriad X instead (smart-camera route)? Then the host NPU would carry only re-ID, tracking and voice, and a lower-power board (RK3576 or RK3588S) would be enough.
Is a Rockchip vendor BSP kernel (Linux 6.1) acceptable for the robot's service life, given that the mainline ISP and RK3576 NPU support are still missing?

Are heavier perception models planned (pose, segmentation, larger detectors, an on-device LLM for voice)? If so, the Jetson's 3-5x detector headroom may justify its roughly 20 W power penalty at 100-120 cm.
Should the 50-100 Hz locomotion MLP run on the host's A76 cores (under 1 ms per step, my estimate, but not hard real-time) or on the Teensy 4.1 for deterministic timing?
Should the OAK-D Pro W draw its power from a dedicated 5 V rail (Y-cable), given the 2 A shared USB budget on Radxa ROCK 5B+/5T?
Accept current stock-outs and RAM-inflated prices, and buy spares of the chosen board now (FriendlyElec and Orange Pi in stock, most Radxa RK3588 boards sold out)?
Which board should be bench-measured first? Whole-set power with the real workload is estimated at 6-9 W, but no board here has a published measurement under a robot-like load.

Models need INT8 (w8a8) quantization and static shapes, and the runtime is version-locked: AI Hub artifacts built with QAIRT 2.45 failed on the board's 2.42 runtime (forum, May-Jun 2026).

options.fit_notes: The best low-power fit for 60-75 cm in this category. It can carry person detection (YOLOv8n/YOLO11n 640 INT8 at 3.6-4.1 ms model-only, about 10 ms in a real ORT pipeline), tracking, OAK-D depth post-processing and local planning on the CPU, plus the 50-100 Hz ONNX MLP policy (trivial on the A78 cores; estimate). Whole-board draw is 3-10 W measured, against the Jetson budget of 31 W before the converter (about 35 W at the battery), so it saves roughly 25 W at the battery (derived). Risks: a single USB 3 port; four big cores with a 2 MB L3 may be tight for Nav2 plus lidar SLAM at 100-120 cm; no QCS6490 re-ID benchmark found; Qualcomm toolchain version lock; no official cooler (94 C in a CPU benchmark); volatile price and stock.

options.fit_notes: The smallest x86 board here (a Pi-like 88x70 mm) with three USB 3 ports and an RP2040 for low-level I/O. On its own it is marginal: an N100-class iGPU runs YOLO11n INT8 at about 21 fps, and the N150 iGPU needs 16 ms for YOLOv9-t at 320 px, before any ROS 2 navigation load. So either run detection at 320-416 px or add an M.2 accelerator (see lattepanda_iota_n150_plus_hailo8). Capping the RAPL limits bounds the draw (4 W idle to 20 W bursts measured). Risks: a single PCIe 3.0 x1 lane for any accelerator, a loud fan under load, and stock and price.

category_findings: Measured whole-board power (third party). Radxa Dragon Q6A (QCS6490): 2.9 W idle, 9.3 W stress-ng and 10.1 W HPL at the wall (https://github.com/geerlingguy/sbc-reviews/issues/85), 10.17 W peak with peripherals and a fan (https://sbcwiki.com/news/articles/radxa-dragon-q6a-full-review). LattePanda IOTA (N150): about 4 W idle and 15-20 W under CPU load at the default 10/20 W limits (https://ounapuu.ee/posts/2025/11/18/lattepanda-iota/, https://boilingsteam.com/lattepanda-iota-sbc-review/). LattePanda Mu (N100, limits removed): 5.5 W idle, 22-25 W under load (https://github.com/geerlingguy/sbc-reviews/issues/42). ASUS NUC 14 Essential (Core 3 N355): 5.4 W idle average, 29.2 W load average, 50.5 W peak (https://www.notebookcheck.net/Asus-NUC-14-Essential-review-An-efficient-mini-PC-as-a-desktop-replacement-that-s-useful-for-everyday-use-and-at-the-office.943361.0.html). ASUS NUC 14 Pro (Core Ultra 5 125H, 64 W limits): 6.4 W idle average, 55.5 W load average, 103.3 W peak (https://www.notebookcheck.net/Asus-NUC-14-Pro-review-NUC-mini-PC-with-Intel-Core-Ultra-5-125H-fast-Intel-Arc-iGPU-and-2x-Thunderbolt-4.881404.0.html).

Against the Jetson budget in the brief (25 W module + 6 W carrier = 31 W, about 35 W at the battery through the 0.88 converter): a QCS6490 board at 3-10 W measured saves roughly 25 W at the battery. An N150 board with a Hailo-8 saves roughly 25 W at typical load (estimate). A Lunar Lake module saves roughly 15-20 W (estimate). Meteor Lake H mini PCs at default limits can draw more than the Jetson. At 60 cm, where walking draws about 96 W, a 25 W saving is about a quarter of the electrical load (derived).

Person-detector speed, Qualcomm. Vendor figures from AI Hub (model-only, w8a8 TFLite, 640x640): YOLOv8n / YOLO11n take 3.6 / 4.1 ms on QCS6490, 1.4 / 1.7 ms on IQ-8275, 1.5 / 1.8 ms on IQ-9075 and 1.3 / 1.6 ms on the QCS8550 proxy (https://huggingface.co/qualcomm/YOLOv8-Detection, https://huggingface.co/qualcomm/YOLOv11-Detection). In a real ONNX Runtime QNN pipeline on the Dragon Q6A, YOLOv8n at 640 INT8 took about 10 ms (https://forum.radxa.com/t/running-custom-frigate-with-full-npu-support-dragon-q6a/31047).

Person-detector speed, Intel OpenVINO. N100: YOLO11n INT8 at about 21 fps on the iGPU and 10 fps on the CPU (vendor blog, https://www.lattepanda.com/blog-323240.html). N150 iGPU: YOLOv9-t at 320 px in 16 ms (https://docs.frigate.video/frigate/hardware). YOLO26n with OpenVINO 2026.2.1 (https://docs.ultralytics.com/integrations/openvino/): Core Ultra 7 155H 5.8 ms iGPU / 11.4 ms CPU; Core Ultra 7 258V 3.3 ms iGPU / 23.7 ms NPU / 8.6 ms CPU; Core Ultra X7 358H 4.0 ms iGPU / 7.7 ms NPU / 10.0 ms CPU. N-series iGPUs on their own are marginal for 640 px detection at 30 fps with navigation running; the QCS6490 NPU and Core Ultra iGPUs handle it comfortably.

M.2 accelerator power, measured in 2026 by one independent tester (Mario Bergeron; INA228 or on-module sensor on the 3.3 V rail; ResNet-50 at saturation; AMD Strix Halo host). Hailo-8: 4.0 W at 1371 fps, idle 0.51 W with ASPM L1 or 0.84 W without. DeepX DX-M1: 4.7 W at 1009 fps, idle 0.74 / 1.04 W. Axelera Metis M.2: 7.6 W at 2050 fps, idle 2.9-3.1 W with ASPM off. MemryX MX3: 11.0 W at 1796 fps in the default 14 TFLOPS mode and 20.2 W at 20 TFLOPS (throttles), idle 1.3-1.9 W. Sources: https://www.hackster.io/AlbertaBeef/edge-ai-power-benchmarking-part-1-hailo-8-the-reference-ee73df, https://mariobergeron.com/posts/edge-ai-power-p04-axelera-metis/, https://mariobergeron.com/posts/edge-ai-power-p05-deepx-m1/, https://mariobergeron.com/posts/edge-ai-power-p06-memryx-mx3. Vendor FPS/W figures count NPU silicon only, without PCIe or LPDDR. One 30 fps camera stream uses a small fraction of any of these modules, so idle power decides: Hailo-8 and DX-M1 should add about 1-1.5 W, Metis about 3.5 W, and MX3 several watts (estimates).

YOLO throughput at 640x640 (vendor figures). Hailo-8: YOLOv8n reaches 1036 fps even at batch 1, but YOLO11n and YOLO26n drop to 185 and 154 fps at batch 1 (541 and 427 at batch 8), so model choice matters on Hailo-8. Hailo-10H: YOLOv8n 378, YOLO11n 309 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hailo-ai/hailo_model_zoo/master/docs/public_models/HAILO8/HAILO8_object_detection.rst). Axelera Metis M.2: YOLOv8n 771-774, YOLO11n 574-724, YOLO26n 485-628 (https://docs.ultralytics.com/integrations/axelera, https://docs.axelera.ai/sdk/reference/models/model-zoo/). MemryX MX3: YOLOv8n 328 (417 at 20 TFLOPS), YOLO11n 212 (325 MXA-optimized) (https://developer.memryx.com/model_explorer/models.html). DeepX lists YOLOv8m at 135 fps with 2.76 W NPU power (https://deepx.ai/?p=2523), but no verifiable YOLOv8n or YOLO11n figure was found. Every module exceeds a 30 fps need by more than 5x, so choose on idle power, toolchain, host fit and supply.

Re-identification, needed for reacquisition without silent target switching. Vendor numbers exist only for Axelera (OSNet x1_0 at 256x128, 1673 fps on M.2, https://docs.axelera.ai/sdk/reference/models/model-zoo/) and Hailo (OSNet x1_0 at 215 fps batch 1 on Hailo-8 and 292 on Hailo-10H; RepVGG-A0 re-ID at 5204 fps on Hailo-8, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hailo-ai/hailo_model_zoo/master/docs/public_models/HAILO8/HAILO8_person_re_id.rst). No re-ID benchmark was found for QCS6490, IQ8 or IQ9, for Intel CPU, iGPU or NPU, or for MemryX or DeepX, so none is given.

New in 2026: Arduino VENTUNO Q (IQ-8275, 40 dense TOPS, 16 GB, STM32H5 with CAN-FD; $399 since 19 Oct 2026, pre-order; https://store-usa.arduino.cc/products/ventuno-q); Radxa AIRbox Q900 (IQ-9075, 36 GB, under 20 W per the vendor, $599; https://www.cnx-software.com/2025/09/30/fogwise-airbox-q900-599-qualcomm-iq-9075-ai-box-delivers-up-to-200-tops-of-ai-performance/); LattePanda Mu Ultra (Lunar Lake, $643 kit, Sept 2026) and Sigma 2 (Panther Lake X7 358H, $2,599 pre-order); Radxa Dragon Q8B (Snapdragon 8cx Gen 3, 29+ TOPS, 100x75 mm, $209 for 8 GB, early-stage software; https://liliputing.com/radxa-dragon-q8b-is-a-single-board-pc-with-snapdragon-8cx-gen-3-pcie-3-0-and-dual-2-5-gbe-lan/, https://hackaday.com/2026/10/10/poking-at-the-radxa-dragon-q8b-raspberry-pi-5-killer/). None of the IQ8, IQ9, Mu Ultra or Sigma 2 has an independent power measurement yet.

QCS8550-class: only dev kits were found, such as the Lantronix Open-Q 8550CS kit ($1,500 on a 200x170 mm carrier with Android 13 or Yocto; SOM from $547.60; https://estore.lantronix.com/products/open-q-8550-development-kit). IQ-8275 and IQ-9075 products give similar AI Hub YOLO latency (1.4-1.8 ms against 1.3-1.6 ms) and come with Ubuntu and ROS 2 support, so they replace QCS8550 for this robot.

Toolchain effort and ROS 2, lowest effort first. (1) x86 with OpenVINO: Ubuntu 22.04/24.04, ROS 2 amd64 binaries, pip install, Ultralytics export format=openvino. (2) Hailo: precompiled HEFs, with the Dataflow Compiler and calibration for custom models; Hailo-8 and Hailo-10H use different compiler generations (DFC 2.20 vs 5.5). (3) MemryX: compiles unmodified ONNX and TFLite models (SDK 2.2). (4) Axelera Voyager 1.9: Linux only, INT8 with 100-400 calibration images. (5) DeepX: the DX-COM compiler runs only on x86-64 Linux, INT8. (6) Qualcomm QAIRT / AI Hub: INT8 w8a8, static shapes, and an artifact/runtime version lock seen on the Dragon Q6A. On the Qualcomm side, ROS 2 is best supported on RB3 Gen 2 and IQ-9075 through the QIR SDK (ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04, https://docs.qualcomm.com/doc/80-90441-2/topic/1-introduction.html). This survey found no accelerator vendor that ships a ROS 2 node.

Supply voltage: almost every option still needs the DC-DC converter. Dragon Q6A and RUBIK Pi 3 take USB-C PD (RUBIK at 12 V 3 A); IOTA takes 15 V PD or 10-15 V DC; Mu Ultra 12-20 V; Sigma 2 15-20 V; AIRbox Q900 12 V. VENTUNO Q accepts 12-24 V on its jack and 7-24 V on its terminal, but a fully charged 6S pack (25.2 V) is above 24 V. Only the UP Xtreme i14 (9-36 V) could run straight from 6S, and not from 12S. Sources are listed in each option.

Video encode for the operator page: QCS6490 encodes H.264/H.265 at 4K30, IQ-8275 at 4K 85 fps, IQ-9075 at 2x 4Kp60. Intel N100, N150 and N355 (ADL-N family in Intel's media driver) encode H.264 and HEVC but only decode AV1; Meteor Lake, Lunar Lake and Panther Lake add AV1 encode (https://github.com/intel/media-driver). The M.2 accelerators have no encoder.

Prices are volatile in 2026 and mostly rising with memory costs. LattePanda IOTA 8 GB is $339 (CNX's review configuration was $166.80 in Nov 2025). The Mu N100 module is $359 (Geerling paid $139 in 2024). RB3 Gen 2 Core Kit is $439 (launch $399) and the Vision Kit $750 (launch $599). VENTUNO Q is $399 (launch $299, raised citing memory costs; https://esp32.co.uk/?p=20261017025). The Dragon Q6A is $249.95 at ameriDroid (launch about $62-124). Sources are listed in each option.

The 50-100 Hz locomotion MLP is a negligible load for any CPU in this category (estimate; no benchmark was sought). Linux scheduling jitter is the real risk, and the deterministic loop stays on the Teensy.

Low-confidence data point: a hobby project on an Advantech ASR-D501 (QCS6490) reports about 7.6 W whole board while running YOLOv8n on the NPU, against 5.8 W idle, without stating a method (https://github.com/Holo911/Drone).

Fit summary for this category. At 60-75 cm: a QCS6490 SBC (Dragon Q6A for size and power; RB3 Gen 2 for the documented ROS 2 SDK), or an N150 board plus a Hailo-8 M.2 if x86 software is preferred. At 100-120 cm, where price is not a constraint: the IQ-9075 box or VENTUNO Q on the Qualcomm side, or Lunar Lake (Mu Ultra) or Panther Lake (Sigma 2) on x86, optionally with a Hailo-8 or Axelera for heavy re-ID. Avoid Meteor Lake H mini PCs at default limits, the UP 7000 (no M.2) and QCS8550 dev kits.
open_questions: No independent power measurement was found for IQ-8275 (VENTUNO Q), IQ-9075 (AIRbox Q900), the Lunar Lake Mu Ultra, the Panther Lake Sigma 2, UP Xtreme i14, UP 7000, RUBIK Pi 3 or RB3 Gen 2. Measure at the DC input with the real pipeline (OAK-D streaming, detector, tracker, Nav2) before committing.

All M.2 accelerator power figures are at saturation (ResNet-50). No partial-load figure was found for a single 30 fps YOLO stream. The Hailo-8 exposes an on-module power sensor through HailoRT, so it can be measured directly.

No verifiable DeepX DX-M1 YOLOv8n or YOLO11n fps was found, and DeepX's tables disagree between versions. Ultralytics' YOLO26n result on a Raspberry Pi 5 host (34.6 ms) is slow next to a Hailo-8 on a Pi 5 in a separate test (9.8 ms model-only). Benchmark on the intended host.
No QCS6490, IQ8, IQ9 or Intel re-ID (OSNet-class) benchmark was found. Check Qualcomm AI Hub and OpenVINO for one before relying on those platforms for reacquisition.
Can the OAK-D Lite or OAK-D Pro W run the person detector on its own Myriad X? That would shrink the host NPU requirement. This is outside this category; check Luxonis RVC2 benchmarks.

Board masses are not published for the Dragon Q6A, RUBIK Pi 3, RB3 Gen 2, AIRbox Q900, UP Xtreme i14, Sigma 2 or the Mu Ultra kit, nor for M.2 modules with coolers; the masses given are estimates. The VENTUNO Q store weight (0.49 kg) may include packaging.
Current prices for the UP 7000 and UP Xtreme i14 could not be verified because AAEON pages refused automated access. The AIRbox Q900's $599 is its 2025 launch price.

Mechanical and electrical fit to check: the Axelera Metis M.2 is 25 mm wide and 25.8 mm tall with its cooler; MemryX MX3 operation in a x1 slot is unverified; and it is unverified whether the LattePanda IOTA M-key expansion board can supply a module rated up to 8.25 W.
No Intel Open Model Zoo person-detection-0200/0201/0202 speeds were found for N150 or Core Ultra; only YOLO-family and MobileNet numbers are given.

The web-search budget for this sub-task ran out before the LattePanda IOTA M.2 expansion-board price, the Hailo-8 module mass and current AAEON prices were found. A follow-up search could fill these gaps.

Rockchip RK3588 / RK3576 SBCs (e.g. Radxa ROCK 5B+/5T, Orange Pi 5 Plus/Max, Radxa ROCK 4D; 6 TOPS NPU via RKNN, Ubuntu with ROS 2). IMX214 13 MP rolling-shutter colour camera: 69 deg HFOV; focus 8 cm to infinity (AF) or 50 cm to infinity (FF). Two OV7251 640x480 global-shutter mono cameras: 73 deg HFOV / 86 deg DFOV, 7.5 cm baseline. Passive stereo (no IR projector), BMI270 IMU, USB-C. The price covers the camera only; the OAK Y-adapter (+$24, for a separate 5 V feed) and a USB 3 cable (+$14) cost extra. Depth per the 2023 spec sheet: ideal 40 cm-6 m; MinZ ~20 cm (480P, extended disparity) or ~35 cm (480P); MaxZ ~10 m at 10% variance. The current docs page lists ~80 cm-12 m with 800P figures that look copied from OAK-D, since this camera's mono sensors are 480P.
options.cpu: Two Leon cores inside the Myriad X run the device firmware and the Script node only. The application runs on the host; the host uploads the pipeline to the camera.
options.ai_accelerator: Myriad X (RVC2): 16 SHAVE vector cores and 2 neural compute engines. FP16 only: Luxonis staff say an INT8 conversion request is ignored on RVC2. Also has a hardware stereo engine, warp engines and an H.264/H.265/MJPEG encoder. With the cameras running, about 13 of the 16 SHAVEs are free for networks.

options.power_basis: Third-party measured: 3.25-3.5 W (650-700 mA at 5 V) at the camera, fed from a separate 5.1 V supply, while depthai-ros published RGB, MobileNet detections and stereo depth (Feb 2024). A USB meter read 5 W max while the camera ran YOLOv4. Vendor spec sheet: 0.6 W standby, 4 W running depthai_demo, 4.5 W max, with occasional 2 W spikes from the encoder or network. Vendor docs: 2.5-3 W base plus camera streaming, AI up to 1 W, stereo up to 0.5 W, encoder up to 0.5 W, up to ~5 W with every feature at 100%. Integrator budget (TurtleBot 4): 3.5 W nominal, 5 W max.
options.interfaces: USB-C, USB 2/3 up to 10 Gbps; 5 V bus power, no barrel jack (the spec sheet notes 900 mA from USB and that a Raspberry Pi may not supply the current spikes). BMI270 6-axis IMU (Kickstarter units have none). No GPIO, CAN, I2C or Ethernet, so the VL53L5CX ToF pair, the lidar and the CAN buses stay on the Teensy or host. A Pi 5 limits total USB current to 600 mA with a 3 A supply (1.6 A with a 5 A supply), which can brown out the camera; feed it 5 V through the Y-adapter.
options.video_encode: On-device H.264, H.265 and MJPEG up to 4K30 or 1080p60 (vendor).
options.software: DepthAI v3 (Python and C++) runs on the host: Linux, macOS or Windows, including ARM64 boards such as Raspberry Pi and Jetson. ROS 2 via depthai-ros (v3 packages for Humble/Jazzy; default on Kilted). Models come from the Luxonis model zoo or HubAI conversion (ONNX/PyTorch to an RVC2 FP16 blob); converting a network takes an export step. YOLO decoding, SpatialDetectionNetwork (XYZ per detection) and ObjectTracker run on the device. The PointCloud node runs on the host only for RVC2. Host requirements: a USB3 port with a host that runs the DepthAI library; there is no standalone operation on this USB camera. Known issue: a DepthAI v3 firmware crash on the OV7251 mono cameras of some units was fixed in DepthAI 3.11.0 (Oct 2026).
options.availability: Orderable from Luxonis: the shop shows Add to Cart, and its page data listed about 87 AF and 194 FF units on 2026-11-07. Intel ended Myriad X manufacturing in 2025. Luxonis placed end-of-life buys that it says cover all expected demand and warranty for five years (post of 2025-01-23). A Luxonis notice raised the price from $169 to $269 from 2026-07-09, citing a finite Myriad X supply. SparkFun and Botland list it as retired or discontinued in their own catalogues. Plan on supply to about 2030, not indefinitely.

options.fit_notes: What runs on the camera: stereo depth (480P); person detection; a 3D position per detection (SpatialDetectionNetwork); an imageless multi-object tracker with 3D velocity but no appearance re-ID; optionally an OSNet re-ID crop network (49 inferences/s network-only, sharing the SHAVEs); and H.264/H.265 encoding of the operator video. Realistic detection rates are YOLOv6n 512x288 at ~35 fps for the whole pipeline; YOLOv8n/YOLO11n at 640x640 only reach 7-14 fps. What stays on the host: target lock and the re-ID gallery behind the no-silent-switch rule, point clouds and the costmap (PointCloud is host-only on RVC2), ToF and lidar fusion, navigation, ROS 2, the web relay, the locomotion MLP and voice. With that split, a Raspberry Pi 5-class host is enough for perception. A third party measured OAK-D Lite plus Pi 5 (depthai-ros publishing RGB, MobileNet and depth) at 9.5 W average and 10.1 W max, with the Pi's load average about 2 of 4 cores; the full navigation and following stack was not measured. At 61 g it suits the 60-75 cm head. Risks: (1) Passive stereo on 640x480 sensors (ideal 0.4-6 m) is weak on textureless floor; the ToF pair covers the near field. (2) Use the fixed-focus variant on a vibrating mount, as Luxonis advises. (3) Powered from a Pi 5 USB port it browns out; feed 5 V through the Y-adapter. (4) Myriad X supply is finite (five-year Luxonis stock bought in 2025; price now $269). (5) Run DepthAI 3.11.0 or later.

options.fit_notes: The workload split is the same as for OAK-D Lite: detection at ~35 fps (YOLOv6n 512x288, whole pipeline), with a user measuring YOLOv6n 640x640 at 23-24 fps on an OAK-D Pro with 1080p colour running; tracker without re-ID; OSNet at 49 inferences/s; on-device H.264/H.265; point clouds on the host. So a Pi 5-class host is enough for perception at 100-120 cm as well. It adds what the larger robots need: a dot projector for depth on textureless floor, flood IR for dark rooms (networks must then use the mono streams), and 1280x800 global-shutter stereo with 127 deg HFOV. The wide FOV puts fewer pixels on a person at range, so detection at 5-10 m needs higher input resolution or crops. The IMX378 colour sensor is rolling shutter on a walking robot, and the global-shutter OV9782 variant is backordered. Power is 5 W nominal and about 7.5 W with IR at 100%. The 91 g is small against a head+neck allowance of 1.5-2.75 kg at these sizes (estimate from REFERENCE.md). If the lidar and ToF make IR unnecessary, the OAK-D W is $100 cheaper. Same Myriad X lifecycle caveat as OAK-D Lite.

USB-C needs 25 W PD for nominal performance; 15 W gives a reduced mode (Luxonis staff: without PD it is limited to 15 W). PoE+ 802.3at gives nominal performance, 802.3af reduced. Network-only whole-board power in model-zoo runs is 2.7-3.4 W for YOLOv6n 512x288. M8 8-pin aux: 5 V GPIO or UART, FSYNC/strobe, a USB 2.0 host (not usable together with USB-C) and a 5 V 5 W output. 9-axis IMU. options.software: Luxonis OS (Linux) with DepthAI v3. OAK Apps are containers based on the Debian 12-based oakapp-base image; oakctl or Luxonis Hub builds and runs them on the camera, and pip packages can be installed. ROS 2 Kilted runs onboard (depthai-ros v3.2.1; Humble/Jazzy hosts use the _v3 packages). Models are converted with HubAI (ONNX, PyTorch or TF to INT8/FP16). The PointCloud node can run on the device on RVC4. Host requirements: none in standalone mode; otherwise an Ethernet (or alpha USB) peer. The software moves fast: DepthAI 3.12.0 (2026-11-06) more than doubled RVC4 NeuralDepth throughput, and a forum thread reports an RVC4 ImageManip crash in DepthAI 3.10.
options.availability: Orderable. The shop page data on 2026-11-07 showed AF 195, FF 67 and Wide 287 units. Prices include a temporary +$200 surcharge since 2026-07-30, attributed to memory and storage markets; the launch price was $849 (Dec 2025). The QCS8550 is in Qualcomm's longevity programme to April 2033. Passed IEC 60068 climate tests and ISO 19014 level 3 vibration with 30 g shock (vendor test, Dec 2025).

options.fit_notes: It can be the whole high-level computer. On the device it runs person detection (YOLOv6n at ~800 inferences/s network-only), OSNet re-ID (571/s), stereo depth with on-device point clouds, tracking, H.264/H.265 4K encoding, and ROS 2 Kilted plus custom container apps on the CPU. It also has a 3-microphone array for the voice stretch goal. Luxonis showed an OAK4-D as the only computer on a Create 3 doing ROS 2 person following (Feb 2026). The locomotion MLP could run on its CPU but has not been benchmarked there; my estimate is that the compute is trivial and the concern is latency and jitter to the Teensy over Ethernet. Problems for this robot: (1) 674 g and 143.5x42.5x67.3 mm in the head. That is more than the whole head+neck allowance at 60 cm (5.0-5.5% of 11 kg = 0.55-0.61 kg, from REFERENCE.md; estimate), about 75-85% of it at 75 cm, ~40-45% at 100 cm and ~25-30% at 120 cm. (2) 10-15 W maximum average (25 W peak) of heat in the head. (3) Power needs a 24 V-to-PoE+ injector or a 25 W USB-PD source. (4) USB was alpha in 2026, so Ethernet is the main link. (5) $1049, against $638 for today's Jetson, integration and OAK-D Lite. Net against Jetson plus OAK-D Lite: roughly 16-24 W less at the load (estimate), with 323 g more mass, all of it moved into the head. With no IR, textureless floor relies on the ToF and lidar. Pick fixed focus on a vibrating mount.

options.fit_notes: This is the most packageable way to put RVC4 in the head. A 36 g board (Q1 2027), or the 215 g Dev Kit available now, drives a custom stereo pair and a colour module through flex cables. Like OAK 4 D, it runs the whole perception, ROS 2 and app stack on the board, and it takes 6S battery voltage directly (6-32 V DC; a 12S pack needs a step-down). Because it has CAN FD, I2C, SPI, UART and GPIO, the VL53L5CX pair and the STL-19P lidar could connect to it directly, and it could exchange commands with the Teensy over CAN FD while the Teensy keeps ownership of the leg buses. Luxonis's own robot head ran 30 cm FFC cables to cameras on a pan-tilt head, so the board can sit in the skull or in the upper neck. The integrator is responsible for cooling 10-15 W, for stereo calibration, for sealing and for EMI. Module and heatsink prices were not found. The Barebone schedule (Q1 2027) is a risk. If it works out, it could replace both the head camera and the Jetson for an estimated 16-24 W saving at the load and far less head mass than the OAK 4 D.

options.fit_notes: Comparison only, and only with a Jetson. GMSL2 needs a ZED Link card on a Jetson, and depth is itself a network on the Jetson GPU: per Stereolabs, NEURAL_LIGHT uses 36% and NEURAL 88% of an Orin Nano 8 GB GPU at 30 fps. That competes with person detection for the same GPU. category_findings: Main result: an RVC2 OAK already carries most of the perception load on the camera. That covers stereo depth, a person detector, a 3D position per detection, an imageless multi-object tracker, and H.264/H.265 encoding of the operator video. The host is left with target-lock and re-ID logic, the costmap and navigation, ROS 2, the web relay and the policy. Third-party evidence that a Raspberry Pi 5-class host can handle this split: OAK-D Lite plus Pi 5 running depthai-ros (RGB, MobileNet detections and depth) drew 9.5 W average and 10.1 W max at the Pi's USB-C input, with a Pi load average of about 2 of 4 cores (https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/3459-can-oak-d-lite-crash-a-raspberry-pi-5). Against the Jetson's 31 W budget that is about 21-25 W less at the load, or about 24-28 W at the battery through the 0.88 converter. That is roughly 25% of the 96 W walking power at 60 cm and 12-16% at 100-120 cm (estimates). The full navigation, following and streaming stack on a Pi 5 has not been measured; the same poster reports a fully loaded Pi 5 at about 7 W.

Real RVC2 detector rates are well below the headline table. The cameras and ISP leave only about 13 of the 16 SHAVEs for networks (Luxonis staff, https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/3129-yolov6n-benchmarks). Luxonis staff measured whole pipelines on an RVC2 OAK-D at about 35 fps for YOLOv6n 512x288, 17 fps for YOLOv8n 512x288, 12 fps for YOLOv6n 640x640 and 7 fps for YOLOv8n 640x640 (Jan 2026, https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/6590). A user measured 23-24 fps for YOLOv6n 640x640 with 1080p colour running on an OAK-D Pro. RVC2 runs FP16 only. For person following on OAK-D Lite or Pro W, YOLOv6n at 512x288 or 416x416 is the practical detector; YOLOv8n and YOLO11n at 640x640 run at only 7-14 fps.

Preventing silent target switches and reacquiring a lost target both need appearance re-ID, which the DepthAI ObjectTracker lacks. It associates by bounding box and motion (SHORT_TERM_IMAGELESS), with optional 3D spatial association and velocity output in m/s (https://docs.luxonis.com/software-v3/depthai/depthai-components/nodes/object_tracker/). OSNet re-ID at 128x256 benchmarks at 49 inferences/s on RVC2 and 571/s on RVC4, network only (https://models.luxonis.com/luxonis/osnet/aim_56shrgyoKdoJrz1Wu8qKWV?backTo=%2F). No benchmark of detector, re-ID and stereo running together on RVC2 was found, so the per-person re-ID budget on OAK-D Lite or Pro W has to be bench-tested. The identity-gallery and lock state machine belongs on the host in every option except the RVC4 standalone ones.

Myriad X lifecycle: Intel stopped manufacturing Myriad X in 2025. Luxonis placed end-of-life buys that it says cover five years of Series 1/2 demand (https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/5747-update-on-our-oak-series-2-supply-chain). On 2026-07-09 it raised the OAK-D Lite from $169 to $269, citing finite Myriad X supply. Both cameras are still orderable today: OAK-D Lite at $269 and OAK-D Pro W at $529. RVC2 is fine for prototypes and a small fleet through about 2030; RVC4 is Luxonis's forward platform, and its QCS8550 SoC is in Qualcomm's longevity programme to April 2033.

RVC4 can replace the Jetson outright. Luxonis demonstrated an OAK4-D as the only computer on an iRobot Create 3 running ROS 2 person following onboard (https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/6695-running-ros2-onboard-oak4-d). RVC4 provides a 48 INT8 TOPS NPU, 8 GB RAM, on-device point clouds and H.264/H.265 4K encoding, at 1.6 W idle, 10-15 W maximum average and 25 W peak (https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/platform/rvc/rvc4). The packaged OAK 4 D and D Pro, however, weigh 674 g and measure 143.5x42.5x67.3 mm. That exceeds the whole 60 cm head+neck allowance (5.0-5.5% of 11 kg = 0.55-0.61 kg, from /home/user/mesozoic-labs/hardware/trex_form_study/REFERENCE.md; estimate) and is about 25-45% of it at 100-120 cm. They need PoE+ or 25 W USB-PD power. They cost $1049-1249, which includes a temporary $200 surcharge since 2026-07-30 (https://shop.luxonis.com/pages/temporary-surcharge-oak-4-line).

For the head, the OAK 4 FFC is the better-packaged RVC4 option. The barebone board is 36 g and 70x53 mm; the dev kit, with heatsink, is 215 g. It has 5 MIPI camera ports for a custom stereo pair plus colour, takes 6-32 V DC (so a 6S pack connects directly), and has CAN FD, I2C, SPI, UART, USB-C and 2.5 GbE. The Dev Kit ($849) ships now; the Barebone ($730) ships Q1 2027 (https://www.luxonis.com/oak4-ffc, https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/platform/deploy/oak4-ffc-getting-started). Luxonis's own OAK4 FFC robot head ran detection, stereo and the app on the board, using 30 cm FFC cables to cameras on a moving head (https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/7078). Cooling for 10-15 W and stereo calibration are the integrator's job.

Video for the operator page is a hidden host cost that only the OAKs remove. The Raspberry Pi 5 has no hardware H.264 encoder; software 1080p30 uses as little as about 60% CPU, per a Raspberry Pi white paper (https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/685-app-notes-guides-whitepapers/documents/RP-010033-WP-1-H.264%20encoding%20performance%20on%20Raspberry%20Pi%205_series%20computers.pdf). The Orin Nano also lists video encode as '1080p30 supported by 1-2 CPU cores' (https://www.stereolabs.com/en-us/store/products/zed-box-mini). The OAK's on-camera encoder (RVC2 4K30 or 1080p60; RVC4 4K120) removes this load from either host. The IMX500 camera and the depth-only cameras have no encoder.

RVC2 hosts still generate the point clouds. DepthAI v3's PointCloud node runs on the host for RVC2 and can run on the device only for RVC4 (https://docs.luxonis.com/software-v3/depthai/depthai-components/nodes/pointcloud/). A Jetson Xavier NX user reported about 50% CPU generating 25 Hz clouds from depthai-ros (https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/1284). On a Pi-class host, decimate the depth image or build the costmap directly from it, and fuse the VL53L5CX pair and the STL-19P lidar there.

Power and wiring: RVC2 OAKs draw up to 5 W (Lite) or about 7.5 W (Pro W with IR at full) from 5 V USB. A Pi 5 limits total USB current to 600 mA with a 3 A supply (1.6 A with 5 A), and that has browned out an OAK-D Lite under load. Feed the camera from the robot's 5 V rail through a Y-adapter (https://github.com/iRobotEducation/create3_docs/discussions/543). The OAK 4 D/D Pro/S need PoE+ (802.3at) or a 25 W USB-PD source; with 15 W they run in a reduced mode (https://discuss.luxonis.com/d/6647).

The Raspberry Pi AI Camera (IMX500, $70) runs YOLOv8n or YOLO11n at 640x640 on the sensor in about 59 ms per frame (https://docs.ultralytics.com/integrations/sony-imx500/), or MobileNet SSD at about 30 fps, at about 1.9 W. However, it is monocular, connects only to a Raspberry Pi CSI port, holds one network at a time in 8 MB, and has no encoder. It can supplement the stereo head camera, for example as a rear view, but not replace it. It stays in production until at least January 2028.

Depth-only comparison: Orbbec Gemini 335/336 ($264/$284, 97-99 g, under 3 W average and 6.5 W peak), Gemini 2 ($234, under 2.5 W) and RealSense D435i/D455 ($399/$499, 75/116 g, about 3.4 W max) all compute depth on an ASIC. None of them run networks or encode video, so they push the design back toward a Jetson or a host with an NPU, not toward a smaller host. RealSense lifecycle: spun out of Intel on 2025-07-11. Cognex agreed on 2026-09-22 to buy it for about $500M, with closing expected Q4 2026 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000851205/000085120526000071/exhibit991-pressrelease.htm). The D435i was backordered on the RealSense store in November 2026.

The ZED X Mini needs a Jetson (GMSL2 through a $139 ZED Link card), and its neural depth runs on the Jetson GPU. On an Orin Nano 8 GB, one camera at 30 fps takes 36% of the GPU in NEURAL_LIGHT mode and 88% in NEURAL mode (vendor, https://docs.stereolabs.com/docs/development/zed-sdk/modules/depth-sensing/depth-modes). It consumes exactly the compute this study is trying to save.

Assessment by size. At 60-75 cm: keep the OAK-D Lite and move detection (YOLOv6n), spatial location, tracking and H.264 encoding onto it, with a Pi 5-class host and a separate 5 V camera feed; the OAK 4 D/D Pro are too heavy for that head. At 100-120 cm: OAK-D Pro W with a small host works the same way. If one device should replace both camera and Jetson there, the OAK 4 D Pro Wide (674 g, $1249) is acceptable on head mass at these sizes, or an OAK 4 FFC build once the Barebone ships (Q1 2027). On a Pi-class host, the open risk is re-ID throughput on RVC2, which needs a bench test.
open_questions: Throughput of the combined RVC2 pipeline on OAK-D Lite and OAK-D Pro W: stereo, YOLOv6n 512x288, OSNet re-ID per tracked person, ObjectTracker and a 1080p H.264 stream running together. No vendor or third-party benchmark was found; bench-test it before committing to a Pi-class host.

Host CPU and power for the full stack on a Raspberry Pi 5: costmap from OAK depth plus the STL-19P lidar and ToF, the person-following and re-ID gallery logic, the web relay of the OAK's H.264, and ROS 2. Only the depthai-ros camera-publishing case has been measured (9.5 W average including the camera).

Measured power of the OAK-D Pro W with the dot projector at the brightness the floor needs. Only vendor figures (up to ~7.5 W, supply sized for 15 W) and an integrator budget (5 W nominal) were found.

Measured power of OAK 4 D/D Pro/FFC running a realistic depth, detection and ROS 2 app. The vendor gives only 10-15 W maximum average and 2.7-3.4 W for network-only runs; no third-party measurement was found.

OAK 4 FFC barebone mass with heatsink, two OV9282 modules, an IMX586 module and cables. Can 10-15 W be dissipated inside the skull shell? What is the longest reliable FFC run if the board sits behind the neck (Luxonis used 30 cm)? Module and heatsink prices were not found.

Luxonis docs mention an 'OAK4 Lite R1' board in the M8 pin table on the OAK 4 D Pro and OAK 4 S pages (https://docs.luxonis.com/hardware/products/OAK%204%20S), but no product page was found. Ask Luxonis whether a lighter RVC4 camera is coming; it would suit 60-75 cm. The web search budget ran out before this could be checked further.
No benchmark was found for YOLOv8n or YOLO11n at 640x640 on RVC4. Only YOLOv6n 512x288, YOLOv8n-pose 512x288 and larger models are published.
OAK 4 USB connectivity was alpha (peripheral mode only) as of DepthAI 3.4.0 in March 2026. Confirm its current status before planning USB rather than PoE+ or Ethernet.

If an OAK 4 in the head becomes the high-level computer, where should the 50-100 Hz locomotion MLP run: on the OAK 4 CPU over Ethernet or CAN FD to the Teensy, on a small separate host, or on the Teensy? Latency and jitter have not been measured.
RealSense D400 supply and roadmap after the Cognex acquisition closes (expected Q4 2026).
Mass of the Raspberry Pi AI Camera module. Retailers list 6 g and 18 g; the product brief gives none.
Whether DepthAI 3.11.0 fully fixes the OAK-D Lite stereo-camera crash reported in Aug-Oct 2026. Pin a DepthAI version for the robot.

Fit (estimate): ~206 g is about 34-37% of the 60 cm head+neck allowance and 23-26% at 75 cm, which makes it the first RVC4 candidate for the small sizes. https://shop.luxonis.com/products/oak-4-lite

RealSense D555 PoE: $649, in stock on the RealSense store (2026-11-07).
