architectures.name: Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit (current), re-budgeted in its 15 W mode
parts: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit 8 GB as sold: module, reference carrier, heatsink with fan, M.2 Wi-Fi card ($399 NVIDIA MSRP since July 2026; SparkFun $399 in stock)
M.2 2280 NVMe SSD for boot and rosbag logging (~$40, the surveys' NVMe estimate from opi6plus_16gb_cix_p1)
Existing DC-DC to 12 V (the carrier accepts 9-20 V; the 12 V converter on 6S, the study's 48-to-12 V converter at 12S); not counted
OAK-D Lite (60-75 cm) or OAK-D Pro W (100-120 cm) for stereo depth and on-camera H.264/MJPEG; camera not counted
Teensy 4.1 control stack (policy, CAN, IMU, ToF stop, watchdogs; firmware still to be written); unchanged, not counted
architectures.where_inference_runs: Person detector (YOLO-nano class, TensorRT INT8/FP16 at 416-640 px) and OSNet re-ID on the Orin's 1024-core GPU. Stereo depth, rectification, RGB-depth alignment and the operator H.264/MJPEG on the OAK-D's RVC2. Ground-frame tracking (camera pose per frame from torso attitude and neck angle), 2.5D grid, arc planner, ROS 2 and the web server on the six A78AE cores. Locomotion MLP, CAN loop, ToF/floor-drop stop and watchdogs on the Teensy.
architectures.power_basis: Board level: measured module basis (jetson_orin_nano_super_devkit) plus an unmeasured allowance. Typical 15.0 W (conservative) = module 12 W (the survey's typical: 11.7-12.3 W whole-module tegrastats running YOLO26s FP16 end to end at 67-75 img/s, host-bound, with locked MAXN SUPER clocks, arXiv 2609.13551; a heavier load than 10-15 Hz nano detection) + 3 W carrier/NVMe/fan (top of the unmeasured 2-3 W estimate; this allowance includes the NVMe). No light-load measurement exists in the 15 W mode. The only light-load figure, 6.2 W VDD_IN with two 8 fps 640x640 FP16 detector streams (NVIDIA forum, third party), was taken in the 7 W mode, which exists only in the non-Super flash configuration (reflash required); on that basis the kit would draw 6.2 + 2 = 8.2 W (low end of the carrier estimate), optimistic because it omits this stack's CPU work. Max 18.0 W = 15 W mode cap (vendor) + 3 W; Hackster measured ~17 W peak at the wall on the original kit (mode not named). 25 W mode (the Super configuration's default): 25 + 3 = 28.0 W at the board, 31.8 W at the battery; MAXN SUPER is uncapped. Idle with PCIe enabled measured 4.7-6.1 W (4.7 W VDD_IN in the 7 W mode, 6.1 W with jetson_clocks locking); 2.5 W was reached only with display, audio and PCIe disabled, which removes the NVMe and Wi-Fi. Not counted here or in B-D: the OAK encoder (vendor 'up to 0.5 W'), which is outside the brief's whole-set definition (host + accelerator + camera inference share); E's and G's host encoders are unmeasured and not counted either. Battery side at 0.88: 15.0/0.88 = 17.0 W typical, 18.0/0.88 = 20.5 W max (8.2/0.88 = 9.3 W on the 7 W-mode basis), against 31/0.88 = 35.2 W budgeted, i.e. 18.2 W less (25.9 W on the 7 W-mode basis). Share of the resulting walking total (study total - 35.2 + 17.0 W): 21.9% (60 cm), 18.0% (75), 11.2% (100), 8.9% (120); the 35.2 W budget is 36.7/31.2/20.6/16.9% of the study's totals. Computed runtime (requirements: 34 min at 96 W and 29 min at 113 W, i.e. 54.4 and 54.6 Wh): 41.9 min at 60 cm (46.6 on the 7 W-mode basis) and 34.6 min at 75 cm (37.6).
architectures.volume_note: NVIDIA's datasheet gives 100 x 79 x 21 mm including carrier, module and thermal solution (0.17 L); the 103 x 90.5 x 34.77 mm reseller figure for the discontinued original kit (0.32 L) is a reasonable packaging allowance. The study's chest tray is sized from that reseller envelope plus fixed margins (designlab/build.py:453), so the kit fits it by construction; the 60 cm clearance screen moved the power board behind the tray (DECISION_LOG F6). 174 g is an NVIDIA-forum figure for the kit as sold (not independently weighed; excludes the NVMe); the study's tray brings it to about 0.29 kg. The stock fan needs a ducted inlet and outlet; at the 18.0 W ceiling the 10 K-rise airflow is 2.6 x 18.0/31 = 1.51 L/s, against the 2.6 L/s sized for 31 W.
architectures.covers_growth_spec: Moderate, as the requirements state for this module: 67 TOPS (vendor) and six A78AE cores carry YOLO-s or pose models at 640, OSNet x1.0 and Whisper on the GPU (YOLOv8n INT8 4.9 ms GPU-only in the 15 W mode, third party; PeopleNet + NvDCF 217 FPS in the pre-Super 15 W mode, vendor, as corrected), and the 2280 slot takes a >= 256 GB NVMe. Limits: 8 GB shared by ROS 2, TensorRT, maps and any LLM/VLM; no hardware encoder; no Orin Nano re-ID benchmark exists (NVIDIA's ReIdentificationNet card gives AGX Orin figures only).
architectures.software_effort: Low. It is the platform PR #662 assumes: JetPack 6.2 (Ubuntu 22.04, ROS 2 Humble, Isaac ROS 3.2), or JetPack 7.2 (Ubuntu 24.04, Jazzy, Isaac ROS 4.6) flashed from a USB ISO because this kit has no 7.2 SD image. The 15 W mode exists in both flash configurations; the 7 W mode needs the non-Super one. Work needed here as on every platform: replace the OpenCV HOG detector with a DNN (ONNX to TensorRT via Ultralytics export or trtexec is routine), move ingestion, grid and planner from Python to C++ or vectorised code, move tracking to the ground frame with per-frame camera pose (the camera now rides on the head), ingest with depthai-ros, and export the ONNX actor plus normalisation arrays to the Teensy. Keep the policy off Linux: PREEMPT_RT plus CUDA is unproven on JetPack 6 (CUDA error 801 reported on 6.2.2; NVIDIA does not maintain nvbuild.sh there).
architectures.lifecycle: In production; NVIDIA lists Orin Nano modules through Jan 2032 and dev kits carry no lifecycle date. MSRP rose from $249 to $399 in July 2026. NVIDIA has announced the Orin Nano 2 for H1 2027 (NVIDIA: 78 TOPS, 8-core CPU, 8 GB, price not announced; Electronic Design adds LPDDR5X, configurable 15-40 W and the same form factor as Orin Nano Super, which NVIDIA has not confirmed). Depth relies on the RVC2 OAK-D: Myriad X is being discontinued (Intel's 2025 plan, per Luxonis) and Luxonis says its end-of-life buys cover about five years of demand from Jan 2025, so plan camera supply to about 2030.
risks: The 31 W budget is about 2.1x this conservative estimate (31/15.0) and 3.8x the 7 W-mode basis (31/8.2); runtime, converter rating and the 2.6 L/s airflow are mis-sized until the kit is measured at the converter input with the real pipeline. The 3 W carrier/NVMe/fan allowance is itself unmeasured.
$399 since July 2026; the dev-kit carrier is not intended for production and its fan needs ducting through the shell.
The 9-20 V input keeps a DC-DC stage (the 12 V converter on 6S; the study's 48-to-12 V converter at 12S).
No hardware video encoder (NVIDIA: 1080p30 on 1-2 CPU cores), so the operator stream should come from the OAK's encoder.
8 GB is shared by ROS 2, TensorRT, maps and streaming; the 7 W mode exists only in the non-Super flash configuration.
Depth depends on the end-of-life Myriad X OAK-D (shared with B-E and G).

architectures.name: Jetson Orin Nano 8GB module on a Connect Tech Super Hadron-DM carrier (10-60 V direct battery input)
parts: Connect Tech NGX027 Super Hadron-DM carrier: 45 g, 87.6 x 58.8 mm, +10 to +60 V input, Super Mode supported, rugged latching connectors, -25 to +85 C ($410 at WDL, 38 in stock)
Jetson Orin Nano 8GB module ($449.82 single-unit at Seeed; NVIDIA's $399 is a 1KU+ price)
Active heatsink with fan: Connect Tech's 49 g unit is unpriced and unverified, so it is priced with Seeed's $28.99 Super-mode heatsink-fan as a proxy (fit on this carrier unverified)
M.2 2242/2230 NVMe (~$40, survey estimate); M.2 Key E Wi-Fi card (not priced)

USB plan: the OAK-D Pro W (or Lite) on one USB 3.1 port with its Y-adapter feed from the robot 5 V rail (the carrier's VBUS current is not stated); a powered hub on the other port for the Teensy (USB serial) and the lidar's USB-UART adapter, or the lidar on a Teensy UART (the carrier's spare serial ports are RS-232, not TTL; its 3.3 V UART is the console). Camera not counted
Teensy 4.1 unchanged

Variants: Seeed reComputer Mini J3011 + Extension ($709 complete with fansink, 128 GB NVMe and enclosure; 462 g; 12-54 V; Super mode not stated, which only matters above the 15 W mode); ARK Just A Jetson ($1,129.82 with module; 75 g carrier; 5.5-75 V; INA238 power monitor; modes above 25 W unlikely on its 5.2 V rail); Seeed Robotics J401 bare build ($674.80; 19-54 V; CAN-FD; 6x USB 3.2; 115 x 115 mm, wider than the dev-kit envelope the 60 cm tray is built around)
architectures.where_inference_runs: Same as A: detector and OSNet re-ID on the Orin GPU; depth, alignment and the operator H.264/MJPEG on the OAK-D's RVC2; ground-frame tracking, grid, planner and ROS 2 on the six A78AE cores; policy and safety chain on the Teensy.
architectures.power_basis: Same module and mode as A, so the same basis: typical 15.0 W = 12 W module (measured under a heavier, host-bound detector load in MAXN SUPER, arXiv 2609.13551) + 3 W carrier/NVMe/fan (unmeasured estimate, includes the NVMe); no light-load measurement exists in the 15 W mode (A's 8.2 W case is a 7 W-mode basis). Max 18.0 W in the 15 W mode; 25 + 3 = 28.0 W in the 25 W mode, 31.8 W at the battery and 3.4 W inside the 35.2 W budget. OAK encoder not counted (see A). The carrier takes the 6S or 12S pack directly, but its own 10-60 V regulator efficiency is unmeasured, so 0.88 is kept as a placeholder: 17.0 W typical and 20.5 W max at the battery, 18.2 W below the budget. Share of the resulting walking total: 11.2% at 100 cm and 8.9% at 120 cm in the 15 W mode; 19.0% and 15.5% in the 25 W mode.
architectures.volume_note: Carrier 87.6 x 58.8 mm (spec sheet); module and heatsink height not published. The footprint is smaller than the dev kit's 100 x 79 mm, so it fits any chest that takes the dev kit; check the height against the chest station. Mass is not computable: 45 g carrier + 49 g heatsink (unverified) = 94 g, plus the module (NVIDIA publishes no mass) and the NVMe; weigh it. Price = $410 + $449.82 + $28.99 + $40 = $928.81. Airflow 2.6 x 18.0/31 = 1.51 L/s at the 18.0 W ceiling (10 K rise).
architectures.covers_growth_spec: Moderate, as A. The same SODIMM socket takes an Orin NX now (Connect Tech lists Super Mode for NX; an NX 16GB also ran Super modes on NVIDIA's own dev-kit carrier, so the upgrade path is not unique to B) and possibly the Orin Nano 2 in H1 2027 (same form factor per Electronic Design; not confirmed by NVIDIA).
architectures.software_effort: Low to moderate, and more than A: the Connect Tech BSP (listed through JetPack 6.2.2 / L4T 36.5.0, a release behind NVIDIA; JetPack 7.2 not confirmed), flashing through the carrier BSP, adding Wi-Fi and NVMe, and routing the Teensy and lidar adapter through a powered hub on the second USB 3.1 port or putting the lidar on a Teensy UART. The ONNX policy goes to the Teensy as in A.
architectures.lifecycle: Module listed through Jan 2032; NGX027 in stock (38 units at WDL, Nov 2026), while the non-Super Hadron NGX012 is out of stock. The socket accepts the Orin NX and, if the form factor holds (Electronic Design; not confirmed by NVIDIA), the Orin Nano 2 (H1 2027). Same RVC2 camera supply caveat as A.
risks: About twice the dev kit's price ($928.81 vs $439) for the same compute; its gains are production fit (latching connectors, -25 to +85 C, 45 g carrier), not speed or software.
Battery-voltage input saves only the compute's share of conversion: at 12S the 48-to-12 V converter stays for the 12 V appendage rail (Dynamixel expression servos at 60-100 cm).
The carrier BSP trails NVIDIA by a release; JetPack 7.2 support is unconfirmed.
Total mass is unknown (module and heatsink masses unpublished; the 49 g heatsink figure is unverified) and the proxy heatsink's fit is unconfirmed; weigh and fit-check before committing.
Only two USB 3.1 ports and an unstated VBUS current: feed the OAK-D from the 5 V rail and put the Teensy and lidar adapter on a powered hub, or the lidar on a Teensy UART.
Same 8 GB, no-encoder and Myriad X caveats as A.

architectures.name: Raspberry Pi 5 8GB + AI HAT+ 13 TOPS (Hailo-8L); OAK-D for depth and video
parts: Raspberry Pi 5 8 GB ($175 list, product brief RP-008348-DS-10, Nov 2026; Adafruit $200 street)
Official Active Cooler ($5 list)

Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ 13 TOPS (Hailo-8L) on the PCIe FFC with the 16 mm stacking header ($70 list; PiShop $76.95). Variants: AI HAT+ 26 TOPS (Hailo-8, $110) or AI HAT+ 2 (Hailo-10H, 20 TOPS INT8 / 40 INT4, 8 GB, $200)
USB 3 SSD on the second USB 3.0 port for boot and logs (~$40, the surveys' NVMe estimate used as a proxy; the HAT occupies the only PCIe lane)
5 V/5 A (>= 25 W) buck from the pack with PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000, sized against the ~18 W worst case and CNX's 16.8 W peak with USB drives attached (not priced)
OAK-D Lite (60-75 cm) or OAK-D Pro W (100-120 cm) on the OAK Y-adapter ($24) fed from the robot 5 V rail; camera not counted
Teensy 4.1 unchanged (USB serial or UART link)
architectures.where_inference_runs: Person detector (YOLOv8n/YOLO11n INT8 HEF; the zoo HEFs are 640x640, so a 416 px input needs a Dataflow Compiler build) and OSNet re-ID on the Hailo-8L, sharing it over the Pi's single Gen 3 x1 link. Stereo depth, alignment and the operator H.264/MJPEG on the OAK-D's RVC2. Detector pre/post-processing (C++), the ground-frame tracker (camera pose per frame from torso attitude and neck angle), grid, planner, ROS 2 and the web relay on the Pi's four A76 cores. Policy and safety chain on the Teensy.
architectures.power_basis: Board level, excluding storage (the USB SSD's draw is unmeasured; A, B and G carry their NVMe inside a 3 W allowance). Typical 8.0 W = Pi 5 host 6.5 W (measured endpoints, Geerling via rpi5_8gb_active_cooler: Pi 5 8GB C1 at 3.2 W idle and 9.8 W stress-ng, interpolated at about 2 busy cores: 3.2 + (9.8 - 3.2) x 2/4; 1.5 cores for the stack per the requirements plus 0.5 core for detector pre/post, an estimate) + 1.5 W Hailo-8L (vendor typical). OAK encoder not counted (see A). Cross-check: Sixfab measured 6.08 W whole-system average for a Pi 5 8GB + Hailo-8L (rpi5_8gb_ai_hat_plus_13tops), which the verification labels a mixed seven-model sync proxy with no OAK attached, so 8.0 W is conservative. Max 18.0 W = the ~18 W worst case the verification sets for any Pi + NPU HAT (Sixfab system peaks of 9.2-17.8 W were not broken out by chip; Pi stress-ng 9.8 W + Hailo-8 maximum 8.25 W = 18.05 W); CNX measured 16.8 W peak with USB drives attached (wall meter, PSU included). Battery side at 0.88: 8.0/0.88 = 9.1 W typical and 20.5 W max, 26.1 W below the 35.2 W budget; share of the resulting walking total 13.0% (60 cm), 10.5% (75), 6.3% (100), 5.0% (120); computed runtime 46.7 min at 60 cm and 37.7 min at 75 cm. Against A in its 15 W mode (17.0 W at the battery) the saving is 8.0 W (4.8 min at 60 cm); only against A's 7 W-mode basis (9.3 W) does it shrink to 0.2 W.
architectures.volume_note: Pi 5 + Active Cooler + AI HAT+ stack 85 x 56 x 30 mm (0.14 L), plus a 5 V/5 A buck and a small USB SSD: a smaller footprint than the dev kit and within its 34.77 mm reseller height, so it fits any chest that takes the dev kit (the study's tray resizes with the selected board). Mass ~100 g is a survey estimate (no measured Pi, cooler or HAT masses exist; the cooler's 29 g is a retailer shipping weight), excluding the SSD. Price = $175 + $5 + $70 + $40 = $290 list (~$323 at observed street prices). Airflow 2.6 x 18.0/31 = 1.51 L/s at the 18.0 W worst case and ~0.67 L/s at the 8.0 W typical (10 K rise); the HAT's 0-50 C ambient rating, not the Pi's 0-70 C, sets the shell temperature limit.
architectures.covers_growth_spec: Partial. 13 TOPS is below the 20-70 TOPS growth floor, and the four A76 cores, 8 GB and single PCIe lane fall short of the growth CPU/RAM/NVMe targets. Accelerator upgrades on the same host: AI HAT+ 26 TOPS (Hailo-8, +$40; vendor zoo YOLOv8s 491 fps and OSNet x1.0 215 fps on an x86 host) or AI HAT+ 2 (Hailo-10H, 20 TOPS INT8, 8 GB, $200; faster than Hailo-8 on YOLO11n, YOLO26n and OSNet at batch 1 but slower on YOLOv8n; Qwen2.5-1.5B prefill 320 ms vs 2039 ms on the Pi CPU, prefill only; Whisper examples in hailo-apps) for on-device voice.
architectures.software_effort: Moderate. ROS 2 Jazzy/Lyrical is Tier 1 only on Ubuntu 24.04/26.04 (Raspberry Pi OS is Tier 3: Docker or source build), while the AI HAT+ is first-class on Raspberry Pi OS and needs its PCIe driver built from source on Ubuntu (2024 Canonical guide; current HailoRT status unchecked). Models: precompiled Model Zoo HEFs at 640x640 (yolov8n, yolo11n, yolo26n, osnet_x1_0, repvgg_a0_person_reid), or ONNX through the Dataflow Compiler on an x86 PC with INT8 calibration for 416 px or custom models. HailoRT must be wrapped in a ROS 2 node (no vendor node), with async, pipelined requests and pre/post in C++. The OpenCV HOG path is replaced; the follower ports to arm64 but needs C++/vectorisation on the slower A76 cores, and its tracker must move to the ground frame with per-frame camera pose. The ONNX policy goes to the Teensy (no RT kernel package for Raspberry Pi OS; stock-kernel worst case 36.8 ms under stress vs 124 us with PREEMPT_RT).
architectures.lifecycle: Pi 5 in production to at least Jan 2036; AI HAT+ to at least Jan 2030 at an unchanged $70; AI HAT+ 2 to Jan 2036. Memory-driven price rises took the Pi 5 8GB from $80 at launch to $175 list; Raspberry Pi says it will reverse them when memory prices fall. Because detection runs on the Hailo, a future depth-only camera (e.g. Orbbec Gemini 335: $264, 97 g, < 3 W average, vendor) could replace the end-of-life RVC2 OAK-D without losing the detector; the on-camera route instead is the OAK 4 Lite watch item under D.
risks: Detector and re-ID share one Hailo-8L over the Pi's Gen 3 x1 link: switching between two networks is unmeasured and multi-context models slow sharply on the single lane. Sixfab's sync end-to-end rate of 12-15 fps (YOLO26n at 640, with video decode on the Pi, which raw OAK frames avoid) is 67-83 ms per frame, leaving only ~17-33 ms of a 100 ms frame for re-ID, grid and planner, so use async, pipelined HailoRT.
The AI HAT+ is rated 0-50 C ambient; a closed torso needs forced air past the stack.
The 16 mm stacking header and PCIe FFC are untested under walking vibration, and Raspberry Pi does not certify the PCIe Gen 3 link the HAT uses.
The HAT takes the only PCIe lane: logging goes to a USB SSD, or to NVMe behind a PCIe packet switch (Geekworm X1004) that drops to shared Gen 2 bandwidth.
Per-chip peak power is unmeasured and the storage draw is not in the 8.0 W; size the 5 V supply and cooling for ~18 W.
The Pi's USB downstream budget is 1.6 A total; a Pi-powered OAK-D Lite browned out the Pi, so the Y-adapter feed from the 5 V rail is mandatory.

Vendor zoo throughput comes from an x86 host on a 2-4x wider PCIe link than the Pi's Gen 3 x1 (Hailo's statements conflict on x2 vs x4), so measured Pi rates are lower (e.g. Hailo-8L YOLOv8n 61.9 fps at batch 1).

architectures.name: Raspberry Pi 5 8GB; OAK-D runs depth, person detection and encoding (no extra accelerator)
parts: Raspberry Pi 5 8 GB ($175 list; the 4 GB board at $110 is a possible production saving)
Official Active Cooler ($5)
Raspberry Pi M.2 HAT+ (from $12; M-key 2230/2242, up to 3 A) with an NVMe SSD for boot and logs (~$40, survey estimate); the PCIe lane is free because there is no NPU HAT
5 V/5 A (>= 25 W) buck from the 6S pack with PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000 (not priced)
OAK-D Lite on the OAK Y-adapter ($24) fed from the robot 5 V rail, running depth, detector and encoder; camera not counted
Teensy 4.1 unchanged (USB serial or UART link)
architectures.where_inference_runs: On the OAK-D's RVC2: stereo depth, a YOLOv6n-class detector at 416x416 or 512x288 as a SpatialDetectionNetwork (box plus 3D position from aligned depth), optionally an OSNet re-ID stage on person crops, and H.264/MJPEG for the operator page. The on-camera ObjectTracker (imageless, camera frame, no ego-motion input) is only an auxiliary cue. The Pi 5 runs the constant-velocity ground-frame tracker and association after composing each frame's camera pose from torso attitude and neck angle (< 1-2 ms per frame, requirements), target lock, the re-ID gallery and ambiguity latch, the grid built directly from the 320x200 depth image (point clouds are host-only on RVC2), the planner, ROS 2 and the web relay. Policy and safety chain on the Teensy.
architectures.power_basis: Board level, excluding the M.2 HAT+ and NVMe (unmeasured; A, B and G carry their NVMe inside a 3 W allowance). Typical 6.7 W = Pi 5 host 5.675 W (Geerling's measured 3.2 W idle and 9.8 W stress-ng for a Pi 5 8GB C1, interpolated at the requirements' ~1.5 busy cores: 3.2 + (9.8 - 3.2) x 1.5/4) + camera inference share 1.0 W (OAK docs: 'AI up to 1 W', vendor) = 6.675 W. Low end 5.9 W with a 0.25 W share: a third party measured the OAK-D Lite at 3.25-3.5 W while depthai-ros published RGB, MobileNet detections and stereo depth (oak_d_lite_rvc2), 0.25-0.5 W over the 3 W the study books for the camera. The study's 3 W camera base excludes the encoder (vendor 'up to 0.5 W'), which is outside the brief's whole-set definition and not counted (see A). Cross-check: post #1 of the same forum thread gives the Pi alone at about 4 W (load 2.0) and 7 W (load 4.0), conditions unstated; with the camera on a separate 5.1 V feed only the camera was measured (3.25 W) and the Pi's draw was not reported; the verification's estimated stable total is 7.3-10.5 W including the camera. Max 10.8 W = 9.8 W stress-ng + 1.0 W, excluding storage, so not a maximum for this parts list; CNX measured 16.8 W peak with USB drives attached (wall meter, PSU included), so size the buck and airflow with margin. Battery side at 0.88: 7.6 W typical (6.7 W low end) and 12.3 W max, 27.6 W below the 35.2 W budget; share of the resulting walking total 11.1% (60 cm), 8.9% (75), 5.3% (100), 4.2% (120); computed runtime 47.7 min at 60 cm and 38.4 min at 75 cm. Against A in its 15 W mode the saving is 9.5 W at the battery (5.8 min at 60 cm), and 1.7 W against A's 7 W-mode basis. D's 1.3 W board margin over C (8.0 - 6.7 W) rests on the assumed 0.5-core difference and sits inside the estimate spread; rank the two by bench test 3.
architectures.volume_note: Pi 5 + Active Cooler 85 x 56 x 20 mm (0.10 L) plus the M.2 HAT+ (height not published) and a 5 V buck: the smallest chest package here, with the head camera unchanged (OAK-D Lite 61 g, 91 x 28 x 17.5 mm). Mass ~75 g is a survey estimate (29 g cooler retailer weight + ~46 g board), excluding the M.2 HAT+ and NVMe (unpublished). Price = $175 + $5 + $12 + $40 = $232 ($195 with a microSD instead, which the requirements reject for logging). Airflow 2.6 x 10.8/31 = 0.91 L/s at the 10.8 W board figure (10 K rise), or 1.41 L/s if sized for CNX's 16.8 W peak with drives; the requirements give ~0.6 L/s for a ~7 W host.
architectures.covers_growth_spec: None. RVC2 is 1.4 TOPS 'for AI' on FP16-only hardware (not an INT8 figure, per the correction), and YOLOv8n/YOLO11n at 640 reach only 7-14 fps; there is no room for pose, larger detectors or full-rate OSNet x1.0 beside the detector. The growth path is to add an AI HAT+ (which turns D into C) or change host. Minimum spec: provisional, so set false until the requirements' acceptance test passes with re-ID added: the detector holding >= 10 Hz and embeddings for up to 5 tracked people at >= 5 Hz (>= 25 crops/s, 51% of OSNet's 49/s standalone network-only rate) alongside stereo, alignment and MJPEG. That combination has never been measured.
architectures.software_effort: Low to moderate, and the lowest-risk Pi software stack: Ubuntu 24.04 + ROS 2 Jazzy (Tier 1) + depthai-ros v3, with no NPU toolchain or out-of-tree driver on the host. The detector becomes a DepthAI SpatialDetectionNetwork with an RVC2 FP16 blob from the Luxonis zoo or HubAI (INT8 requests are ignored on RVC2). Detection and per-detection XYZ come from the camera, while the ground-frame Kalman tracker and association stay on the Pi with ego-motion from the Teensy's odometry; re-ID runs as a second on-camera stage or on the Pi; the identity gallery and no-silent-switch logic stay on the host. The OpenCV HOG path goes; the follower ports to arm64 but needs C++/vectorisation. Pin DepthAI >= 3.11.0 (OAK-D Lite OV7251 crash fix). ONNX policy on the Teensy.
architectures.lifecycle: Pi 5 to at least Jan 2036; M.2 HAT+ to at least Jan 2032. Detector and encoder live on the RVC2 OAK-D, so this is the most camera-dependent option: Myriad X is being discontinued and Luxonis stock covers about five years from 2025 (OAK-D Lite now $269; SparkFun lists it as retired). Successors: a depth-only camera plus an accelerator (C), or, as a watch item, the OAK 4 Lite (RVC4, EVT prototype, one unit per order; vendor figures: $779 AF/FF, $879 Wide, ~206 g with USB, 4 GB / 128 GB, 8 W / 20 TOPS sustained at 25 C and 4 W / 10 TOPS at 50 C, 25 W USB-PD for full compute), which would keep detection and re-ID on the camera and remove the Myriad X dependency; its ~206 g is an estimated 34-37% of the 60 cm head+neck allowance and 23-26% at 75 cm, and it would put up to 8 W of sustained heat in the head.
risks: The combined RVC2 load is unmeasured: the ~35 fps YOLOv6n 512x288 figure is a detection-only pipeline (no stereo, encoder, tracker or re-ID), and the cameras take 3-6 of the 16 CMX slices, leaving about 10-13 for networks (6 SHAVEs x 2 threads recommended).

Re-ID budget: 49/s is OSNet's standalone network-only rate on RVC2. With the detector, stereo and encoder sharing the 10-13 free CMX slices, the available re-ID rate is lower and unmeasured, so 5 crops at 5 Hz (25/s) may already exceed it; test it in bench test 2, or keep re-ID on an AI HAT+ (C).

The on-camera ObjectTracker works in the camera frame with no ego-motion input; on the moving head its tracks and velocities would carry neck and body motion into target-lock and ambiguity decisions, so tracking stays on the host.
FP16-only RVC2: the detector must be YOLOv6n-class at 416 or 512x288 and validated on truncated bodies at 1.0-2.5 m.
Most exposed of all options to the Myriad X end of life.
No growth headroom; the Pi's 1.6 A USB budget makes the Y-adapter feed mandatory.

architectures.name: Orange Pi 5 Max (RK3588, 6 TOPS NPU); OAK-D for depth
parts: Orange Pi 5 Max, RK3588, 6 GB LPDDR5 ($168.99 on Amazon US, listings showing 'only 2-5 left'; the 16 GB SKU at $346.99 is the fallback, $396.99 as configured)
Aluminium heatsink + 5 V fan (~$10 and ~20 g, survey estimates)
M.2 NVMe on the PCIe 3.0 x4 slot (~$40, survey estimate)
24 V-to-5 V buck rated >= 25 W (not priced)
OAK-D Lite or Pro W for depth on its own 5 V feed; camera not counted
Teensy 4.1 unchanged
Variant for 100-120 cm: FriendlyElec NanoPC-T6 LTS ($272.50 with heatsink-fan; 12 V DC input; 64 GB eMMC; in stock; power unmeasured)
architectures.where_inference_runs: Detector (YOLOv8n/YOLO11n RKNN INT8) on NPU core 0 and re-ID on core 1 (one context per core raises throughput; spreading one model over cores cut latency only 0-18%; re-ID conversion is untested and unbenchmarked on RK3588), core 2 spare, e.g. Whisper base (vendor RTF 0.196). Depth on the OAK-D's RVC2; the operator H.264 on the RK3588 hardware encoder; ground-frame tracking, grid, planner and ROS 2 on 4x A76 + 4x A55. Policy and safety chain on the Teensy.
architectures.power_basis: Board level, excluding storage unless stated. Typical 8.0 W is the survey's estimate for the full autonomy load (opi5_max_6gb: 6-8 W), checked bottom-up at 7.24 W: 3.68 W measured whole-device during continuous YOLOv8n INT8 640 NPU inference (Sci. Rep. 2026, an unnamed 16 GB RK3588 board) + 1.5 cores x 2.375 W ((10.9 - 1.4)/4: Geerling's stress-ng minus idle on this board, all attributed to the four big cores, an upper bound) = 7.24 W; the hardware encoder is unmeasured and not counted (as the OAK encoder in A-D). With the NVMe in this parts list, one report puts idle at ~5 W without ASPM L1.2 against 1.4 W, so the typical becomes up to 8.0 + 3.6 = 11.6 W until ASPM L1.2 is confirmed (or boot from microSD or eMMC and drop the $40 NVMe). Max 15.7 W = 12.8 W HPL measured at the wall (Geerling #49) + an NPU increment of up to 4.27 - 1.4 = 2.87 W (Sci. Rep. maximum across nine models minus this board's 1.4 W idle; cross-board, so an estimate), excluding storage. Battery side at 0.88: 9.1 W typical (up to 13.2 W with the NVMe penalty) and 17.8 W max, 26.1 W below the budget (22.1 W with the penalty); share of the resulting walking total 13.0% (60 cm), 10.5% (75), 6.3% (100), 5.0% (120), or 17.8/14.5/8.8/7.1% with the NVMe penalty.
architectures.volume_note: Board 89 x 57 mm (cooler height not stated) plus a 5 V buck; a smaller footprint than the dev kit. Mass 82 g = 62 g board (vendor) + ~20 g cooler (estimate), excluding the NVMe. Price = $168.99 + $10 + $40 = $218.99 ($188.99 with a ~$10 microSD in place of the NVMe, survey estimate). Airflow 2.6 x 15.7/31 = 1.31 L/s at 15.7 W (10 K rise).
architectures.covers_growth_spec: Partial. The 6 TOPS NPU is below the 20-70 TOPS floor, but the eight-core CPU, the 16 GB SKU and the vendor model zoo (YOLOv5-v11/YOLO26, pose, segmentation, Whisper base and zipformer speech) cover voice and some perception growth. A Hailo-8 M.2 on the PCIe 3.0 x4 slot could add 26 TOPS if storage moves to eMMC or microSD. Re-ID, which the minimum spec's no-silent-switch rule needs, is unverified: no RK3588 re-ID benchmark exists and its conversion is untested.
architectures.software_effort: Moderate to high. The NPU needs the Rockchip vendor BSP kernel (6.1) under Orange Pi's Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 images; the community Ubuntu-Rockchip project was archived on 2026-04-29, and the mainline Rocket NPU driver (Linux 6.18, Mesa 25.3 Teflon) supports only MobileNet/SSDLite, not YOLO. Models are converted with RKNN-Toolkit2 on an x86 host: Ultralytics format='rknn' INT8 decodes boxes on the CPU and measured YOLO26n at 41.2 ms on a ROCK 5B vs 18.2 ms for Rockchip's zoo recipe (2.3x), so use the zoo's restructured heads. Re-ID conversion is untested. ROS 2 Humble/Jazzy from Ubuntu arm64; depthai-ros for the OAK; ONNX policy on the Teensy.
architectures.lifecycle: RK3588 is 2022 silicon. Orange Pi publishes no end-of-supply date, and the 6 GB SKU appears only on Amazon (Orange Pi lists 4/8/16 GB). Radxa guarantees ROCK 5B/5B+/5T/CM5 to Sept 2032, but most were sold out on 2026-11-07; FriendlyElec's NanoPC-T6 LTS and CM3588 are in stock. The 2026 DRAM shortage inflated SBC prices about 1.5-2.5x. RVC2 camera caveat for depth.
risks: Vendor-kernel lock-in: the NPU, and in practice the board, depends on Rockchip's 6.1 BSP.
The export recipe changes NPU speed about 2.3x; Frigate rates RKNN 'community supported'; no re-ID benchmark exists on RK3588, so the no-silent-switch requirement is unverified here.
Thin stock for the 6 GB SKU and no longevity statement; buy spares.
Possible NVMe idle penalty (~5 W idle without ASPM L1.2, one report), which would erase its power parity with C.
The 5 V/5 A input needs a dedicated >= 25 W buck, and the OAK-D needs its own 5 V feed.

architectures.name: Luxonis OAK 4 D Pro Wide (RVC4, QCS8550) as camera and high-level computer, plus the Teensy
parts: Luxonis OAK 4 D Pro Wide: QCS8550, 48 INT8 TOPS, 8 GB LPDDR5, 128 GB storage, IP67 ($1,249 = $1,149 + $100 Wide, including the temporary +$200 surcharge since 2026-07-30); replaces the OAK-D Pro W ($529) and the Jetson set

Power: PoE+ (802.3at) from a DC-input injector on the 12S bus (not found, so price and mass are not counted; Luxonis's $29.99 injector is mains-only, 138 g); a 25 W USB-PD source is the alternative, and 15 W gives a reduced mode
Data: a small Ethernet switch on the injector's data side (not found, not counted) linking the camera to the Teensy 4.1 over 100 Mbit Ethernet, one of the requirements' listed host links
USB Wi-Fi dongle on the M8 USB 2.0 host for the operator page (not priced; that host cannot run together with USB-C, which this plan leaves unused)
Teensy 4.1 unchanged; ToF, IMU and the STL-19P lidar (on a Teensy UART) stay on it; no prototype M8 CAN adapter

Lighter RVC4 routes, not production-ready: OAK 4 FFC Dev Kit ($849, 215 g, plus $139.97-169.97 of camera modules, i.e. $988.97-1,018.97; 36 g Barebone at $730 ships Q1 2027; 6-32 V input; 1.8 V I2C needs level shifting) and OAK 4 Lite (EVT prototype, ~206 g, $779-879, one per order)
architectures.where_inference_runs: All high-level work on the camera: stereo depth with on-device point clouds, the person detector and OSNet re-ID (vendor 571 inferences/s, network only) on the 48 TOPS eNPU, H.264/H.265 encoding, and the follower, ground-frame tracker (camera pose from the Teensy's timestamped neck-angle and IMU stream), grid, planner and ROS 2 (Kilted, onboard) as OAK App containers on the QCS8550 CPU; the on-camera ObjectTracker is at most an auxiliary cue. The Teensy keeps the policy, CAN, ToF/IMU, lidar parsing, request expiry and the stop chain.
architectures.power_basis: Vendor figures only (OAK 4 D Pro docs, RVC4 page): 1.6 W average idle, 10-15 W maximum average, 25 W peak, 12 W boot peak; vendor model-zoo and marketing network-only runs report 2.7-3.4 W for YOLOv6n 512x288 (measurement point not stated); no third-party measurement of a depth + detection + app pipeline exists. F replaces the head camera, which the study books at its 3 W base (requirements: '2.5-3 W base'; study catalog parts[9]) inside a sensor line of 5.85 W at 100-120 cm (round-one power.aux.loads.sensors); the other 2.85 W (ToF, foot sensing, lidar) stays. So whole-set power = device - 3 W: typical 15 - 3 = 12.0 W (top of the vendor maximum average used as a planning value; 10 - 3 = 7.0 W at its low end), max 25 - 3 = 22.0 W. Battery side at 0.88: 13.6 W typical (8.0 W low end) and 25.0 W max, 21.6 W below the budget; share of the resulting walking total 9.1% at 100 cm and 7.3% at 120 cm. PoE+ injector or USB-PD conversion losses are unmeasured.
architectures.volume_note: 143.5 x 42.5 x 67.3 mm (0.41 L) IP67 housing in the head; it frees the chest compute bay entirely. 674 g replaces the 91 g OAK-D Pro W, so +583 g in the head, or +293 g overall against the Pro W plus the 290 g Jetson tray; the DC-input injector and switch add mass not counted here. Net price over the camera it replaces: $1,249 - $529 = $720, before the injector and switch. Head heat 10-15 W on average (25 W peak); 10 K-rise airflow 2.6 x 15/31 = 1.26 L/s at 15 W.
architectures.covers_growth_spec: Mostly, for perception: 48 INT8 TOPS NPU + 4 FP16 TOPS GPU, 8 GB and a strong CPU (vendor: YOLOv8-large pose 170 fps at 640x352, open-vocabulary YOLOE-v8-large 85 fps). Storage (128 GB) is below the 256 GB target, voice/LLM on RVC4 is unbenchmarked, and the 3-microphone array is reported only by CNX. Minimum spec: conditional, so set false, because three host items are not met as written: it runs Luxonis OS rather than the Ubuntu + ROS 2 pairing, Wi-Fi needs a USB dongle, and USB data was at alpha.
architectures.software_effort: High. The follow stack must be rebuilt as DepthAI v3 on-device pipelines plus OAK App containers (oakctl or Luxonis Hub) on Luxonis OS (Linux 5.15) rather than Ubuntu, with ROS 2 Kilted onboard (Humble/Jazzy peers use the _v3 packages) and models converted through HubAI (INT8/FP16). The ground-frame tracker needs the Teensy's timestamped neck and IMU stream over Ethernet. The Teensy link moves from USB to 100 Mbit Ethernet (the M8 UART's rate is not stated against the >= 2 Mbit/s requirement). DepthAI changes quickly (3.12.0 on 2026-11-06 more than doubled RVC4 NeuralDepth throughput), so pin versions. The ONNX policy stays on the Teensy.
architectures.lifecycle: QCS8550 is in Qualcomm's longevity programme to April 2033 (read from a search result); RVC4 is Luxonis's forward platform and removes the Myriad X dependency. The OAK 4 D Pro was in stock on 2026-11-07 (AF 237, FF 87, Wide 132 units); prices carry a temporary +$200 surcharge (launch $949).
risks: 674 g in the head: more than the whole 60 cm head+neck allowance (0.55-0.61 kg), ~75-85% of it at 75 cm, ~40-45% at 100 cm and ~25-30% at 120 cm (survey estimates from REFERENCE.md).
10-15 W average (25 W peak) of heat inside the skull, with no third-party power data.
Power plumbing: PoE+ needs a DC-input injector that is not yet sourced (Luxonis's own is mains-only), or a 25 W USB-PD source; Luxonis's own Create 3 demo ran from a PoE power bank.

The one Ethernet port is both the PoE+ input and the only fast data link, so the Teensy shares it through a switch; the single M8 aux port cannot host the Wi-Fi dongle, a Teensy UART, the CAN adapter and the lidar at once, so this plan uses it for Wi-Fi only.
USB data was alpha (peripheral mode) in 2026 and there is no built-in Wi-Fi.

Highest porting effort, off the Ubuntu + ROS 2 pairing the minimum spec assumes, with a short-support ROS 2 distribution onboard (Kilted); confirm Luxonis's move to an LTS release (Lyrical is supported to May 2031).
Camera and computer are one device: its failure removes all high-level perception, so the Teensy's stop-and-stand must be solid.

architectures.name: Jetson Orin NX 16GB (Super) on a Seeed reComputer Robotics J401 carrier (19-54 V, 12S direct)
parts: Jetson Orin NX 16GB module ($1,077.02 single-unit at Seeed; $999 at 1KU)
Seeed reComputer Robotics J401 carrier: 19-54 V input, CAN-FD with transceivers, 6x USB 3.2, 2x GbE, M.2 Key M/E/B ($195.99)
Seeed Super-mode heatsink with fan ($28.99)
M.2 NVMe (~$40, survey estimate); M.2 Key E Wi-Fi card (not priced)
OAK-D Pro W for depth, fed through the Y-adapter from a 15 W 5 V supply; camera not counted
Teensy 4.1 unchanged

Variants: boxed reComputer Robotics J4012 ($1,657.99); the same module on the 87.6 x 58.8 mm, 10-60 V CTI Super Hadron-DM ($1,556.01 with the proxy heatsink and NVMe), or on NVIDIA's own Orin Nano Super dev-kit carrier (an NX 16GB ran Super modes there at 19 V; stock-heatsink headroom unverified)
architectures.where_inference_runs: A fixed person detector on one of the two DLAs (keeping the GPU free); OSNet x1.0, pose, Whisper or a small LLM and larger detectors on the GPU; the operator stream on NVENC. Ground-frame tracking, SLAM, Nav2-style planning and ROS 2 on eight A78AE cores. Depth on the OAK-D Pro W's RVC2. Policy and safety chain on the Teensy.
architectures.power_basis: No idle or detector-load measurement exists for the Orin NX 16GB (an NX 8GB idles at ~5 W, method not stated). Typical 28 W is a planning value for everyday running in the 25 W mode: 25 W mode cap (vendor) + 3 W carrier/NVMe/fan (unmeasured estimate, as for A). On the minimum-spec workload alone the NX draw is unmeasured, expected near the Orin Nano's 15 W-mode estimate (up to 15 W at the board, A). Max 43 W = 40 W mode (vendor; the mode the GPU-heavy growth loads need, 4 TPCs at 1173 MHz vs 408 MHz in the 25 W mode) + 3 W. A third party measured 31.9-32.2 W VDD_IN under full CPU+GPU stress in Super mode on the Orin Nano dev-kit carrier (35.2 W with the 3 W allowance); MAXN_SUPER is uncapped. NVENC draw is unmeasured and not counted (as the OAK encoder is not counted in A-D). Battery side at 0.88: 28/0.88 = 31.8 W in the 25 W mode (3.4 W inside the 35.2 W budget) and 43/0.88 = 48.9 W in the 40 W mode (13.6 W over it); share of the resulting walking total 19.0% at 100 cm and 15.5% at 120 cm in the 25 W mode, 26.5% and 21.9% in the 40 W mode (resulting totals 184.6 W and 222.6 W).
architectures.volume_note: J401 carrier 115 x 115 x 38 mm (0.50 L): wider than the dev kit's 100 x 79 mm datasheet and 103 x 90.5 mm reseller envelopes that the study's 60 cm tray is built around, so it is meant for the larger 100-120 cm chests (check it against the chest station); the CTI carrier (87.6 x 58.8 mm) takes the same module if space is tight. Mass not computable: 200 g carrier (Seeed wiki) plus the module and heatsink (unpublished); Seeed's 1,100 g label is implausible (2.19 g/cm3 over the 115 x 115 x 38 mm envelope, about 81% of solid aluminium) and is probably a packaged weight, so weigh it. Price = $195.99 + $1,077.02 + $28.99 + $40 = $1,342. Airflow 2.6 x 43/31 = 3.61 L/s at 43 W (10 K rise), 2.35 L/s at 28 W.
architectures.covers_growth_spec: Full, as the requirements state for the NX 16GB at 100-120 cm, but only with the 40 W mode for the GPU-heavy parts: 157 TOPS sparse / 78 dense (vendor, Super), eight A78AE cores, 16 GB, two DLAs (vendor PeopleNet + NvDCF 153 FPS per DLA) and NVENC, enough for YOLO-s/m and pose at 640 and 15-30 Hz, OSNet x1.0 for 10 people, slam_toolbox or VIO, and Whisper plus a small LLM. In the 25 W mode it adds 8 cores, 16 GB, two DLAs at 614.4 MHz and NVENC but has less GPU than the Orin Nano 8GB in the same mode (4 TPCs at 408 vs 918 MHz, 44% of its TPC-MHz).
architectures.software_effort: Low: the same JetPack/TensorRT/Isaac ROS stack as A (JetPack 6.2 preinstalled, 7.2 supported; Isaac ROS 3.2, 4.6 and 5.0), the Seeed BSP, and DLA deployment through TensorRT or DeepStream. ONNX policy on the Teensy.
architectures.lifecycle: NX modules listed through Jan 2032; J401 carrier and J4012 in stock at Seeed (Nov 2026). The Orin Nano 2 (H1 2027; NVIDIA: 78 TOPS, 8-core CPU, 8 GB) may cover much of this tier at lower cost. RVC2 camera caveat for depth.
risks: Under the 15/25 W caps the NX 16GB has less GPU than an Orin Nano 8GB (25 W: 4 TPCs at 408 vs 918 MHz); its advantage needs the 40 W mode, 12 W above the 31 W budget at the board (+13.6 W at the battery).
No NX 16GB idle or detector-load measurement; the figures are vendor caps and one stress test.
Mass unverified (see volume note); weigh before committing.
The 19 V minimum input is marginal on 6S (fine on the 12S pack of the 100-120 cm robots).
43 W in a closed chest needs about 3.6 L/s at a 10 K rise; throttling and temperature at 40 W in the closed chest are untested.
$1,342 bare to $1,657.99 boxed; the owner has said price is not a constraint at these sizes.

synthesis.recommendation:
Re-budget first, move to a Raspberry Pi at 60-75 cm, and stay on NVIDIA at 100-120 cm, where the owner has said price is not a constraint.

1. Fix the budget. The study's 31 W Jetson line (35.2 W at the battery: 36.7% of the study's walking total at 60 cm, 31.2% at 75, 20.6% at 100, 16.9% at 120) is a mode ceiling plus allowance, not a draw. Third-party measurements put the Orin Nano module at 4.7-6.1 W idle with PCIe enabled (2.5 W only with display, audio and PCIe disabled), 10.3-12.3 W running YOLO26s end to end (host-bound) and 12.5-14.1 W with YOLOv8n flat out, both in uncapped MAXN SUPER. Capped in its 15 W mode, the dev kit should draw about 15 W at the board on a conservative estimate (17.0 W at the battery; no light-load measurement exists in that mode), with an 18 W ceiling; the forum's 6.2 W light-load figure was taken in the non-Super 7 W mode (reflash required), about 8.2 W at the board on that basis (architecture A). If the dev kit is on hand, measure it at the converter input with the real pipeline (bench test 1). The conservative re-budget alone moves the 60 cm runtime from about 34 to about 42 min, or about 47 min on the 7 W-mode basis (computed from the requirements' 34 min at 96 W).

2. 60 and 75 cm: primary C, a Raspberry Pi 5 8GB with the $70 AI HAT+ 13 TOPS (Hailo-8L) running the person detector and OSNet re-ID, while the head OAK-D Lite still computes depth and encodes the operator video. It has measured Pi + Hailo evidence (YOLOv8n 61.9 fps at batch 1 on a Pi 5; 12-15 fps sync and 20-23 fps async end to end for YOLO26n at 640 with video decode on the Pi) and keeps the detector if the end-of-life RVC2 camera is later replaced by a depth-only unit. The cost-down alternative D drops the HAT and runs the detector on the camera; its minimum-spec coverage is provisional until the requirements' acceptance test passes with re-ID added (detector >= 10 Hz and >= 25 re-ID crops/s alongside stereo, alignment and MJPEG; never measured). C and D draw about 8.0 and 5.9-6.7 W at the board excluding storage, weigh ~100 and ~75 g (estimates, excluding the SSD, or the M.2 HAT+ and NVMe) and cost $290 and $232, against 15.0 W (conservative), 174 g and $439 for the dev kit. Against the 15 W-capped Jetson the battery-side gain is 8.0 W (C) and 9.5 W (D), 4.8-5.8 min at 60 cm; it shrinks to 0.2-1.7 W only if the Jetson runs in the 7 W mode at the measured light-load draw, so mass, cost and heat matter as much as power. Keeping the dev kit (A) is the zero-porting fallback. For a production small-robot build the same software can move to a Compute Module 5 (8 GB / 32 GB eMMC, $205, -20 to +85 C) on a custom carrier with the 5 V buck, locking connectors and an M.2 slot (the official CM5 IO Board is the reference design).

3. 100 and 120 cm: compute is about 9-19% of the resulting walking total on the Jetson options (22-26% with the NX in its 40 W mode), and the growth spec matters most here. 100 cm: the Orin Nano 8GB, staged. Prototype on the dev kit (A: NVIDIA BSP, 174 g, $439, on the study's 12 V rail), then move to B (the module on Connect Tech's 10-60 V carrier: latching connectors, -25 to +85 C, 45 g carrier, $928.81) for production once B is weighed and its heatsink fit confirmed. Its 25 W mode, for growth features, reaches 31.8 W at the battery (19.0% of the walking total), just inside the existing budget. 120 cm: G, the Orin NX 16GB, only if mapping, voice and larger detectors are committed. Its GPU advantage needs the 40 W mode (43 W at the board, 48.9 W at the battery, 13.6 W over today's budget, 21.9% of a 222.6 W total); in the 25 W mode it fits the budget (31.8 W) and adds 8 cores, 16 GB, two DLAs and NVENC, but has less GPU than the Orin Nano. Without committed growth loads, use B as at 100 cm. F, the OAK 4 D Pro as a single camera-computer, is the beyond-Jetson alternative at 120 cm: 48 INT8 TOPS for about 8-14 W at the battery over the camera's 3 W budget line (vendor figures), against G's 48.9 W in the 40 W mode, but 674 g in the head, a DC-input PoE+ supply not yet sourced, Luxonis OS rather than Ubuntu (minimum spec only conditionally met) and the highest porting effort.

4. Considered, not shortlisted: RK3588 boards (E: 8.0 W excluding storage, up to 11.6 W with an NVMe lacking ASPM L1.2; 82 g; $219; capable, but a vendor 6.1 kernel, a 2.3x export-recipe spread, unverified re-ID and thin stock); Qualcomm QCS6490 boards (Dragon Q6A: 2.9 W idle and YOLOv8n ~10 ms in an ONNX Runtime QNN pipeline, but one USB 3 port, an artifact/runtime version lock and no official cooler; RB3 Gen 2: the best-documented Qualcomm ROS 2 SDK, $439, unmeasured power); IQ-9075 and IQ-8275 products (AIRbox Q900: only 'under 20 W' from the vendor, since its '100 TOPS at 25 W' line described an Orin NX; VENTUNO Q: now a QIR ROS 2 SDK target, but its 24 V input limit is below a full 6S pack and its power is unmeasured); Intel N150 + Hailo-8 ($541.90-554.15, Hailo-8 module price unverified; >= 137 g; never measured as a system; board out of stock) and Lunar/Panther Lake modules ($643-2,599, unmeasured); Google Coral (software archived); AGX Orin and Thor (forum quick measurements of ~7 W and ~16 W idle; $3,499 and $5,499).

5. Invariants for every option: the plan puts the policy, CAN loop, ToF stop and watchdog chain on the Teensy, but that firmware and the ONNX export do not exist yet; until they do, a Linux crash publishes nothing and does not end in a controlled stop (PREEMPT_RT plus CUDA is unproven on JetPack 6; the Pi's stock kernel showed a 36.8 ms worst case under stress). HOG must give way to a DNN detector on an accelerator on any ARM host. Track in the gravity-aligned ground frame on the host (or in F's onboard app) with per-frame camera pose, because the camera now rides on the moving head. Feed the OAK from the robot 5 V rail through the Y-adapter. All options except F rely on the RVC2 OAK-D for depth, whose Myriad X is being discontinued (Luxonis stock for about five years from 2025): buy spare cameras. Successors: a depth-only camera (Orbbec, RealSense) with a host NPU or GPU, which favours C over D, or, as a watch item, the OAK 4 Lite (RVC4 EVT prototype; vendor: $779-879, ~206 g, 8 W sustained at 25 C, 25 W USB-PD, one per order), which would keep detection on the camera. NVIDIA has announced the Orin Nano 2 for H1 2027 (vendor claims); keep Jetson carriers SODIMM-compatible and re-check it before a production buy.

per_size.primary: C: Raspberry Pi 5 8GB + AI HAT+ 13 TOPS (Hailo-8L) running the person detector and OSNet re-ID, with the OAK-D Lite computing stereo depth and the operator H.264/MJPEG; ground-frame tracking on the Pi.
per_size.alternative: D: the same Pi without the HAT, with the detector on the OAK-D Lite's RVC2, as a cost-down ($58 and ~25 g less, ~1.3 W less at the board, estimates) once the requirements' acceptance test passes with re-ID added (detector >= 10 Hz and >= 25 re-ID crops/s alongside stereo, alignment and MJPEG); on-camera re-ID has never been measured. Storage moves from C's USB SSD to an NVMe on the M.2 HAT+.
per_size.why: At 60 cm compute is the largest discretionary load: the 31 W budget is 35.2 W at the battery, 36.7% of the 96 W walking total. C carries the minimum spec at ~8.0 W at the board excluding storage (9.1 W at the battery, 13.0% of the resulting 69.9 W total; computed runtime ~46.7 min against 34 min on the budget), ~100 g (estimate, excluding the SSD) and $290, with measured Pi + Hailo detector rates and vendor re-ID rates, and its detector survives a later switch to a depth-only camera. D would draw ~5.9-6.7 W (6.7-7.6 W at the battery, ~11.1%; ~47.7 min), ~75 g (excluding the M.2 HAT+ and NVMe) and $232, but its 1.3 W margin over C sits inside the estimate spread. Against the existing dev kit capped in its 15 W mode (A: 15.0 W at the board, conservative; ~41.9 min) C saves ~8.0 W at the battery (~4.8 min), ~74 g (estimates) and $149; only if the Jetson is reflashed to the 7 W mode and draws like the forum measurement (~46.6 min) does the gain shrink to ~0.2 W. If the dev kit is already owned, the Pi route adds $290 (C) or $232 (D) to the first robot and saves $149-207 on later builds. A remains the zero-porting fallback; the growth tier is not needed at this size (the requirements keep it to 100-120 cm).

per_size.primary: C: same as 60 cm, a Raspberry Pi 5 8GB + AI HAT+ 13 TOPS with depth and video on the OAK-D Lite (same camera, drives and software as 60 cm).
per_size.alternative: D: drop the HAT and run detection on the OAK-D Lite once the RVC2 acceptance test, including re-ID at >= 25 crops/s, passes.
per_size.why: Same sensors and drives as 60 cm (OAK-D Lite, RMD-X4), so one software stack serves both sizes. The budget is 31.2% of the 113 W walking total; C brings compute to 10.5% of the resulting total (9.1 W at the battery; computed runtime ~37.7 min vs 29 min on the budget) and D to ~8.9% (~38.4 min), against 18.0% (~34.6 min) for a conservatively estimated dev kit capped at 15 W and ~37.6 min on its 7 W-mode basis. D's extra saving over C (~1.5 W at the battery, 1.3 W at the board, estimates; ~0.7 min) matters even less here than at 60 cm, so start on C and move to D only if the camera passes its acceptance test. Keeping the dev kit in its 15 W mode (A) is the no-porting fallback.

per_size.primary: Orin Nano 8GB, staged: prototype on A (the existing dev kit: NVIDIA BSP, 174 g as sold, $439, on the study's 12 V rail from the 48-to-12 V converter), then B (the same module on the Connect Tech Super Hadron-DM 10-60 V carrier) for production once B is weighed and its heatsink fit confirmed; 15 W mode by default, 25 W for growth features; OAK-D Pro W for depth and encoding.
per_size.alternative: G: Orin NX 16GB if mapping, voice and larger detectors will run together (its GPU advantage needs the 40 W mode).
per_size.why: Compute is 20.6% of the 171 W walking total on the budget but ~11.2% of the resulting total for the Orin Nano in its 15 W mode (17.0 W at the battery, conservative), and the owner has said price is not a constraint at this size, so headroom and robustness are worth more than the last few watts. The Orin Nano covers the minimum spec and moderate growth (67 TOPS and six cores: YOLO-s/pose, OSNet x1.0, Whisper, slam_toolbox); its 25 W mode reaches 31.8 W at the battery (19.0%), just inside the existing budget. A has the lowest porting effort (NVIDIA BSP) and a known kit mass. B's case is production fit, not speed or software: latching connectors, a -25 to +85 C rating, a 45 g carrier and 10-60 V input, against a dev-kit carrier not intended for production, for $928.81 and an unknown total mass. Its battery input saves only the compute's share of conversion, because the 12S bay keeps its 48-to-12 V converter for the Dynamixel appendage rail. On B, put the OAK-D Pro W on one USB 3.1 port with its Y-adapter feed and the Teensy and lidar adapter on a powered hub, or the lidar on a Teensy UART. Both carriers take an Orin NX, and possibly the Orin Nano 2 (same form factor per Electronic Design, not confirmed by NVIDIA). G's 25 W mode fits the same 31.8 W but gives less GPU than the Orin Nano; its growth advantage needs the 40 W mode (48.9 W at the battery, 26.5%). If growth is dropped, C with the AI HAT+ 26 TOPS ($330; ~8.5-9.8 W at the board and 9.6-11.1 W at the battery, 6.6-7.6%: C's 8.0 W plus Sixfab's 0.45 W Hailo-8-over-Hailo-8L proxy difference, up to 6.5 W host + the Hailo-8's 3.3 W vendor typical at ResNet-50) is the low-power option, though its four-core CPU falls short of the growth CPU target.

per_size.primary: G: Jetson Orin NX 16GB (Super) on the 19-54 V Seeed J401 carrier (12S direct), only if growth loads (mapping, voice, larger detectors) are committed; 25 W mode for everyday following and 40 W for the growth workloads; OAK-D Pro W for depth; NVENC for the operator stream. Without committed growth loads, use B as at 100 cm.
per_size.alternative: F: Luxonis OAK 4 D Pro Wide (RVC4) as the single camera-computer, with the Teensy unchanged; minimum spec only conditionally met (Luxonis OS, Wi-Fi by dongle, USB data at alpha).
per_size.why: With 209 W walking, the flagship is where the owner's growth features (voice, mapping, larger models) would live and price is not a constraint. G is justified only by those committed loads: its GPU advantage over the Orin Nano needs the 40 W mode, 43 W at the board and 48.9 W at the battery, 13.6 W over today's budget and 21.9% of a 222.6 W walking total, with 3.6 L/s of chest airflow. In its 25 W mode it fits the existing budget (31.8 W at the battery, 15.5%) and adds 8 cores, 16 GB, two DLAs at 614.4 MHz and NVENC, but has less GPU than the Orin Nano 8GB (4 TPCs at 408 vs 918 MHz). Like for like: B in its 15 W mode is capped 11.4 W below G's 25 W-mode ceiling (20.5 vs 31.8 W at the battery); at their growth ceilings B's 25 W mode is 31.8 W against G's 48.9 W in the 40 W mode; on the same minimum-spec load the difference is unmeasured. F trades CUDA and 16 GB for one device that replaces both the OAK-D Pro W and the computer: 48 INT8 TOPS for ~8-14 W at the battery over the camera's 3 W budget line (vendor figures only; 7.3% of the resulting total at the planning value), about 35 W below G's 40 W-mode figure. Its 674 g is ~25-30% of the head+neck allowance here, the most tolerable of the four sizes, but it needs a DC-input PoE+ injector and switch (not yet sourced), the follow stack rebuilt as on-camera containers on Luxonis OS, and 10-15 W of skull cooling.

bench_tests_before_committing: Jetson re-budget (first; no purchase if the dev kit is on hand): measure the Orin Nano Super dev kit at the DC-DC input and with tegrastats VDD_IN (to split the module from the unmeasured 2-3 W carrier/NVMe/fan overhead) while running the real pipeline: OAK-D Lite at 640x400 RGB + 320x200 depth at 10-15 Hz, YOLO-nano TensorRT at 416, OSNet on <= 5 crops, ground-frame tracker, grid and planner, operator stream from the OAK encoder, rosbag2 MCAP to the NVMe. Repeat in the 15 W, 25 W and MAXN SUPER modes (and in the non-Super 7 W mode if a reflash is acceptable), with PCIe and the NVMe enabled; log idle, mean, p99 and peak power, temperatures and throttling inside the closed shell. Re-set the 31 W compute line, runtime and the 2.6 L/s airflow from the result.

RVC2 acceptance test (the requirements' own gate, and the gate for moving from C to D) on an OAK-D Lite and an OAK-D Pro W with DepthAI >= 3.11.0: stereo depth with RGB alignment, YOLOv6n at 416x416 and 512x288 (plus YOLOv8n/YOLO11n at 416) as a SpatialDetectionNetwork, OSNet re-ID on up to 5 crops, and MJPEG/H.264 for the operator page, all at once, with neck expression motion and walking. Pass: >= 10 Hz detections and, at the same time, embeddings for up to 5 tracked people at >= 5 Hz (>= 25 crops/s), <= 60 ms acquisition age, p95 chain <= 200 ms, no crash in a 1 h run. Log the SHAVE/CMX allocation (cameras take 3-6 of 16 slices) and camera current on the Y-adapter feed. Fail: keep the AI HAT+ (C).

Pi 5 host load: the full follow stack on Ubuntu 24.04 + ROS 2 Jazzy (depthai-ros C++ ingest, 2.5D grid from the 320x200 depth image, arc planner, ground-frame tracker with per-frame camera pose, re-ID gallery and ambiguity latch, the 25 ms TwistStamped timer, web relay of the OAK bitstream, compressed rosbag2 at 1-5 MB/s to the SSD) on a Pi 5 8GB with Active Cooler inside the closed shell, first with the detector on an AI HAT+ (C), then on the camera (D). Measure CPU load, 25 ms timer jitter, end-to-end latency, 5 V input power including the SSD (to check the 5.7-6.5 W host estimates and rank C against D), SoC temperature and throttling; size the 5 V supply against CNX's 16.8 W peak with drives and the ~18 W HAT worst case.

Hailo specifics (C): YOLOv8n/YOLO11n HEFs compiled at 416 px with the Dataflow Compiler (the zoo HEFs are 640x640) plus OSNet x1.0, end to end with async, pipelined HailoRT and C++ pre/post (not hw-only). Pass: detector >= 10 Hz with re-ID on <= 5 crops at >= 5 Hz running at the same time on the one Hailo-8L, mean per-frame time < 100 ms, p95 chain <= 200 ms. Also log per-chip peak power (Sixfab's 9.2-17.8 W system peaks were not broken out), HAT temperature against its 0-50 C rating, HailoRT and its PCIe driver on the chosen OS, and PCIe Gen 3 link errors under vibration (shaker or walking).

Detector accuracy on the real head geometry: truncated bodies at 1.0-2.5 m (where HOG's full-body template fails), people out to 5.5 m, and the Pro W's 150 deg lens after on-camera undistortion, for each precision used (RVC2 FP16, Hailo INT8, TensorRT INT8/FP16, RKNN INT8).

Re-ID and no-silent-switch behaviour: crossing and occlusion trials with the chosen OSNet variant on the chosen accelerator, with the ground-frame tracker running while the robot walks and moves its neck; pass >= 80% reacquisition after <= 2 s occlusion and stop-and-report within 0.5 s on ambiguity. No Orin Nano, Pi CPU, RK3588 or QCS6490 re-ID benchmark exists.

Camera power and USB: feed the OAK from the robot 5 V rail through the Y-adapter (a Pi-powered OAK-D Lite browned out the Pi), and log current with the Pro W's dot projector at the brightness the floor actually needs (DepthAI 3.12.0 warns that full power on both emitters can crash RVC2 devices).

Teensy link and failure handling: the firmware (CAN loop, policy, request expiry, watchdogs) does not exist yet and gates every option. Test the clock-sync ping over USB serial, UART or Ethernet, neck-encoder and IMU timestamps aligned to camera frames within 10-20 ms, MCU request expiry <= 200 ms, and a Linux kill / power-pull test that must end in the MCU's controlled stop-and-stand.

Supply rails: 6S sag to end of discharge and 12S at 50.4 V against each carrier's input range (the Seeed J401's 19 V minimum is marginal on 6S); efficiency of the actual buck or carrier regulator at the measured load, to replace the 0.88 placeholder; the Pi 5 on a non-PD 5 V/5 A buck with PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000.

Storage under vibration: compressed rosbag2 at 1-5 MB/s with raw RGB-D bursts at ~13 MB/s to the NVMe or USB SSD while walking, logging the storage's own draw (C, D and E exclude it); on an RK3588 board, measure the NVMe idle penalty (one report: ~5 W idle without ASPM L1.2).

If F is pursued: OAK 4 D Pro power at the PoE+ or USB-PD input with the real app (stereo, detection, re-ID, ground-frame tracker, ROS 2 container, encoder), skull temperature in the closed head, Ethernet latency and jitter to the Teensy through the switch, and the efficiency and mass of a DC-input PoE+ injector on the 12S bus.

If G is pursued: the growth workload (YOLO-s at 640, OSNet x1.0 for up to 10 people, slam_toolbox, Whisper) in the 25 W and 40 W modes (GPU 408 vs 1173 MHz) and with the detector on a DLA; idle and mean input power, since no NX 16GB measurement exists; and a closed-chest throttle and temperature run at 40 W with the 3.6 L/s airflow it needs.
synthesis.answer_to_owner:
Short answer: yes for the two small robots, mostly no for the two big ones, and the first fix is the power budget rather than the computer.

The Jetson is not as hungry as the study assumes. The study books it at 31 W (35 W from the battery). Independent measurements of the same module show about 5-6 W at idle, 10-12 W running a mid-size detector end to end, and 12.5-14 W with a small detector flat out, all with no power cap; the follower needs much less. Capped in its 15 W mode, the dev kit should draw no more than about 15 W at the board while following, with a hard ceiling near 18 W (my estimates; nobody has measured it at light load in that mode). If you already have the dev kit, measure it on the bench before buying anything: on that conservative estimate alone the 60 cm robot goes from about 34 to about 42 minutes of walking (computed).

60 and 75 cm: a Raspberry Pi 5 makes sense. I would start with a Pi 5 8GB plus Raspberry Pi's $70 AI HAT+ (a 13 TOPS Hailo chip) that finds people and recognises who it is following, while the OAK-D Lite in the head keeps computing depth and compressing the video for the operator page. That is about 8 W, about 100 g and $290 (estimates; the SSD's power and weight are extra), against about 15 W (conservative), 174 g and $439 for the Jetson kit. The OAK-D Lite's own chip may be able to find people too, which would let you drop the HAT (about 6-7 W, about 75 g, $232), but nobody has measured it doing depth, video, detection and the re-identification that prevents silent target switches all at once, so treat that as a later cost-down after a bench test. Against the 31 W budget either one frees about 26-28 W from the battery (about 47-48 minutes at 60 cm, computed). Against a properly capped Jetson the gain is about 8-9.5 W, or 5-6 extra minutes at 60 cm, and only 0.2-1.7 W if the Jetson can run in its 7 W mode (which needs a reflash) at the low measured draw, so the lower weight, cost and heat are as much the reason as the power. If you already own the dev kit, the Pi route adds $232-290 for the first robot; the $149-207 saving applies to later builds.

100 and 120 cm: stay with NVIDIA. There, computing is about 9-19% of walking power, the growth features (mapping, voice, bigger vision models) matter most, and you have said price is not a constraint. At 100 cm, keep the Orin Nano: prototype on the dev kit, then move to the same module on a rugged carrier that takes battery voltage directly (Connect Tech, about $929) for production, mainly for its locking connectors and temperature rating. At 120 cm, the larger Orin NX 16GB is worth it only if mapping, voice and bigger models are definitely coming: its extra graphics speed needs its 40 W mode, about 49 W from the battery or 13.6 W more than today's budget, while in its 25 W mode it fits the budget but is slower on graphics than the Orin Nano. Otherwise use the 100 cm Orin Nano setup. NVIDIA has also announced an Orin Nano 2 for the first half of 2027 (NVIDIA claims 78 TOPS and 8 cores; a trade outlet says it is the same size as today's module, which NVIDIA has not confirmed), so re-check it before a production buy.

The interesting non-Jetson option there is Luxonis's OAK 4 D Pro, a camera with a 48 TOPS computer inside that could replace both the head camera and the Jetson for roughly 8-14 W more than the 3 W the study books for the camera (Luxonis's own figures; nobody has measured it independently). It costs $1,249, puts 674 g in the head, needs a battery-powered PoE+ injector that still has to be found, and runs Luxonis's own Linux rather than Ubuntu, so the follow software would have to be rebuilt as apps on the camera. Treat it as an experiment.

Other boards: Rockchip RK3588 boards such as the Orange Pi 5 Max (about $219) are in the same power range as the Pi plus Hailo, but they rely on vendor kernels, their re-identification path is untested, stock is patchy, and an NVMe drive may add a few watts at idle. Avoid Google Coral (its software is archived) and the big Jetsons such as AGX Orin or Thor (overkill: about 7-16 W at idle in quick forum measurements, and $3,499-5,499).

What does not change: the plan puts the walking policy, the motor CAN loop, the ToF stop and the watchdogs on the Teensy. That firmware still has to be written whichever computer you choose, and until it exists a Linux crash does not end in a controlled stop. The current HOG person detector has to move to the camera, a Hailo chip or a GPU, because it is too slow on any of these ARM boards, and the tracker has to account for the camera now riding on the moving head. Every option except the OAK 4 depends on the OAK-D's Myriad X chip, which is being discontinued; Luxonis says its stock covers about five years from 2025, so buy spare cameras, and keep an eye on the lighter OAK 4 Lite (an early prototype today) as a possible successor. Prices also jumped in 2026: the Jetson kit went from $249 to $399 and a Pi 5 8GB from $80 to $175.
