issues.where: F_oak4_d_pro_camera_computer: power_w_typical 10.6, power_w_max 20.6 and power_basis; also recommendation item 3 ('about 6-12 W at the battery over the camera line'), per_size[120].why ('~6-12 W ... 5.8% at the planning value') and answer_to_owner ('roughly 6-12 W more than the camera alone uses')
issues.problem: Wrong subtraction. The 4.4 W subtracted as the 'camera line' is the study's whole 60-75 cm sensor line (camera + two ToF + foot sensing), not the camera. The study books the OAK-D Pro W at a 3.0 W base. At 100-120 cm, where F is proposed, the sensor line is 5.85 W, and the ToF, foot-sensing and lidar loads in it stay when F replaces the camera. F's increment is therefore understated by 1.4 W at the board (1.6 W at the battery). The hedge 'If the study's Pro W line is above 4.4 W, the increment is smaller' points the wrong way: the Pro W line is below 4.4 W, so the increment is larger.
issues.evidence: Input requirements workload[0].compute_need: 'Camera power: 2.5-3 W base, up to +0.5 W stereo, +0.5 W encoder, +1 W NN'. Survey oak_d_pro_w_rvc2 power_basis: 'Vendor: 2.5-3 W base plus streaming'. Study catalog hardware/trex_form_study/designlab/data/parts.json: luxonis_oak_d_lite and luxonis_oak_d_pro_w at 3 W typical (research parts_2026-11-07.json parts[8], [9]: power_typ_w 3); st_vl53l5cx_carrier 0.5 W; ldrobot_stl19p 1.45 W. Round-one outputs hardware/trex_form_study/round1/stage_a/candidates/*.json, power.aux.loads.sensors: 4.4 W at 60/75 cm (= 3.0 camera + 2 x 0.5 ToF + 2 x 0.2 foot sensing, designlab/build.py:386-388, 485-487, 505-507) and 5.85 W at 100/120 cm (+1.45 W lidar).
issues.fix: Subtract the 3.0 W camera base. Board: typical 15 - 3 = 12.0 W (low end 10 - 3 = 7.0 W), max 25 - 3 = 22.0 W. Battery at 0.88: 13.6 W typical (8.0 W low end), 25.0 W max, 21.6 W below the 35.2 W budget. Shares on the synthesis's basis: 8.0% at 100 cm and 6.5% at 120 cm (9.1% and 7.3% of the re-budgeted totals). Change '6-12 W' to '8-14 W' in recommendation 3, per_size[120] (where '5.8%' becomes '6.5%') and answer_to_owner. Replace the hedge with: 'the study books the Pro W at 3 W base (parts[9]); the other 2.85 W of the 5.85 W sensor line (ToF, foot sensing, lidar) stays.'

issues.where: Every 'share of walking power' figure: A/B 18.3/15.6/10.3/8.4%, C 10.1/8.5/5.6/4.6%, D 8.5/7.2/4.8/3.9%, E 9.5/8.0/5.3/4.3%, F 7.0/5.8%, G 18.6/15.2% (28.6/23.4% at 40 W); the per_size why fields; recommendation item 3 ('8-19%'); answer_to_owner ('about 8-19%')
issues.problem: Inconsistent basis. Each option's battery-side power is divided by the study's walking totals (96/113/171/209 W). Those totals include the 35.2 W Jetson budget. The runtimes printed beside the shares, however, use the re-budgeted total (total - 35.2 + option). So the shares are not shares of the option's own walking power, and they disagree with the runtimes. The low-power options come out understated and G's 40 W ceiling overstated.
issues.evidence: The brief says the walking totals include the Jetson set ('of which the Jetson set is budgeted at 31 W'). The synthesis's runtimes reproduce only with re-budgeted totals, e.g. D at 60 cm: 34 x 96 / (96 - 35.23 + 8.15) = 47.4 min. On that basis the shares are: A/B 22.5/18.5/11.5/9.2%; C 13.7/11.0/6.6/5.3%; D 11.8/9.5/5.7/4.5%; E 13.0/10.5/6.3/5.0%; G typical 19.0% (100 cm) and 15.5% (120 cm); G at 40 W 26.5% and 21.9%. The budget shares 36.7/31.2/20.6/16.9% are correct, because there the 35.2 W is part of the total.
issues.fix: Either relabel every option share as '% of the study's budgeted walking power (96/113/171/209 W)', or recompute against the re-budgeted totals (values above). On the recomputed basis, the Jetson options at 100-120 cm span about 9-19%, D at 60 cm is 11.8% (not 8.5%), and G at 40 W is 26.5% at 100 cm (not 28.6%).

issues.where: D_pi5_oak_on_camera_inference power_basis, the cross-check sentence ('with the camera on its own 5.1 V feed, a forum user measured the Pi alone at 4 W at load 2.0 and 7 W at load 4.0 while depthai-ros published RGB, detections and depth')
issues.problem: Verification correction misapplied: the measurement conditions are misstated. The 4 W and 7 W figures come from post #1 of the thread. In the stable separate-feed setup only the camera was measured (3.25 W); the Pi's own draw was not reported.
issues.evidence: Smart-camera verification, oak_d_lite_rvc2 correction of the 9.5/10.1 W readings: 'The stable setup fed the camera from a separate 5.1 V supply, with 3.25 W measured at the camera, and the Pi's own draw was not reported. Estimated stable total: Pi at 4-7 W (the poster's load-2 and load-4 figures) plus about 3.3 W for the camera, so about 7.3-10.5 W.' Evidence line: 'Post #1 also gives the Pi alone: 4W for 2.0 load, and 7W at 4.0 load'.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: 'Cross-check: post #1 of the same thread gives the Pi alone at about 4 W (load 2.0) and 7 W (load 4.0). With the camera on a separate 5.1 V feed only the camera was measured (3.25 W), and the Pi's draw was not reported. The verification's estimated stable total is 7.3-10.5 W including the camera.' Keep the note that NVMe and M.2 HAT+ draw are excluded.

issues.where: C power_basis (8.5 W typical / 18.5 W max), D power_basis (7.2 W / 11.3 W) and D volume_note (0.95 L/s airflow), E power_basis (8.0 W / 15.7 W)
issues.problem: Storage power is counted unevenly. A, B and G carry a 3 W carrier/NVMe/fan allowance that includes the NVMe. C (USB SSD), D (NVMe on the M.2 HAT+) and E (NVMe) price their storage at $40 but add no storage power. D's 11.3 W 'max', and the airflow and buck sizing taken from it, are bare-board stress-ng plus camera shares, so they are not a maximum for D's own parts list. E's parts list includes the very NVMe whose idle penalty the synthesis marks 'not included'. These omissions widen the C/D/E advantage over A/B.
issues.evidence: jetson_orin_nano_super_devkit power_basis: 'Kit power at the DC input is module power plus carrier, NVMe and fan overhead; that overhead is unmeasured, estimated at 2-3 W'. rpi5_8gb_active_cooler power_basis: CNX '16.8 W peak with USB drives attached' (wall meter, PSU included) against 9.8 W stress-ng for the bare board. opi5_max_6gb power_basis: 'about 5 W idle with an NVMe SSD fitted (no ASPM L1.2)' against 1.4 W, i.e. +3.6 W; its fit_notes say 'Leave out the NVMe SSD if idle power matters'.
issues.fix: Label the C, D and E power figures 'excluding storage', and say that A, B and G include the NVMe inside their 3 W. For E, show 8.0-11.6 W at the board (9.1-13.2 W at the battery) until ASPM L1.2 is confirmed, or return to the survey's microSD build and drop the $40 NVMe from the price. Present D's 11.3 W as 'excluding the NVMe', not as a maximum, and size its 5 V buck and airflow with margin, noting CNX's 16.8 W peak with drives attached.

issues.where: A_orin_nano_super_devkit power_basis, light-load case (8.7 W board, 9.9 W battery, 25.3 W saving, 46.2/37.4 min). Carried into C ('about 0.2 W'), D ('1.7 W'), recommendation items 1-2 ('8.7-15.5 W', '0-9 W'), per_size 60/75 and answer_to_owner ('9-16 W')
issues.problem: Basis mismatch. A is defined in the 15 W mode of the Super flash configuration. Its light-load case rests on 6.2 W VDD_IN measured in the 7 W mode, which exists only in the non-Super flash configuration (the synthesis's own risk list says so). No 15 W-mode light-load measurement exists. So the low end of A's range, and the near-zero lower bound of the Pi's advantage built on it, come from a mode A does not run. The 2 W carrier figure used there is also the unmeasured low end of the 2-3 W estimate.
issues.evidence: jetson_orin_nano_super_devkit power_basis: '4.7 W idle and 6.2 W with two 8 FPS 640x640 FP16 detector streams on a 7 W-mode configuration'. Software field: 'the Super flash configuration offers 15 W, 25 W (default) and MAXN_SUPER; the non-Super configuration offers 15 W and 7 W'. The Jetson verification's 7 W-mode note also places the 6.2 W measurement in the 7 W mode.
issues.fix: Label the 8.7 W case '7 W mode, non-Super flash (reflash required)'. Present A's 15 W-mode figure as 'up to 15.5 W conservative; light-load draw unmeasured'. Make the Pi's 0.2-1.7 W lower-bound advantage explicitly conditional on running the Jetson in the 7 W mode.

issues.where: D_pi5_oak_on_camera_inference risks[1] ('the zoo OSNet runs 49 inferences/s network-only on RVC2 while sharing SHAVEs, so <= 5 crops at 5-10 Hz (25-50/s) is at the limit')
issues.problem: Overstated margin. 49/s is a standalone network-only rate, not a rate measured while sharing SHAVEs. Sharing with the detector, and with cameras that take 3-6 of the 16 CMX slices, can only lower it, so 25-50/s is at best at the limit and possibly beyond it. The combined rate is unmeasured.
issues.evidence: oak_d_lite_rvc2 benchmarks: 'OSNet person re-ID (market1501) ... 49.09 ... vendor model zoo, network only, one person crop per inference'. Fit_notes: 'optionally an OSNet re-ID crop network (49 inferences/s network-only, sharing the SHAVEs)'. Smart-camera verification: whole-pipeline figures are 'the ceiling for a detection-only pipeline. Rates with stereo, encoder and tracker running are unmeasured and will be lower'; 'about 10 remain with a 4K colour stream ... 6 SHAVEs x 2 threads'.
issues.fix: Write: '49/s is the standalone network-only rate. With the detector, stereo and encoder sharing the 10-13 free CMX slices, the available re-ID rate is lower and unmeasured, so 5 crops at 5 Hz (25/s) may already exceed it.' Then point to bench test 2 or to architecture C.

issues.where: per_size[100].why: 'C with the AI HAT+ 26 TOPS ($330; ~9.7 W at the battery, 5.6%)'
issues.problem: Unsupported as stated. The 9.7 W and 5.6% are architecture C's Hailo-8L figures, built on the Hailo-8L's 1.5 W vendor typical, reused for the Hailo-8 with no basis given. The Hailo-8's supported typical figures are higher. The $330 price ($175 + $5 + $110 + $40) is correct.
issues.evidence: C power_basis: '1.5 W Hailo-8L (vendor typical)'. For the Hailo-8, the verification (rpi5_8gb_hailo8_m2_on_m2_hat_plus) gives datasheet typical 2.4 W at MobileNet-SSD 996 fps and 3.3 W at ResNet-50, maximum 8.25 W. Sixfab system averages: 6.53 W (Hailo-8) against 6.08 W (Hailo-8L). hailo8_m2_mkey: 'The 1.5 W typical figure is my estimate for one 30 fps stream'.
issues.fix: Either cite the hailo8_m2_mkey estimate (1.5 W for one 30 fps stream, an estimate) as the basis for 9.7 W, or use the vendor typical: 6.5 + 2.4 + 0.5 = 9.4 W at the board, 10.7 W at the battery, 6.2% of 171 W (7.3% re-budgeted). The max stays about 18.5 W.

issues.where: A_orin_nano_super_devkit power_basis ('The default 25 W mode lifts the ceiling to the study's 31 W'); per_size[100].primary ('15 W mode, 25 W for growth features')
issues.problem: Internal inconsistency. A mixes the study's 6 W allowance with the synthesis's own 3 W + 0.5 W allowance. For the same module and mode, B gives 28.5 W. The 100 cm recommendation runs B in the 25 W mode for growth features but quotes only its 15 W-mode share (10.3%).
issues.evidence: B power_basis: '28.5 W (25 + 3 + 0.5) in the 25 W mode'. 28.5 / 0.88 = 32.4 W at the battery: 18.9% of 171 W (19.3% re-budgeted) and only 2.8 W below the 35.2 W budget.
issues.fix: In A, write '25 W mode: 28.5 W at the board (32.4 W at the battery)'. In per_size[100], add that B's 25 W growth mode reaches 32.4 W at the battery (about 19% of walking power), close to the existing budget.

issues.where: A, B and C power_w_typical/power_w_max (each includes '+0.5 W OAK encoder share'); D power_basis hedge ('If the study's 4.4 W camera line already includes the encoder, subtract 0.5 W'); E and G power_basis
issues.problem: Deviates from the brief's rule and is applied unevenly. The brief defines whole-set power as host + accelerator + camera inference share. A, B and C add a 0.5 W camera encoder share although no inference moves onto the camera in those architectures. E and G carry no allowance for their host encoders (RK3588 VPU, NVENC), so A-D are 0.5 W heavier than E and G. D's hedge rests on the misread camera line: the study books the camera at its 3 W base, which excludes the encoder.
issues.evidence: Requirements workload[0].compute_need: '2.5-3 W base, up to +0.5 W stereo, +0.5 W encoder, +1 W NN'. Study catalog designlab/data/parts.json: both OAK cameras at 3 W typical. E power_basis: 'plus the hardware encoder (unmeasured)'. G power_basis: 'NVENC replaces the OAK encoder share', with no NVENC power added.
issues.fix: Either follow the rule and drop the encoder share (A and B 15.0 W typical / 18.0 W max; C 8.0 W; D 6.7 W at the board), or keep it as an explicitly stated deviation and add a matching host-encoder allowance (or an 'encoder unmeasured' flag) to E and G. Delete D's hedge and state that the study's 3 W camera base excludes the encoder.

issues.where: Recommendation item 2 ('Against a measured, capped Jetson the battery-side gain is only about 0-9 W (0-6 min at 60 cm)'); per_size[60].why ('roughly 0-9 W ... ~$150-200'); A risks[0] ('The 31 W budget overstates the measured draw about 2-3x'); per_size[75].why ('C's extra ~1.3 W')
issues.problem: Mislabelled and mis-rounded summaries. A is not a measurement of the Jetson set: the module was measured, but the carrier, NVMe and fan are an unmeasured 2-3 W estimate. The figures also fall outside or short of their own computed ranges: the battery-side gain computes to 0.2-9.5 W, the budget-to-A ratio is 2.0-3.6x, and D saves $207 against A. The 75 cm '~1.3 W' is board-side while every figure around it is battery-side.
issues.evidence: Battery side: A 17.61 W (9.89 W light-load), C 9.66 W, D 8.15 W. C saves 0.23-7.95 W and D 1.73-9.46 W. Runtime gains at 60 cm: 0.15-5.72 min. 31/15.5 = 2.0 and 31/8.7 = 3.56. $439 - $232 = $207 and $439 - $290 = $149. C - D = 8.5 - 7.175 = 1.33 W at the board, 1.51 W at the battery.

issues.where: A_orin_nano_super_devkit power_basis ('Idle is 2.5-6.1 W measured'); recommendation item 1 ('2.5-6.1 W idle'); answer_to_owner ('about 2.5-6 W at idle')
issues.problem: Lower bound not applicable. The 2.5 W idle was measured with display, audio and PCIe disabled in the device tree. A's parts list needs PCIe for the M.2 2280 NVMe and the M.2 Key E Wi-Fi card, so 2.5 W is not reachable in this configuration. The applicable measured floor is 4.7 W.
issues.evidence: Jetson verification, power_w_idle correction: '4.7 W VDD_IN in 7 W mode on JetPack 6.2, and 2.5 W after disabling display, audio and PCIe in the device tree'.

issues.where: Recommendation item 1 ('10-14 W with a detector saturated'); answer_to_owner ('10-14 W with a detector running flat out'); key_sources hokwangchoi entry ('(6.13 ms FP16 / 4.9 ms INT8 in 15 W mode; 12.5-14.1 W flat out)')
issues.problem: Mislabelled conditions. The 10.3-12.3 W runs were YOLO26s end-to-end, where pre/post-processing was the bottleneck, so the detector was not saturated. Only the YOLOv8n runs (12.5-14.1 W) were flat out. Both sets were measured in uncapped MAXN SUPER, yet the key-source line puts '12.5-14.1 W flat out' straight after '15 W mode'.
issues.evidence: Jetson verification, YOLO26s correction: 'INT8 gave no end-to-end gain (74.54 vs 74.56 img/s), so pre/post-processing was the bottleneck'. jetson_orin_nano_super_devkit power_basis: '14.1 W FP16 and 12.5 W INT8 with YOLOv8n running flat out at 225 and 286 FPS', in the MAXN SUPER benchmark rows.
issues.fix: Write '10.3-12.3 W running YOLO26s end-to-end (host-bound) and 12.5-14.1 W with YOLOv8n flat out, both in uncapped MAXN SUPER'. In key_sources, write '12.5-14.1 W flat out in MAXN SUPER'.

issues.where: A volume_note ('Both fit the 117 x 99 x 51 mm (0.59 L) chest tray at 60 cm next to the existing 12 V DC-DC'); G volume_note ('wider than the 99 mm of the 60 cm tray'); B variants ('too wide for the 60 cm tray'); the 'fits the tray' claims in B, C, D and E
issues.problem: Unsupported. The 117 x 99 x 51 mm tray appears in no survey or verification. issues.where: per_size[120].why ('If growth features are not committed, B as at 100 cm saves ~14 W at the battery')
issues.problem: Basis mismatch. The 14 W compares B's measured-basis 15 W-mode typical (17.6 W) with G's 25 W-mode cap plus allowance (31.8 W), which the synthesis itself calls a planning value. It measures the gap between two modes and two bases, not between the boards. On the same minimum-spec load, the synthesis expects G at roughly the Orin Nano's 9-16 W.
issues.evidence: G power_basis: 'Typical 28 W is a planning value for the growth workload: 25 W mode cap ... on the minimum-spec workload alone expect roughly the Orin Nano's 9-16 W (unmeasured on NX)'. Caps at the battery: B in the 15 W mode 21.0 W, G in the 25 W mode 31.8 W, a 10.8 W difference.
issues.fix: Write 'B in its 15 W mode is capped about 10.8 W below G's 25 W-mode ceiling (21.0 vs 31.8 W at the battery); on the same minimum-spec load the difference is unmeasured (G expected near 9-16 W at the board)'.

issues.where: F_oak4_d_pro_camera_computer power_basis ('model-zoo network-only whole-board runs are 2.7-3.4 W for YOLOv6n 512x288 (vendor)')
issues.problem: Unsupported label. The verification lists 'whole board' as unverifiable, because the zoo pages do not say what was measured.
issues.evidence: Smart-camera verification, unverifiable: 'Model-zoo RVC4 power figures (3.38 W, 3.37 W, 3.13 W) described as whole board: the pages give power without saying what was measured.'

issues.where: A lifecycle ('Orin Nano 2 (vendor: 78 TOPS, 8 cores, LPDDR5X, 15-40 W, same form factor)'); B covers_growth_spec and lifecycle ('per NVIDIA, the Orin Nano 2' in the same socket)
issues.problem: Misattributed. LPDDR5X, the configurable 15-40 W range and the same form factor come from Electronic Design, not from NVIDIA. Labelling them 'vendor' or 'per NVIDIA' misattributes the power range and the socket compatibility that B's upgrade path relies on.
issues.evidence: Jetson verification missing_options[0]: 'NVIDIA (vendor) gives 78 TOPS, an 8-core Arm CPU and 8 GB ... Electronic Design adds: Ampere GPU, 8x Cortex-A78, LPDDR5X up to 120 GB/s, configurable 15-40 W, same form factor as Orin Nano Super.'
issues.fix: Write 'NVIDIA: 78 TOPS, 8-core CPU, 8 GB, H1 2027 (vendor); Electronic Design: LPDDR5X, 15-40 W, same form factor (socket compatibility not confirmed by NVIDIA)'.

issues.problem: Unverified input. $541.90 depends on a $179 Hailo-8 list price that the verification could not confirm. Its alternative total uses Mouser's $191.25, which is also unverified.

Using the $191.25 Mouser figure the total would be $554.15.' Unverifiable list: 'Hailo-8 $179 list price ... the cited Hailo page shows no price'; 'Every Mouser figure ... Mouser returned HTTP 503'.

issues.where: architectures[D].covers_minimum_spec; per_size[60] and per_size[75] primary; recommendation point 2; answer_to_owner (60-75 cm paragraph); bench_tests_before_committing[1] pass criteria
issues.problem: D is marked true for the minimum spec, but two of the spec's items are unproven on the camera. (1) The detector must hold >= 10 Hz with stereo, alignment and MJPEG running, and the ~35 fps figure comes from a detection-only pipeline. (2) The light re-ID net must run on <= 5 crops at 5-10 Hz, which on RVC2 needs 51-102% of the network-only OSNet rate while sharing SHAVEs with the detector. D's own text calls its coverage 'provisional'. The owner answer says the camera 'can also find people, track them and compress the video', mentions only a detection-rate test, and never mentions re-ID, which the smart-camera survey names as the open risk. The RVC2 acceptance test runs OSNet, but its pass line has no re-ID rate. The fallback is not free either: going from D to C moves the NVMe off the Pi's only PCIe lane. C has measured Pi+Hailo evidence and costs about $58, 25 g and 1.3 W more (estimates). D as the unqualified primary at both small sizes is weaker than the text presents.
issues.evidence: Smart-camera verification correction (oak_d_lite_rvc2 benchmarks): the 35/17/12/7 fps figures are 'camera plus DetectionNetwork pipeline only ... No StereoDepth, VideoEncoder, ObjectTracker or re-ID'. CMX correction: cameras use 3 (1080p) to 6 (4K) of the 16 slices. oak_d_lite_rvc2: OSNet at 49.09 inferences/s, network only. Requirements minimum_spec (b): OSNet x0.25-x0.5 on <= 5 crops at 5-10 Hz = 25-50 crops/s; 25/49.09 = 51% and 50/49.09 = 102%. smart_cameras category_findings: 'On a Pi-class host, the open risk is re-ID throughput on RVC2'. C evidence: rpi5_8gb_ai_hat_plus_13tops measured YOLOv8n at 61.9 fps (batch 1) on a Pi 5; raspberry_pi findings report Sixfab at 12-15 fps sync and 20-23 fps async end to end. Deltas: 290-232 = $58, 100-75 = 25 g, 8.5-7.175 = 1.3 W. C.parts: 'the HAT occupies the only PCIe lane'.
issues.fix: Set D.covers_minimum_spec to provisional, false until the acceptance test passes. Add to the pass line of bench test 2: embeddings for up to 5 tracked people at >= 5 Hz (>= 25 crops/s), running alongside detection, stereo and MJPEG. Then either make C the default build at 60-75 cm with D as a cost-down once it passes, or keep D first but state in per_size and in the owner answer that on-camera re-ID is unproven and that C ($290, ~100 g, ~8.5 W, estimates; storage moves to a USB SSD) is the planned fallback. Add to the owner answer that the camera must also run the re-identification network that prevents silent target switches, and that this combination has never been measured.

issues.where: per_size[120] primary and why; recommendation point 3; answer_to_owner (100-120 cm paragraph: 'in its 25 W mode it fits inside the existing budget'); per_size[120] 'B as at 100 cm saves ~14 W'
issues.problem: The 120 cm case presents G's 25 W mode as giving the flagship 'full growth headroom' inside the existing budget. The owner is told to use the NX if 'mapping, voice and bigger models will run together' and that 'in its 25 W mode it fits inside the existing budget'. The Jetson verification shows that at a 25 W cap the NX 16GB has less GPU than the Orin Nano 8GB, and G's own growth claim depends on the 40 W mode, which runs over the budget. Separately, 'B saves ~14 W' compares B's measured-basis estimate for the minimum workload with G's cap-based planning value for the growth workload.
issues.evidence: Jetson verification correction, seeed_recomputer_robotics_j4012_orin_nx_16gb fit_notes: NX 16GB Super runs 4 TPCs at 408 MHz in the 25 W mode and 4 TPCs at 1173 MHz in the 40 W mode; Orin Nano 8GB Super runs 4 TPCs at 612 MHz in the 15 W mode and at 918 MHz in the 25 W mode. In TPC-MHz that is 4x408 = 1632 against 4x918 = 3672, so G at 25 W has 44% of B's GPU clock at 25 W, and 67% of B's at 15 W (2448). G.covers_growth_spec: 'Full ... provided the 40 W mode is allowed'. G.power_basis: 43 W at the board in the 40 W mode, so 43/0.88 = 48.9 W at the battery, 48.9-35.2 = 13.6 W over the budget, and 48.9/209 = 23.4% of walking power. G.power_basis also puts the minimum workload at 'roughly the Orin Nano's 9-16 W (unmeasured on NX)', which is 10.2-18.2 W at the battery against B's 17.6 W.
issues.fix: State at 120 cm and in the owner answer that G is justified only by committed growth loads. Those need the 40 W mode: 43 W at the board, 48.9 W at the battery, 13.6 W over today's budget, 23.4% of 209 W, for a total of about 209-35.2+48.9 = 222.7 W. In its 25 W mode G adds 8 cores, 16 GB, two DLAs at 614.4 MHz and NVENC, but less GPU than B. Replace 'saves ~14 W' with like-for-like figures. On the same workload B and G are about equal. At their growth ceilings, B's 25 W mode is 28.5 W at the board (32.4 W at the battery) against G's 48.9 W at the battery. Compare F with G at G's growth figure, 48.9 W against 12.0 W (vendor), about 37 W apart. Add a closed-chest throttle and temperature run at 40 W (3.6 L/s) to G's bench test.

issues.where: architectures[F] covers_minimum_spec, parts, power_basis; per_size[120] alternative
issues.problem: F is marked true for the minimum spec but misses three of its host items, and its I/O plan over-subscribes one connector. It runs Luxonis OS, not the Ubuntu + ROS 2 pairing the spec requires; F's own risks admit this. It has no Wi-Fi without an unpriced USB dongle, and its USB data path is at alpha. The single M8 aux port is proposed for the Wi-Fi dongle, the Teensy UART, the $99 prototype CAN adapter and the lidar, and its USB host cannot run at the same time as USB-C. The M8 UART rate is never checked against the link requirement. The only Ethernet port is also the PoE+ power input, and no battery-fed injector is costed. The 2.7-3.4 W model-zoo figures are called 'whole-board', which the verification says the pages do not state.
issues.evidence: Requirements minimum_spec (c): 'USB or UART to the MCU, Wi-Fi, and Ubuntu + ROS 2 support'. software_constraints[0]: 'Any host needs a supported arm64 Ubuntu/ROS 2 pairing'. interfaces[1]: USB 2.0 HS, UART >= 2 Mbit/s or 100 Mbit Ethernet, with 1-2 KB sent up at 50-100 Hz (2 KB x 8 x 100 = 1.6 Mbit/s of payload). oak4_d_rvc4 interfaces: 'M8 8-pin aux: 5 V GPIO or UART, FSYNC/strobe, a USB 2.0 host (not usable together with USB-C) and a 5 V 5 W output'; 'CAN only through the M8 CAN adapter ($99, prototype access)'; USB at alpha. Smart-camera correction (oak4_d_rvc4): Luxonis's $29.99 PoE+ injector has US/EU mains plugs and weighs 138 g. smart_cameras unverifiable: the RVC4 model-zoo pages 'give power without saying what was measured'.
issues.fix: Mark F as conditional and list the exceptions: Luxonis OS instead of Ubuntu, Wi-Fi only through a dongle, USB data at alpha. Commit to one costed wiring plan. For example: PoE+ from a DC-input 802.3at injector on the 12S bus; the Teensy 4.1 on 100 Mbit Ethernet through a small switch on the injector's data side; the Wi-Fi dongle on the M8 USB host; the lidar on a Teensy UART; no prototype CAN adapter. Carry the injector and switch in price and mass as 'not found' until they are sourced. Relabel the 2.7-3.4 W figures as vendor model-zoo power with the measured scope unstated.

issues.where: answer_to_owner (Jetson paragraph, 60-75 cm paragraph, OAK 4 sentence, closing 'What does not change' paragraph); recommendation point 5
issues.problem: Several statements read as settled when the inputs say otherwise. (a) 'The Teensy keeps the walking policy, motors, ToF stop and watchdogs ... so a Linux crash still ends in a controlled stop': none of that firmware exists, the policy has no ONNX export, and today a crash publishes nothing. (b) 'The dev kit you already own': ownership is not established. If it is owned, the Pi route adds $232-290 to the first robot, and the ~$150-200 saving applies only to later builds. (c) 'Roughly 6-12 W' for the OAK 4 is a vendor maximum average minus the camera line, with no independent measurement. The answer omits its PoE+/25 W PD supply and the rebuild on Luxonis OS. The Pi's 'about 7 W' and 8.5 W are interpolation estimates and are not labeled as such. (d) The Orin Nano 2 is left out, although it bears on both 'stay with NVIDIA' and the power case for the small robots.
issues.evidence: Requirements realtime_layer: 'None of this exists yet. The only watchdogs are inside the Linux Python process ... a process crash publishes nothing'. Requirements workload (policy): 'No ONNX export exists and no policy bundle is committed'. growth_spec: 'Jetson Orin Nano Super 8 GB (current choice)'. oak4_d_pro_rvc4 power_basis: 'No third-party power measurement was found'. D and C power_basis: Geerling endpoints, interpolated. jetson verdict missing_options[0]: Orin Nano 2 announced 25 Aug 2026; vendor claims 78 TOPS, 8 cores and 'the same performance at 40% less power in the 15 W mode'; same form factor; due H1 2027; price not announced.
issues.fix: Rewrite the closing paragraph as: 'The plan puts the walking policy, the motor CAN loop, the ToF stop and the watchdogs on the Teensy. That firmware still has to be written whichever computer you choose, and until it exists a Linux crash does not end in a controlled stop.' Make the ownership conditional and give the first-unit cost. Label the OAK 4 and Pi watt figures as vendor figures or estimates, and name the OAK 4's power-supply and software costs. Add one line: NVIDIA has announced an Orin Nano 2 for H1 2027 (vendor claims); keep carriers SODIMM-compatible and re-check it before a production buy.

issues.where: architectures[D].where_inference_runs and software_effort ('tracking and 3D association move onto the camera'); bench_tests_before_committing[1]; also F's on-device ObjectTracker
issues.problem: D moves tracking onto the camera's ObjectTracker. The camera now sits on a moving head, and the requirements call for constant-velocity tracks in the gravity-aligned ground frame, with ego-motion compensation from MCU odometry and a per-frame camera pose. The surveys describe the ObjectTracker as associating by box, motion and optional camera-frame 3D position, with no ego-motion input, and it has no access to the neck encoder or leg odometry. On-camera tracks and velocities will therefore carry head and body motion into the target-lock and ambiguity decisions.
issues.evidence: Requirements workload (tracking): 'Constant-velocity Kalman tracks in the gravity-aligned ground frame, with ego-motion compensation from MCU odometry'; compute '< 1-2 ms per frame on one Linux core for <= 10 tracks; no accelerator'. Workload (time sync): camera pose = torso attitude x neck forward kinematics at the frame timestamp; neck motion of +/-9.7 deg at 0.55 Hz is ~1 deg per 30 ms, ~3.5 cm at 2 m. smart_cameras category_findings: the ObjectTracker 'associates by bounding box and motion (SHORT_TERM_IMAGELESS), with optional 3D spatial association and velocity output'.
issues.fix: Keep detection and spatial XYZ on the camera. Run the ground-frame Kalman tracker and association on the Pi, after composing each frame's camera pose. The requirements cost this at < 1-2 ms per frame, so D's host budget barely changes. Use the on-camera tracker ID only as an auxiliary cue. Run bench test 2 with neck expression motion and walking. For F, state that the follower app on the QCS8550 does the ground-frame tracking from the Teensy's neck and IMU stream.

issues.where: per_size[100] why; architectures[B] covers_growth_spec, risks, parts
issues.problem: The case for B over the dev kit A at 100 cm rests on points A shares or that do not hold. 'Lowest porting effort' belongs to A: B uses Connect Tech's BSP, which trails by a release, and JetPack 7.2 support is unconfirmed. The NX and Orin Nano 2 upgrade socket is not unique to B. 'Removes the 48 V converter' is a small gain, because the 12S bay keeps a 48->12 V converter for the 12 V appendage rail. Against that, B's mass is unknown, its heatsink is a Seeed part priced as a proxy with unverified fit, it costs $928.81 against $439, and its two USB 3.1 ports must carry the OAK-D Pro W, the lidar's USB-UART and the Teensy (its RS-232 headers are not TTL). B's real advantages are not the reasons given: latching connectors, a -25 to +85 C rating, a 45 g carrier and 10-60 V input, against a dev-kit carrier 'not intended for production'.
issues.evidence: cti_super_hadron_dm_orin_nano_8gb: 2x USB 3.1, 2x RS-232, latching connectors, -25 to +85 C; BSP through JetPack 6.2.2, 7.2 not confirmed. jetson verdict missing_options[2]: an Orin NX 16GB ran Super modes on NVIDIA's own Orin Nano Super dev-kit carrier at 19 V, ~32 W VDD_IN. missing_options[0]: Orin Nano 2 'same form factor'. jetson unverifiable: CTI's 49 g heatsink unverified; Orin Nano module mass unpublished. Requirements interfaces: 'At 12S the 48 V power bay carries a 48 -> 12 V converter'; Dynamixel TTL 'on the 12 V appendage rail' at 60-100 cm; STL-19P via USB-UART or an MCU UART. Price: 410+449.82+28.99+40 = 928.81.
issues.fix: Rewrite the 100 cm reason around ruggedness and production fit, and drop 'lowest porting effort' and the claim that the socket is unique. Consider A for the first 100 cm prototype (174 g as sold per a forum figure, NVIDIA BSP, $439) and B for production, once B has been weighed and its heatsink confirmed. State the USB plan: the OAK-D Pro W on its Y-adapter feed, plus a powered hub for the lidar adapter and the Teensy, or the lidar on a Teensy UART.

issues.where: architectures[D].power_basis ('Cross-check (smart-camera verification) ...') and power_w_typical
issues.problem: The cross-check misreads the verification. It says that with the camera on its own 5.1 V feed the poster measured the Pi at 4 W (load 2.0) and 7 W (load 4.0) while depthai-ros published. The verification says the Pi's draw in that stable setup was not reported; 4 W and 7 W are the poster's general Pi-alone figures. The camera share also likely double-counts. The measured OAK-D Lite drew 3.25-3.5 W while running RGB, detections and stereo, already under the 4.4 W camera line, yet D adds the vendor's 1.0 W AI and 0.5 W encoder on top. That makes 4.4+1.5 = 5.9 W, above the vendor's ~5 W all-features maximum and the 4.5 W spec-sheet maximum. With D's host at 1.5 cores against C's 2, the '1.3 W below C' ranking falls inside the estimate spread.
issues.evidence: smart_cameras verdict correction (oak_d_lite_rvc2 fit_notes): 'The stable setup fed the camera from a separate 5.1 V supply, with 3.25 W measured at the camera, and the Pi's own draw was not reported ... Post #1 also gives the Pi alone: 4W for 2.0 load, and 7W at 4.0 load'. oak_d_lite_rvc2 power_basis: 3.25-3.5 W measured with RGB, MobileNet detections and stereo; vendor 'up to ~5 W with every feature at 100%'; spec sheet 4.5 W max. D.power_basis: 5.675+1.0+0.5 = 7.175 W. C.power_basis: host at 2 cores, 6.5 W.
issues.fix: Rewrite the cross-check as: 'the poster quotes the Pi alone at 4 W (load 2.0) and 7 W (load 4.0), conditions unstated; the Pi's draw in the separately fed setup was not reported.' Show the camera increment as 0-1.5 W, with the measured camera as the low end. Give D as about 5.7-7.2 W at the board (6.4-8.2 W at the battery), and say that D and C cannot be ranked on power until bench test 3.

issues.where: architectures A/B power_basis vs C/D/E power_basis and mass_g; recommendation point 2; per_size[60]/[75] why; answer_to_owner ('about $232 with an SSD, about 75 g')
issues.problem: A and B include a 3 W carrier/NVMe/fan allowance, but C and D carry no storage power, and E's typical ignores the NVMe idle penalty that E itself flags. The A-vs-Pi gaps ('9.5 W ... to 1.7 W', '0-9 W') therefore credit the Pi with storage power that A is charged for. C's 18.5 W maximum may not cover a Pi with a USB drive attached. D's 75 g excludes the M.2 HAT+ and NVMe, although the rules say mass includes the carrier, and the owner answer pairs that 75 g with a $232 price that includes the SSD.
issues.evidence: A.power_basis: '+ 3 W carrier/NVMe/fan'. D.power_basis: 'NVMe and M.2 HAT+ draw are not in these measurements'. D.volume_note: 75 g 'excluding the M.2 HAT+ and NVMe'. C.parts: the USB 3 SSD is absent from power_basis. rpi5_8gb_active_cooler power_basis: CNX measured a '16.8 W peak with USB drives attached'. opi5_max_6gb power_basis: ~5 W idle with an NVMe lacking ASPM L1.2, against 1.4 W.
issues.fix: Apply the same storage allowance to C, D and E, or take storage out of A and B's 3 W and say so, then restate the A-vs-Pi gaps. In the owner answer, label D's mass as excluding the M.2 HAT+ and NVMe. Have bench test 3 measure the Pi while the SSD writes compressed rosbag2 at 1-5 MB/s. Size C's 5 V supply against both the 16.8 W USB-drive peak and the 18 W worst case.

issues.where: architectures[C] risks and where_inference_runs; bench_tests_before_committing[3] (Hailo specifics)
issues.problem: C runs the detector and OSNet x1.0 on one Hailo-8L, but its risks never mention that the two networks will share the chip over a single Gen 3 x1 link. On that link per-call overhead is already large, and switching between two networks has not been measured. The latency budget (mean < 100 ms per frame to hold 10 Hz, <= 140 ms for detection, tracking and planning) is tight against Sixfab's sync end-to-end rate. The '416 px input' advice requires a Dataflow Compiler build, because the zoo HEFs cited are 640x640. Bench test 4 lists measurements but sets no pass criteria.
issues.evidence: Requirements workload (person detection): '<= ~140 ms ... average < 100 ms to hold 10 Hz with the single latest-frame worker'. raspberry_pi category_findings: Sixfab YOLO26n at 640 ran 12-15 fps sync and 20-23 fps async end to end, i.e. 1000/15 = 67 ms to 1000/12 = 83 ms per frame. rpi5_8gb_ai_hat_plus_13tops: YOLOv8n at 61.9 fps (batch 1) against 121.4 fps (batch 8) on a Pi 5; 'Multi-context models ... slow sharply on the single lane'; custom models go through the DFC on an x86 PC.
issues.fix: Add a risk: the detector and re-ID share one Hailo-8L over Gen 3 x1 (model switching), and sync inference leaves only about 17-33 ms of a 100 ms frame for re-ID, grid and planner, so use async, pipelined HailoRT. Give bench test 4 pass criteria: detector >= 10 Hz with re-ID on <= 5 crops at >= 5 Hz running at the same time, mean per-frame time < 100 ms, p95 chain <= 200 ms, using 416 px HEFs compiled with the DFC.

issues.where: architectures A, C, D, E volume_note ('117 x 99 x 51 mm (0.59 L) chest tray at 60 cm'); G volume_note ('wider than the 99 mm of the 60 cm tray')
issues.problem: This tray envelope is in neither the surveys nor the verifications, and it is not the study's tray. The repository sizes the tray as the selected compute part plus fixed margins, using the dev kit's 103 x 90.5 x 34.77 mm envelope, which gives 120 x 110.5 x 64.8 mm (0.86 L). 117 x 99 x 51 mm is NVIDIA's 100 x 79 x 21 mm plus the same margins. The conclusions survive (the small boards fit, and the 115 mm J401 still exceeds 110.5 mm), but the figure is wrong and unsourced. 'Fits the tray' is also circular, because the tray resizes with the board.
issues.evidence: '117 x 99' does not occur in all_surveys.json. designlab/build.py:453: tray = compute dims + (0.017, 0.020, 0.030) m. data/parts.json, nvidia_orin_nano_super_devkit: dims_m [0.103, 0.0905, 0.03477]. In the built 60 cm model, round1/review/mjcf/60-M-S-10-serial.json, compute_tray has size [0.12, 0.1105, 0.06477] m. 100+17 = 117, 79+20 = 99, 21+30 = 51.
issues.fix: Replace the figure with the study's 120 x 110.5 x 64.8 mm tray, cited to build.py and the round-one model, or drop it. Judge packaging against the chest station instead, since the tray resizes with the board.

issues.where: per_size[100] why ('C with the AI HAT+ 26 TOPS ($330; ~9.7 W at the battery, 5.6%)')
issues.problem: The 9.7 W reuses C's Hailo-8L power basis for a Hailo-8 HAT, and no arithmetic is shown.
issues.evidence: C.power_basis uses 1.5 W, the Hailo-8L vendor typical. Raspberry Pi verification correction (rpi5_8gb_hailo8_m2_on_m2_hat_plus): Hailo-8 typical is 2.4 W at MobileNet-SSD 996 fps and 3.3 W at ResNet-50 915 fps. other_edge_ai correction (hailo8_m2_mkey): 'Neither datasheet states 2.5 W typical'. Sixfab system averages (mixed-model proxy): 6.53 W for Hailo-8 against 6.08 W for Hailo-8L. Arithmetic: 6.5+2.4+0.5 = 9.4 W, or 10.7 W at the battery (6.2% of 171 W); 6.5+3.3+0.5 = 10.3 W, or 11.7 W (6.8%); 8.5+0.45 = 8.95 W, or 10.2 W (6.0%).
issues.fix: Give the 26 TOPS variant its own basis: about 9.0-10.3 W at the board, 10.2-11.7 W at the battery, 6.0-6.8% of 171 W, labeled as vendor or proxy figures.

issues.where: architectures[E] best_for_sizes, power_w_typical, covers_minimum_spec vs recommendation point 4
issues.problem: E carries best_for_sizes [60, 75] and covers_minimum_spec true, but the recommendation lists it as 'not shortlisted'. Its 8.0 W typical leaves out the NVMe idle penalty, although its configuration includes an NVMe. Its re-ID path is untested, so its coverage of the no-silent-switch requirement is unverified.
issues.evidence: E.parts: M.2 NVMe on PCIe 3.0 x4. E.power_basis: 'an NVMe without ASPM L1.2 may raise idle from 1.4 W to ~5 W'. That adds 5-1.4 = 3.6 W, so 8.0+3.6 = 11.6 W at the board (13.2 W at the battery), above C's 8.5 W. E.software_effort: 'Re-ID conversion is untested'. rockchip_and_arm_npu category_findings: 'No person re-ID network benchmark was found for any board in this category'.
issues.fix: Clear best_for_sizes to mark it not shortlisted. Give the typical as 8.0-11.6 W with the NVMe fitted, or configure eMMC or microSD instead. Mark re-ID as unverified.

issues.where: 'share of walking power' in every architecture and in the per_size why texts; A.power_basis light-load case
issues.problem: Each share divides the new compute draw by the budgeted walking total, which still contains the 35.2 W Jetson line, so it understates compute's share of the robot that results. Separately, A's 8.7 W light-load bound comes from the 7 W mode, which the Super flash configuration (the one A uses for its 15/25 W modes) does not offer.
issues.evidence: D at 60 cm: written as 8.15/96 = 8.5%, but 8.15/(96-35.2+8.15) = 8.15/68.9 = 11.8% of the resulting total. A: 17.6/96 = 18.3% against 17.6/78.4 = 22.5%. G at 120 cm: 31.8/209 = 15.2% against 31.8/205.6 = 15.5%. jetson_orin_nano_super_devkit software: 'the Super flash configuration offers 15 W, 25 W (default) and MAXN_SUPER; the non-Super configuration offers 15 W and 7 W'. A.power_basis: 6.2 W VDD_IN 'in the 7 W mode'.
issues.fix: Label the shares '% of the budgeted walking total', or recompute them against the total after the change. Label A's 8.7 W as a 7 W-mode measurement used as a lower bound.

issues.where: architectures[D] lifecycle; architectures[C] lifecycle; recommendation point 5 (camera replacement path)
issues.problem: For the end-of-life RVC2 camera at 60-75 cm, the plan offers only a depth-only camera plus a host NPU. It leaves out the OAK 4 Lite, which the smart-camera verification calls the first RVC4 candidate for the small sizes. The OAK 4 Lite would keep detection and re-ID on the camera and remove the Myriad X dependency.
issues.evidence: smart_cameras verdict missing_options[0], OAK 4 Lite (EVT): $779 AF/FF, $879 Wide; ~206 g (USB); 4 GB / 128 GB; 8 W / 20 TOPS sustained at 25 C ambient, 4 W / 10 TOPS at 50 C; 25 W USB-PD for full compute; one unit per order; an estimated 34-37% of the 60 cm head+neck allowance and 23-26% at 75 cm; 'the first RVC4 candidate for the small sizes'. D.lifecycle: 'Replacing the camera later with a depth-only unit means adding an accelerator (C)'.
issues.fix: Add the OAK 4 Lite as a watch item for the D path's camera successor (vendor figures, EVT, one per order). Note its 25 W PD supply, up to 8 W of sustained heat in the head and ~206 g of head mass. Keep C plus a depth-only camera as the alternative.
